The Democrats hold a narrow lead over the Republicans in the US Senate race in Mississippi, with both sides in a dispute over the counting of the remaining votes which could decide the outcome.
Lawyers for each campaign are preparing for a possible legal battle over the final results and weighing in on the examination of ballots.
The result could mark the end of almost 40 years of Republican control over Mississippi's senate seats and will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the upper house.
Mississippi is the only US state which does not have a set procedure in place to trigger a recount - and the pressure is on to declare a winner with the state's 13 November deadline for certification approaching.
What ballots are left to count?
With 97% of the votes counted as of Friday, Democratic candidate Scott Colom is about 2,500 votes ahead of the incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson said on Wednesday that 3,600 "absentee-by-mail ballots" were still to be counted. The state can accept these votes so long as they were postmarked by election day and are received by 10 November.
Watson said there are also an "unknown" number of provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, to be counted. These are typically cast when a voter lacked the required identification to cast their vote. The deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues with provisional ballots, usually by providing acceptable photo identification, is also 10 November.
Mississippi Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst said on Thursday that they estimated there could be "approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted".
Hyde-Smith's campaign said the same day that "thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties" and it is "confident" this will secure her re-election. She has held the seat since 2018.
Colom said the election saw "historic voter turnout" and he is "confident that when votes are counted, we will flip this seat". If he wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in the state since 1875.
What have the campaign lawyers requested?
Colom said his campaign has an "an army of lawyers" ready to act - while the state Republican party said it has sent more than 50 volunteers, attorneys and observers across the state.
Lawyers from both campaigns have sent letters to Mississippi election officials about the counting of outstanding provisional ballots.
The Hyde-Smith campaign lawyers have requested that all 82 counties in the state keep all provisional ballots separate from regular or absentee ballots.
Their letter also requested that election officials preserve various records - including information on how the votes were processed - associated with the provisional ballots as "potential evidence" in a possible legal dispute.
The Colom campaign lawyers responded saying the move has "no legal authority whatsoever".
"Mississippi law does give any candidate a right to examine ballot boxes and their contents within 12 days after the relevant canvass and examination," says Ronald Rychlak, a law professor at the University of Mississippi. "Mississippi's affidavit-ballot statute also requires eligibility review and records concerning whether affidavit ballots were counted."
"Neither law, however, establishes a blanket requirement to segregate all affidavit ballots after they have been accepted," he adds.
The Colom campaign has said the request from Hyde-Smith's team could allow "a particular ballot to be traced to a particular voter", in violation of ballot secrecy laws.
"That's where he does have a more reasonable argument," says Rychlak, "as ballots in the US are private by law and when there's no clear procedure in place there could be a possibility a voter's privacy might be breached."
Could there be a recount?
Recounts rarely succeed - just three out of 37 completed state-wide recounts across the US since 2000 have reversed a result., external
However, in many states automatic recounts are triggered if a vote is very close, and in others there is an official process for campaigns to request one in a tight race.
Two states, Illinois and Tennessee, allow recounts if a candidate mounts a formal legal challenge.
Mississippi doesn't have a set procedure in place which allows for a result to be automatically recounted even if it's tight or contested.
It is effectively left up to judges in the state to decide how specific disputes should be resolved.
"Mississippi's lack of a formal recount procedure does not leave either campaign without a possible avenue to challenge the result," says Rychlak, "Ballot-box examination is an available post-election mechanism, and that can lead to discoveries that may result in a recount."
There could also be a legal challenge raised at a federal level - with the US Senate potentially having authority to determine who is entitled to the seat.
This would fall under Article I of the US Constitution as there is a provision which gives each chamber of Congress the power to be the "judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members".
Additional reporting by Krystal Campos.

185a68ef5964.text: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/seeds-and-preserved-hair-in-tomb-point-to-oldest-signs-of-cannabis-high-2800-years-ago-study-suggests Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests Science Nov 6, 2026 5:19 PM EST GENEVA (AP) — People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests. Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes. The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands. The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies. "It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern. It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said. The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians — ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine. READ MORE: A $28 billion hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe. Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said. "It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said. Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said. Results were published Thursday in the journal Science. Not all independent experts were convinced. A preserved human hair braid dating to about 2,800 years ago at the site of an ancient Scythian burial mound, in the Valley of the Tsars, the Republic of Tyva, south of Siberia, Russia, in this handout image released on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Frozen Corpses Golden Treasures, T.Wallace & G. Caspari/Handout via Reuters The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email. "For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)." Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses — seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth — their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use. Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure — in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange. But Elisa Guerra Doce of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study. In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite." Jenne reported from Vienna, Austria. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press

51efe7201652.text: Angered over his midterm losses, President Trump announced Friday he was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with longtime adviser Stephen Miller. Why it matters: Trump is trading one of his few moderating forces with one of the most maximalist champions of his agenda, a striking signal that the president may double down on the hardline policies that helped Republicans lose control of Congress on Tuesday. Driving the news: Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night. Sources told Axios her departure was a mutual decision, but driven by Tuesday's election results, for which Trump blamed her. Sources said Trump began expressing discomfort with the scale of the midterm losses and the money his political team spent on Wednesday. Wiles offered to quit for two days before she resigned. Trump accepted her decision on Friday. Trump did not ask for her resignation, said one informed source who spoke with Wiles, "but he couldn't get it out of his head that she was to blame, not him." "Susie could've stuck around, but what's the point?" that person said. "Whether it's right or wrong, Susie knows that serving the president means it's at his pleasure. And if she couldn't change the way he felt, there was no reason to stay." What they're saying: "I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that Wiles will move to the Trump Political Operation. Wiles said in a statement posted to X that "[s]erving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together." Zoom in: Miller, who served in Trump's first administration, was already a co-equal of Wiles' in some respects. No one in Trump's government knows the levers of power, the operation of the White House and the bold use of the executive branch better than him. An architect of Trump's explosive first hundred days exerting executive authority, Miller has been working on plans to keep operating a muscular White House even in the face of big Democratic majorities. "Trump needs to prepare for war with the Democrats in Congress with all their investigations they're going to launch, and Stephen is a wartime adviser," a Trump adviser explained. Zoom out: Wiles is widely viewed as the most powerful person in the White House outside the president himself, and she achieved something few in his orbit could: earning his trust, influencing his decisions and bringing discipline to an administration defined by historic infighting and upheaval. She was Trump's longest-serving chief of staff, and commanded an extraordinary level of trust from Trump, often serving as the last person he consulted before making major decisions. Her exit also ends the tenure of the first woman ever to hold the powerful position. Her influence stemmed from a relationship with Trump that stretched back to his 2016 campaign when she led his efforts in Florida, and again when she agreed to manage his political comeback following the Jan. 6 riot. Between the lines: Wiles' strength was understanding how to navigate Trump rather than trying to control him. She avoided public confrontations, offered disagreements privately and sought to carry out Trump's priorities rather than restrain them. But her influence had limits. She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller. Friction point: In a grand irony, the very Trump decisions she opposed —the Iran war and the brutality of immigration enforcement — drove Tuesday night's midterm shellacking that led the president to lose confidence in her. Catch up quick: As recently as Oct. 16, Trump emphatically denied reports he was considering replacing Wiles. Trump noted at the time that Wiles would stay as long as she wanted, and he praised her toughness in surviving cancer while serving as his staff chief. Context: Wiles spent decades mastering the art of influencing powerful men while staying out of the spotlight. The daughter of famed NFL broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles has credited growing up with an alcoholic father with teaching her how to handle larger-than-life personalities. In Florida, she became a powerful behind-the-scenes operator for two moderate Republican mayors in Jacksonville, helped elect Rick Scott as governor in 2010, and rescued Ron DeSantis' struggling gubernatorial campaign in 2018. ba229bd58fc2.text: By — Josh Funk, Associated Press Josh Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/dad-of-20-year-old-co-pilot-in-florida-jet-crash-says-her-final-radio-calls-showed-shes-tough Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida jet crash says her final radio calls showed 'she's tough' Nation Nov 6, 2026 4:52 PM EST The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot who died along with eight others when their Learjet crashed in Florida said Friday he has listened to his daughter's heartbreaking final radio transmissions "many times" since the crash. Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach his daughter to fly, was searching for answers as to why the plane plunged from the sky on Sunday. Instead, he found immense pride in how his daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, handled the crisis. "I did listen to that many times trying to find a clue. In my head. How'd that happen? And wow, she's tough," Allan Filgueiras said at a news conference Friday. "I wanted to be by her side," he said, at times holding back tears. "Inside the plane. To help." READ MORE: Parts of jet's tail found more than a mile from plane crash site in South Florida, official says In her conversation with air traffic control, Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly reporting ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm and turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters). The situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. "Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!" she said. Her father and aviation safety experts are impressed that Filgueiras continued to call out updates on what was happening even as she realized the plane's fate was sealed. "For the family — it's like having the heart torn from my chest," her father said in Spanish. "I have to find a way to go on living." The family wants to push back against online criticism over whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot's license and get certified for a Learjet. The plane's captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls in the aircraft's final minutes. So, on Friday, her father held a news conference that his lawyer said was intended to "preserve not just her memory, but her reputation." "She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," attorney Stuart Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans to file a lawsuit over the crash. It's far too early in the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation to know what caused the crash. As it fell, the Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits and pieces of the plane's tail were found miles away from the crash site. READ MORE: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says Allan Filgueiras said he first took his daughter flying at age 12 and later started teaching her to fly. After she got a job as a pilot, she told her dad she couldn't believe she was getting paid to do something she loved. "It was her happiest moment, to fly," he said. Retired airline pilot John Cox, who is now the CEO of Safety Operating Systems, said earlier this week that his career began similarly to Filgueiras, as he started flying professionally at age 19. He said she was doing quite well to earn that co-pilot's seat. "To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that's a good ride. I mean, that's great. I know she loved it," Cox said. Her father believes she handled the crisis better than most. "She showed me what it is to be a hero because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can't handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting," Allan Filgueiras said. The crash victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family's nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. 4237ed0b752b.text: Congressional Democrats see a target-rich environment next year. But they're also worried that if they investigate everything , they may appear to investigate nothing. Why it matters: Democrats want to move beyond the one-off hearings, fist-pounding document demands and subpoena threats that defined much of their oversight during President Trump's first term. The goal, according to senior Democrats, is to build a sustained narrative around the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption" — while showing voters they have legislative solutions to the problems they uncover. "We're trying to get to the answers that point to solutions," a senior Democratic aide said. Zoom in: Senate Democrats are actively coordinating investigations across committees and with their House counterparts, looking to turn Day One oversight of the Trump administration into a sustained case for their own legislative agenda. Think more Jan. 6 committee investigation, with slick videos and compelling witness testimony, than impeachment 1.0. The coordination, underway for months, is increasingly happening at the senator level, with lawmakers working to divide investigative responsibilities and avoid overlapping efforts. "We want to deconflict these with some of the other committees, right? We don't want to be duplicative with other committees," Sen. Chris Van Hollen told Axios. The other side: Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely chair of the House Oversight Committee, has a four-pronged plan to investigate the Trump administration. But he has a two-word taunt: "LAWYER UP." Between the lines: Nearly every House committee has the power to subpoena without getting sign-off from the minority party. In the Senate, only the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (PSI) can issue subpoenas unilaterally. Trump's war in Iran will likely be the Senate's first focus, with the Senate Armed Services Committee preparing for hearings — and planning to call Hegseth to testify — in January. There will also be an immediate vote on a war powers resolution. "I've been very clear that we need to use every tool at our disposal to end the illegal [incentives] war in Iran, and that's beginning day one," Van Hollen said. What's next: As the scope of their victory comes into focus, Democrats across committees are eager to get to work. "I'm looking at you — Big Tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations. If you break the law, there will be consequences," Sen. Elizabeth Warren thundered on X .

d1bc5c81963a.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-faculty-vote-no-confidence-in-university-leadership-after-alleged-fraternity-gang-rape Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell faculty vote 'no confidence' in university leadership after alleged fraternity gang rape Nation Updated on Nov 6, 2026 4:59 PM EST — Published on Nov 6, 2026 4:28 PM EST Cornell University's Faculty Senate approved a resolution Friday declaring "no confidence" in the school's top leaders, a symbolic gesture reflecting deep discontent on campus in the wake of a former student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024. The resolution passed 75-50, with five faculty senators abstaining and five others not voting, according to an email sent to Faculty Senate members on Friday afternoon. The vote followed weeks of debate among professors over whether Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators handled the woman's allegations properly and have done enough to curtail sexual misconduct at the prestigious university. READ MORE: Woman who accused Cornell students of rape says university president's response made her feel 'unsupported' While the faculty body has no power over the university's top leaders, backers of the resolution had said they hoped it would pressure Cornell's trustees to address longstanding institutional failures they identified. Board of Trustees Chair Anne Smalling said in a statement the faculty vote "reflects the deep anger across our campus" and sent a clear signal that what happened to the woman was unacceptable, but added that Kotlikoff and his administration were the right leaders to "thoughtfully and comprehensively" address the issue. Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for the woman who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement Friday that "we are hopeful that this will be yet another step forward to educate and support the Cornell community by addressing the longstanding scourge of sexual assault on campus." Lawsuit sparked outrage on campus The Cornell community has been distressed since mid-September, when a former student, identified only by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, filed a lawsuit against the university and seven former members of the Chi Phi fraternity, saying she was given ketamine and raped at a fraternity house in October 2024. All of the men have denied her allegations, saying the sex was consensual or that they weren't involved. The local district attorney initially decided the woman had consented to the encounter and that no crime had been committed, but the investigation has since been reopened and handed to New York's attorney general. WATCH: Fraternity culture under scrutiny in wake of Cornell allegations Cornell disciplined several of the accused students following a monthslong Title IX investigation. Two were expelled, two received suspensions and probation, and two were required to write "reflection" papers and complete bystander training. A seventh man had already graduated and was barred from campus, according to records obtained by The New York Times. Kotlikoff also convened a task force to study the problem of sexual misconduct on campus, which released certain recommendations. Some faculty members have criticized Kotlikoff for not acting more forcefully to strengthen the school's disciplinary process, push for criminal investigations and change campus party culture. Paul Ortiz, a labor history professor who co-sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said last week that hundreds of students, staff, alumni and faculty approached the resolution's sponsors to emphasize that "the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg" and that "a veritable fortress of silence has been breached" around sexual violence since the resolution's introduction. Cornell's president defended his leadership Speaking to Faculty Senate members on the first day that they debated the no-confidence resolution, Kotlikoff pledged to make the university a leader in addressing sexual assault and asked for more time to make changes. Kotlikoff defended his leadership, arguing that replacing him would do little to solve complex problems and could damage Cornell's reputation. He acknowledged he had not read the campus police report, explaining that university policy barred top administrators from interfering in criminal investigations. He also rejected suggestions he had been indifferent to the woman's case, though he acknowledged only recently learning she had left Cornell. READ MORE: A gang rape allegation at Cornell highlights how Title IX guides campus sex assault cases Kotlikoff said the university needed to determine whether fraternities could operate safely and left open the possibility of sweeping restrictions on Greek life. He argued that decisions should be based on research and evidence rather than emotion. Some professors had said faculty should wait to vote until the release of an independent investigation by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, whom the university hired to examine both how Cornell responded to the woman's initial rape report in 2024 and its overall procedures for handling similar reports from other students. The no-confidence resolution did not call for Kotlikoff's resignation. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.
He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.
The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.
In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

Blue wave presages a defense-spending showdown
A reconciliation bill is likely off the table, and the presumed HASC chair is talking about a $1-trillion cap.
The Democrats' impending takeover of the House and the Senate will have sweeping effects on the Pentagon, from budgets to leadership to defense policy. The biggest near-term issue is the fate of the proposed reconciliation bill, which the Trump administration is counting on for $350 billion of its plans to spend $1.5 trillion on defense spending in fiscal 2027.
Even before the election, some Republican lawmakers doubted their ability to pass a bill through the reconciliation process, which is rarely used for defense funding. A lame-duck effort is unlikely to succeed, and January's seating of the new Democrat-controlled Congress is expected to kill the bill for good.
Defense spending
The administration pushed many top priorities into the unusual reconciliation bill, including:
• Munitions funding. The bill is a major conduit for money that would nearly double munitions spending to $76.3 billion to help rebuild stockpiles following several years of equipment transfers to Ukraine and a depletion of inventories during the war with Iran. It was meant to underwrite a production surge for air and missile defense munitions such as Patriot, THAAD, SM-3, and SM-6; plus strike weapons such as hypersonic missiles. Munitions funding is also included in a proposed Iran supplemental that faces resistance from Democrats who oppose the war.
• Golden Dome homeland missile defense system. The proposal includes $17 billion for a new Golden Dome for America Fund plus investment for related programs such as a Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator capability and a revamped Space Data Network that would serve as the communications layer of the defense system.
• Unmanned systems. The bill includes nearly $54 billion for the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group.
• Aircraft: several F-35s and KC-130Js for the Air Force.
• Warships: The Medium Landing Ship and some investment in the Virginia-class submarine.
If the reconciliation bill is dead, lawmakers will have to decide whether to move any of those items into the defense appropriations bill.
The Pentagon’s $1.1 trillion base budget request—that's $242.4 billion, or 28 percent, over the FY26 defense appropriations bill enacted by Congress—will face more resistance. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., who is expected to once again lead the House Armed Services Committee after two years as its ranking member, said this week that he wants to keep total defense spending to $1 trillion in fiscal 2027.
The administration proposed to offset the Pentagon increase with reductions in domestic non-defense discretionary spending. The guns-versus-butter debate will be reignited, and it is unclear whether base budgets will stay above $1 trillion.
Political headwinds
Several programs are likely to face increased scrutiny in the new Congress.
Golden Dome’s space-based interceptors are a likely target for Democratic opposition. The Pentagon initially selected a dozen companies to work on SBIs, including Anduril, General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, and SpaceX. SpaceX, which has received $6.5 billion for the Space-Based Air Moving Target Indicator and Space Data Network programs, could face new roadblocks.
Also at risk: the Navy’s Trump-class battleship, the signature component of the proposed Golden Fleet. This author has already raised concerns about the practicality and affordability of the battleship, and Democrats are likely to push back on the program’s rapid development and construction plans. The Navy has chose General Dynamics Bath Iron Works and Huntington Ingalls Industries to build the ships, which would use a distributed construction approach. Leidos’ Gibbs & Cox was tasked with supporting ship design and engineering. If this program falls through, the Navy may revisit plans for the DDG(X) destroyer, which had been shelved in favor of the battleship.
The next Congress will also push the administration to end the war with Iran, which continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Democrats have been unwilling to act on the Iran-war supplemental request without establishing guardrails or an exit strategy. At the same time, Democratic majorities in the House and Senate are more likely to push for greater support for Ukraine, which could include more money, faster arms transfers, and pressure on the White House to avoid actions that could harm Kyiv.
Areas of alignment
The new Democratic minority is expected to continue to fund replenishing munitions stockpiles depleted during operations against Iran, despite Democratic opposition to the war itself. Counter-unmanned aircraft systems investment will remain a priority, from low-cost munitions to directed energy. Congress, which has long supported Navy shipbuilding, can be expected to add money for it, even if lawmakers disagree about specific platforms. There will also be continued support for developing autonomous gear and the networks that support them.
More budget delays expected
Congress failed to pass most budget legislation before the 2027 fiscal year began on Oct. 1, and the government is currently operating under a continuing resolution through December 11. That's not enough time to finalize a full spending plan, so the lame-duck Congress will likely pass another CR that extends into the next calendar year. Under the new Congress, passage of a final spending bill could be hindered by negotiations over the status of the Iran war, topline spending levels, the debt ceiling, or other policy issues.
Lawmakers might also pass a long-term CR, covering several months or even the rest of fiscal year. These stopgap spending bills typically restrict new start programs and production rate increases. 0b937070ad8e.text: Between the GOP's thrashing at the polls, another one of President Trump 's planned D.C. construction makeovers being halted and an uphill battle to overturn his conviction on 34 felony counts, this week has netted a string of setbacks for the president. Why it matters: Trump's administration is entering its lame-duck era, facing criticism and potential investigations as its power to reshape the federal government dwindles . But Trump is showing little inclination to change course. Driving the news: Trump has remained defiant about the midterms, blaming the Iran war and the GOP's candidates for the losses while spending a lot of time discussing planned D.C. construction projects . On Friday, Trump announced he would replace White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller , a champion of his most hard-line policies. The move could signal that the president plans to push even harder on some of his unpopular policies, Axios' Marc Caputo and Andrew Pantazi write. Zoom in: Voters told Trump loud and clear they're dissatisfied with his policies, particularly on the Iran war, cost of living and economy. Roughly two-thirds of voters said Trump's agenda had fueled inflation, per the AP's Voter Poll. Trump admitted the unpopular war helped Republicans lose their majorities. With Democrats poised to control Congress and potentially restrict war funding, he has few good options for a decisive win. As one of his former advisers told Axios' Barak Ravid: "It's one thing to lose the midterms. But Trump doesn't want to look like a loser twice." What they're saying: "I don't think conciliatory is in [Trump's] vocabulary or ethos," Republican strategist Barrett Marson told Axios, calling Miller's appointment evidence that Trump won't "go away quietly." "He's taken the architect of many of the worst policies and elevating him. I'm not really sure how that is sort of acknowledging voters' discontent," Marson said. Marson said Trump's inability to run for president again could make him even less concerned about political consequences. He also noted that Trump has a massive war chest that he could wield to control GOP politicians as the 2028 election cycle begins. Republican strategist John Feehery , who spoke to Axios before Friday's chief of staff shake-up, said Trump could still cut deals with Democrats to cement his legacy, but acknowledged his influence over congressional Republicans could wane. "I don't think he's going to control the Republicans to the extent that he did, I think Republicans are going to try to figure out their own brand," Feehery said. Zoom out: The president's headaches also extend to his legal battles and ambitious construction projects. A New York appeals court heard arguments Thursday in Trump's bid to overturn his conviction on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records. His lawyers argued the conviction was tainted by legal errors and inadmissible evidence, but the court has yet to rule. In the wee hours of Friday, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order barring construction on Trump's planned 250-foot Triumphal Arch for 14 days, just hours after the National Capital Planning Commission approved the project. The order was in response to a lawsuit brought by D.C. and Virginia and blocked construction, excavation, and road closures related to the arch. The project would tower over a road leading to Arlington National Cemetery and has drawn opposition from preservation groups, military veterans and families of people buried at the cemetery. The other side: "As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." On the arch, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle blasted the judge's ruling, saying the administration was confident it would be "fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The bottom line: Trump is the political comeback king — and no one should expect him to roll over during his lame-duck season. Go deeper: Trump, under pressure, embraces Builder-in-Chief role

Please check your inbox to confirm. In her first term, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs had vetoed more than 540 measures passed by the Republican-led Legislature on policies including taxes, immigration and voting laws. Hobbs has said she's looking to address water issues and affordability, and take on fraud and abuse in the state's school voucher program. The Associated Press called enough legislative races to confirm that both chambers flipped on Friday. The news organization calls races individually and it can take several days after voting, depending on when election officials tally the votes and how close the elections are. Besides Arizona, those wins were in the battleground states of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Wisconsin. READ MORE: Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House The flips weren't just in states that are normally competitive. Democrats won control of the Texas House, which Republicans have held since 2003, and elected Gina Hinojosa as the state's first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994. Republicans held onto the state Senate. Democrats also flipped the lower chambers of the legislatures in Maine and North Carolina and both chambers in New Hampshire, where Republican Kelly Ayotte was reelected. The count could grow as results are tallied in additional states. The National Council of State Legislatures says it's likely to end up as the election with the most legislative seats and chambers changing parties since the 2010 election, when Republicans took over governments across the country amid the Great Recession. Democrats will also hold the governor's office in at least 28 states. Results are still pending in Alaska and Kansas. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. State Department's push to cancel hundreds of contracts left behind a trail of mistakes, watchdog finds
Several government oversight reports have found costly operational errors as agencies implemented administration directives.
Widespread errors in State Department efforts to terminate contracts may have wasted money and exposed the agency to lawsuits, its inspector general said in a report published on Monday.
Within a month of Donald Trump taking office for the second time, the department began reviewing some contracts for termination, particularly ones regarding foreign aid and diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Then Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to review their contracts and grants for cancellation or modification “to reduce overall federal spending or reallocate spending to promote efficiency and advance the policies of my administration.”
This led State workers to review nearly 5,600 contracts worth a total of about $65 billion. From Jan. 20 to June 15, 2025, the department terminated almost 400 contracts, totaling roughly $360 million. But auditors found several instances where employees didn’t rescind obligated funds.
Across at least six terminated contracts, there was about $8.1 million that still had not been deobligated as of August 2026, the IG reported.
“Because [contracting officers] did not take timely action to deobligate excess funds, the department’s ability to redirect those resources to other mission priorities was limited and the risk that the funds would expire before they could be used increased,” auditors wrote.
The watchdog recommended that officials repurpose the $8.1 million, which the department agreed to do, except for nearly $50,000 that it determined was owed to the contractor as part of the termination settlement.
Auditors also found that, out of a sample of 30 terminated contracts, 25 lacked adequate written termination notices. For example, the paperwork for 10 of the cancellations listed two different termination dates, which increases “the risk of disputed costs, administrative delays or contractor claims.”
The IG also highlighted four terminated contracts in which State employees didn’t ensure that contractors returned their government-issued laptops and phones. Similarly, the IG for the IRS reported in August that the agency could not account for nearly 600 agency electronic devices valued at more than $270,000 from employees who separated in spring 2025.
Auditors acknowledged that State, while undergoing the contract review, also was dealing with the Trump administration’s reductions to the civil service, a department reorganization and taking over the U.S. Agency for International Development’s operations. But they also emphasized that the agency did not standardize contract cancelation procedures and that some contracting officers had never terminated a contract before.
The IG recommended that State specify steps for returning government-issued property due to a contract termination, set procedures for reviewing unused funds from a canceled contract and establish a process for tracking deobligation actions. Officials concurred with all three.
The Government Accountability Office recently criticized State for entering inaccurate information into its grant management system following significant cuts to foreign assistance grants, contracts and cooperative agreements. For example, more than 4,000 awards (out of around 10,000) were categorized as both active and terminated.
The IG for the Veterans Affairs Department in September similarly reported on the VA’s contract cancellations, finding that employees generally complied with termination requirements but that, in some cases, they had “only a few hours” to complete reviews.

Watch the video in the player above. The shift in the nation's fourth-largest city is one of the first actions to restrict U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations since Democrats' rout in Tuesday's midterm elections. It also is a sign that results are already having an impact in Texas, where Republican leaders have enthusiastically embraced President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. "I've said many times, elections matter," Mayor John Whitmire said. ICE would only be contacted for jailable offenses Whitmire, a Democrat, said the city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education." In the case of a traffic incident, "you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way," he said. Under the mayor's new directive, Houston police should contact ICE only if the person it stops is arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing or if ICE issues an administrative warrant, which is an order signed by a senior ICE official indicating that the person is wanted by immigration officials. READ MORE: Democrats win full control of more state governments and the Texas House "The fact that a person is, or is suspected to be, subject to immigration enforcement shall not, by itself, be a basis to contact ICE, to prolong any detention, or to take any person into or hold any person in custody," the two-page order states. The Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Houston has sparked protests after an ICE officer fatally shot a Mexican homebuilder this summer and another struck a man with a car. Spokespersons for ICE did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the mayor's announcement. Cooperation with ICE has sparked protests in Texas cities A grand jury last week indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Prosecutors say Morales intentionally rammed his car into Miguel Parra Hernandez, whose leg was broken. ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Despite a one-time $75 billion infusion from Congress, ICE remains heavily dependent on local police to find people subject to deportation and turn them over. It has done so partly by signing about 2,600 agreements — many in Texas — to deputize local police and other state and local agencies to enforce immigration laws. Texas has been a primary target for ICE arrests. Abbott has closely aligned the state with the Trump administration to collaborate on enforcing federal immigration laws. In April, he had threatened to take away nearly $200 million in public safety grants from Austin, Dallas and Houston after city officials in Houston tried to limit police officers' cooperation with ICE. READ MORE: ICE officer charged with ramming man with SUV in Houston turns himself in Houston's City Council passed an ordinance eliminating the requirement for Houston police officers to wait 30 minutes for ICE agents to pick up someone with a nonjudicial administrative warrant. If ICE agents didn't show up in time, police officers took a detained person's information and were able to release them. Abbott said the ordinance violated the terms of millions of dollars in state grants Houston had received for police and security during the World Cup games the city hosted in June. Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit, accusing the city of violating a 2017 state law that prevents cities from adopting policies that limit the enforcement of immigration laws. The city changed the ordinance two weeks after passing it to delete language stating that administrative warrants — which ICE agents use to take individuals into custody, unlike warrants signed by a judge — are not enough for officers to arrest or detain an individual. Advocate calls the change a 'sigh of relief' for immigrant communities FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family of Parra Hernandez, planned to hold a press conference Friday afternoon in light of the announcement. Prior to the changes, immigration enforcement "looked like a complete collaboration between Houston Police Department and ICE," Cesar Espinosa, executive director at FIEL, said in an interview with The Associated Press. He said the collaboration paralyzed communities too afraid of getting stopped for a traffic ticket or getting referred to ICE when calling for help when witnessing a crime. "It gives our community a sigh of relief in that we know of many people in the city of Houston that will not even go to the grocery store because they're afraid that they're going to get caught up by ICE or they're gonna get pulled over by HPD

The site's debut is yet another sign of how much Trump is leaning into his efforts to make over the White House and Washington to his own gilded tastes, even after his party lost control of Congress in a midterm-election drubbing. It was the fourth day this week alone that the administration promoted his projects. The website declares that the 250-foot (76-meter) structure — which is slated to rise in a mass of blindingly gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery — will be formally known as the United States Military Triumphal Arch. Describing the arch as "an American vision finally realized," the site offers bird's-eye views of the proposal from many angles and shows off the declarations it will feature: "One Nation Under God" on one side and "Golden Age of America" on another. It's also set to have towering gold doors complete with panels of sculptures at its base. At its very top, the structure features a golden-hued cherub hoisting a flaming torch that recalls a smaller version of the Statue of Liberty. The website does not say how much the project will cost or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100 million. READ MORE: Trump's Washington projects are a likely casualty as Democrats claim Congress The White House highlighted the website the morning after U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order that prohibits work on the site for 14 days. That order followed a vote to approve the arch by a federal planning commission that is stocked with Trump's allies. With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Trump's renovation projects will encounter far more scrutiny and roadblocks — from his effort to put his own name on the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and building his massive White House ballroom and the arch. The arch will feature an event space — and 'provisions for a sniper nest' The president on Monday focused his final remarks before the midterm elections talking up his costly and problem-plagued effort to overhaul the Lincoln Memorial's Reflecting Pool. The day after the losses, on Wednesday, he took reporters on a tour of the ballroom's construction site. And his first official action after his party lost control of Congress was to declare, on Thursday, that the Oval Office would become a national monument. The arch website features the word "Triumph" in gold cursive script recalling the typeface used at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida and similar flourishes that have been affixed to the White House as part of his overhaul of the Oval Office and West Wing. The arch plans feature an event space in the horizontal part of the structure reached by elevators and stairs. But inside its "massive columns will be storage for munitions," the site states, as well as areas on the pedestal and observation deck that will be "set aside for snipers, countersnipers, and provisions for a sniper nest." READ MORE: Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin An open ground area at the monument's base "will be designed for launching drones and other homeland security assets," the site says, while also noting that the arch "will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before." "It is long overdue, and has been sought for many years, especially by the Military," it says. Trump has said for months that the monument would be inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris and that Washington has wanted a similar structure for centuries — even though that's not true. He previously joked that it might be called the "Arc de Trump." The website repeats Trump's inaccurate claims. It also features a picture of the president and quotes him as saying, "This will be the greatest and most beautiful triumphal arch, anywhere in the world." a04ea90910d5.text: Americans on both sides of the political aisle are watching the nail-bitingly close Mississippi Senate race , where a controversial voter-roll cleanup has come under scrutiny after some voters reported problems casting their ballots. Why it matters: The cliffhanger has exposed concerns about relying on third-party data to determine where voters live and how states maintain voter rolls. Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom are locked in a razor-thin race to be the state's junior senator. As of 2 p.m. ET Friday, Colom led by a little over 2000 votes, according to Associated Press data. The big picture: More than 230,000 Mississippians were listed as inactive ahead of the midterms, according to an analysis by Mississippi Today. That's up from roughly 166,000 in the 2024 election, according to federal data . Those voters weren't removed from the rolls, but they were required to cast affidavit ballots in Tuesday's election. Election workers review those ballots after Election Day, checking voter information against registration records. In some cases, voters must verify their identity with their county circuit clerk's office, slowing vote counting and — in this case — determining the winner. The intrigue: The inactive voter total shot up after the state's March primaries, months after Secretary of State Michael Watson's office inked a $50,000 deal with credit reporting company Experian to help verify voter addresses. "The increase in inactive registrations across the state of Mississippi raised some concerns because it seemed unusually high compared to other cycles and in such a small amount of time," Thessalia Merivaki, an elections research expert and former professor at Mississippi State University, tells Axios. She says there were concerns about "how reliable" these data brokers are, and whether relying on them had "resulted in erroneously placing eligible voters on an inactive status." How it works: Experian's data was intended to flag voters who might have moved, not automatically establish an address change. Local election officials were supposed to compare those records with other information, such as death records, Social Security records and the National Change of Address database to maintain voter lists, but counties have discretion over how to proceed. Merivaki says officials in Oktibbeha County knew some records were inaccurate because they recognized the voters. An election official in Oktibbeha County confirmed that information to Axios on Friday. Case in point: Jarvis Dortch, executive director of the ACLU of Mississippi, told Axios that a longtime Chickasaw County voter was told he lived in a different county, despite never having moved. Dortch suspects a car loan the man co-signed for his sister in Lee County likely caused the mix-up. He said the state ultimately let him vote. Dortch also said some voters were turned away instead of offered affidavit ballots. Yes, but: It's unclear how many of the newly inactive registrations are due to Experian data. An Experian spokesperson told Axios that the company "has not provided services to the State of Mississippi since early 2025. The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records." "Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws." Watson's office later told WAPT-TV it no longer uses Experian data, switching to IDI Data and U.S. Postal Service records. His office did not respond to Axios' questions about when it stopped using the data or other detailed questions about the contract and its terms. What they're saying: Watson defended the state's system Tuesday, saying , "The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Go deeper: Magic in Mississippi: Democrat locked in Deep South Senate stunner

President Donald Trump has named Stephen Miller, the architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new chief of staff following historic losses in the US midterm elections.
Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who submitted her resignation after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a blow to the prospects for Trump's agenda in his final two years in the White House.
Speaking to reporters, Trump said Wiles had "done a very good job", but "we've got to make moves sometimes".
Miller, a Trump loyalist and deputy chief of staff who served as a senior adviser during his first administration, is set to take on the new role on Monday.
One of Trump's closest aides, Miller, 41, stuck by the president following his 2020 election defeat and followed Trump back into power last year.
On X, Miller called Trump "the most transformative political leader in American History" who has "single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it".
He thanked Wiles for her years of devoted service to the president, country and for her friendship.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic," he wrote.
Wiles gave her resignation to Trump on Thursday night, a US official told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. Three sources told CBS she quit because of the election losses.
Trump said in a statement that Wiles would be moved to the "Trump Political Operation". He told reporters that Miller "gets it, very good politically".
Wiles said being on Trump's team was "the honor of a lifetime".
"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together," she said.
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she added.
It was unclear if her deputies would remain at the White House.
Wiles, 69, is seen as among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.

2fae4a97943c.text: Navajo Nation voters made history this week by choosing their first woman president, handing Crystalyne Curley a groundbreaking victory — and a political fight before she even takes office. Why it matters: Curley's victory breaks a barrier in the Navajo Nation, where women hold deep cultural influence, but men have long dominated the presidency. Driving the news: Curley, 40, and running mate Chris Deschene defeated Justin Jones and Emily Ellison in the Nov. 3 election, according to unofficial Navajo Election Administration results . Curley won 50.88% to Jones' 49.12% — a margin of just 1,115 votes across the Nation's 110 chapters. She will succeed President Buu Nygren, whose turbulent bid for a second term ended with a third-place finish in July's primary. Her running mate, former Arizona legislator and energy attorney Chris Deschene, returns to tribal leadership politics 12 years after a Navajo-language qualification dispute derailed his presidential campaign. The Navajo Nation, the country's largest Native American reservation, spans more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah and has nearly 430,000 enrolled members , according to June 2026 tribal figures. Yes, but: Jones refuses to concede and has threatened a legal challenge, alleging irregularities in the vote count. The Navajo Times reported he initially offered no specific discrepancies. Tribal election law prevents certification until at least 10 days after the election, leaving time for challenges, according to the site . Zoom in: Curley now faces a tougher challenge: tackling poverty, delivering basic services and healing a government fractured by years of infighting. About 35.2% of residents of the Navajo Nation Reservation live below the poverty line, compared with 12.5% nationally, according to 2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates . Between 30% and 40% of Navajo families lack running water at home, according to an April 2026 statement from the outgoing administration. An estimated 10,000 families still lack electrical service, according to the American Public Power Association . What they're saying: "This could not have been possible without the Navajo People. This is your victory. We worked hard because we said we wanted a positive direction," Curley said in a statement. "Thank you for believing in this team. This is a new direction for our people." What's next: Curley faces a high-stakes battle over drilling near sacred sites in the Southwest. The Trump administration is reviewing whether to reverse federal protections covering roughly 336,400 acres around Chaco Culture National Historical Park in New Mexico, potentially reopening federal lands to new oil and gas leasing. Curley joined Nygren in 2023 in criticizing the 10-mile drilling buffer created by then-Interior Secretary Deb Haaland. (Haaland was herself elected governor of New Mexico this week.) Navajo leaders raised concerns over sovereignty and the economic interests of individual Navajo landowners, while other Indigenous advocates backed stronger protections. The federal restrictions do not directly prohibit drilling on Navajo allotted lands.

This article originally appeared in the Chicago Sun-Times. It has been republished with permission.
Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.
“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”
The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the south branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the south fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.
It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.
Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”
More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.
Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it’s calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.
“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”
The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water—both wastewater and stormwater—to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.
But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.
And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That’s more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.
Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district’s North Branch pumping station—at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square—has spewed nearly 2 billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the north branch of the Chicago River.
And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayer money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution.
The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.
But climate change has complicated those efforts. It’s contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes.
These intense storms can bring us more than 8½ inches of rain in just 24 hours.
But Chicago’s sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just 2 inches of rain before flooding is likely.
All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the north branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the last three decades to restore.
Tara Hoffmann, executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast cancer survivors, says she worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.
Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.
“One of the first things you notice,” she says, “is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”
A Threat to Wildlife
Both the Racine and North Branch pumping stations are owned by the water reclamation district. Since 2011, the independent government body that’s in charge of treating sewage and reducing flooding around Chicago has operated under a binding agreement with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency over federal clean water violations related to the sewage.
District officials say the more intense storms we’re seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood prevention measures in addition to the Deep Tunnel, like creating green spaces and tapping other strategies in an effort to capture water before it reaches the sewers. The district has designed nearly 300 flood mitigation projects, many of them still in the planning stages.
Raw sewage is a clear threat to the river’s water quality, says Phil Nicodemus, who’s the research director for the organization Urban Rivers, which works to turn urban waterways in Chicago into wildlife sanctuaries.
“It dumps a bunch of nutrients into the water at the same time,” Nicodemus says of the sewage. “That causes a massive oxygen drop, which causes a huge die-off. If that happens enough times throughout the year, you might be talking about a whole summer without much oxygen at all. That creates an enormous problem for wildlife.”

c546131a6feb.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/schumer-says-democrats-will-stop-trump-from-placing-right-winger-on-the-supreme-court Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Schumer says Democrats will stop Trump from placing 'right-winger' on the Supreme Court Politics Nov 6, 2026 2:46 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer is vowing that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put "a right-winger" on the Supreme Court once they take power, raising the possibility that his party could block a presidential nominee if there is a vacancy in the next two years. In an interview with The Associated Press on Thursday, Schumer would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are "not going to allow any crappy nominees" to be confirmed to the Supreme Court — or to the lower courts or Trump's Cabinet, either. "The bottom line is we're not going to allow a right-winger on the court," Schumer said. Please check your inbox to confirm. Schumer's pledge came two days after Democrats won a decisive Senate majority in the midterm elections — a feat few predicted a year ago, when Schumer was facing intense criticism from progressives within his party and Senate Republicans were betting that a favorable map and backing from Trump would help them keep power. While there is still frustration with Schumer in some corners of the party, the New Yorker is expected to easily be reelected as leader by his caucus after leading them to wins in Republican-leaning states across the country. Democrats could have as many as 56 seats in the Senate if they win Mississippi and Alaska, which still have not been called — "a durable majority," Schumer predicts, that has been 20 years in the making as he has been directly or indirectly in charge of his party's Senate campaign operation. With so many seats, Schumer is betting that "it's not just a flip of the Senate once." And the party will have the power not only to reject any of Trump's nominees, forcing him to seek more moderate choices, but also to halt the Iran war and alter policies that they have been unable to counter in the minority. Navigating divided government, Schumer says focus will be on costs Schumer says the party's agenda will center around lowering prices, along with five issues that they have focused on in the minority — healthcare, housing, Trump's tariffs, childcare and lowering energy bills. He has said Democrats will try to ban federal elected officials from stock trades, and limit consumer costs from data center expansion. Democrats also want to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids across the country and scrutinize the Trump administration, which he says is the "most corrupted administration by far in American history." But Schumer would not get into specifics, or how he plans to get around Trump — who posted a picture of a red hat with the word "veto" in large letters on election night. Beyond Trump, Schumer will also have to navigate his own caucus, including progressives who have criticized him and incoming freshman who won red states and would not commit to supporting him for leader during their campaigns. And to pass any legislation, he will still have to win Republican support as well. He predicts that Republicans will suffer more losses "and keep following Trump over the cliff" if they don't work with Democrats in a bipartisan way. But that will not be easy. Schumer would not say if he would try and eliminate the filibuster, which he tried and failed to do when he was majority leader during President Joe Biden's term, to allow Democrats to pass legislation with a simple majority instead of 60 votes. "The focus has got to be on getting things done," he says. "That's all I am saying." Asked if he would support a third Trump impeachment after Trump was impeached and acquitted twice during his first term, Schumer responds that he would support an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an effort that House lawmakers have already launched. And Trump? "That's up to the House," Schumer said. Election wins two decades in the making Schumer first led his party's campaign arm in the 2006 cycle and has had a hand in every election since then, with mixed results. He attributes this year's wins to good candidates and a focus on local issues in Republican states — the effect of Trump's tariffs on farms in Iowa, where Democrat Josh Turek won, Trump's war with Canada in Maine, where Democrat Troy Jackson beat Republican Sen. Susan Collins, and data centers in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown won after losing his seat two years ago to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. Still, the party's focus on lowering costs was "a message that resonated everywhere," he says. "That's a big difference than in the past." The Democrats who won were not all his recruits — in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed represents the progressive wing of the party and beat Schumer's original choice for the seat, Haley Stevens, in the primary. But Schumer poured $67 million into that race to help El-Sayed and the two "talk regularly," he said. Schumer's future is unclear Even with his winning record this year, it is still unclear how long he will stay in power — and how long the party will support him as some call for a new generation of leadership. He is up for reelection in 2028, and he won't say if he'll run again for a sixth term. "I'm focused on 2027," said Schumer, who became the party's Senate leader in 2015. edbb8ad8eb52.text: By — Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Seung Min Kim, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-names-stephen-miller-his-next-chief-of-staff-after-major-republican-midterm-losses Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump names Stephen Miller his next chief of staff after major Republican midterm losses Politics Nov 6, 2026 2:17 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, mere days after Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections. On his social media site, Trump praised Wiles and said she'd continue to work for his political organization. Wiles also released a social media statement Friday. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," Wiles said in a social media post shortly after Trump's announcement. She added that her commitment to "the President and the mission" will not change. Miller, long a key member of Trump's inner circle, is a key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies. President Donald Trump's hand reaches toward White House chief of staff Susie Wiles as they both attend a lunch with the Kennedy Center board members in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., March 16, 2026. File photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters Wiles, the steely political operator and longtime adviser to Trump, was the first woman to ever serve in that post. Wiles' departure comes almost immediately after the GOP's midterm thrashing on Tuesday. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime trusted aide to Trump. The departure also came months after Wiles indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease, a diagnosis she went public with in March 2026. Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term. Miller is one of Trump's closest and longest-serving advisers, jumping on board during his longshot 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He currently serves as White House deputy chief of staff, and though he has a wide-ranging portfolio, Miller is most closely aligned with Trump's immigration policy and rhetoric on immigration. Miller is a former aide to hardliner former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who would go on to serve as Trump's first attorney general. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
