Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/latino-voters-propel-democrats-to-big-wins-with-leftward-swing Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Latino voters propel Democrats to big wins with leftward swing Politics Nov 6, 2026 2:07 PM EST AN JUAN, Texas (AP) — Latino voters moved sharply to the left in the midterm elections, propelling Democrats to an improbable electoral sweep in Texas and in battleground House races from coast to coast. It's a remarkable pivot for a demographic that had shifted toward President Donald Trump just two years ago. "We showed our power and flexed our muscle during this election," said Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who won his battleground district in New Mexico by around 17 percentage points after winning by less than 1 percentage point in 2022. Democrats capitalized on voters' angst over rising prices and government corruption, riding a wave of frustration to retake control of the House and the Senate. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Hispanics joined in that decisive repudiation of Trump and his Republican Party. In Texas, every county voted more Democratic than it did two years ago, when Trump beat Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the presidential race. But the more heavily Hispanic the county, generally the heavier the shift. "This is our lightning-in-the-bottle moment, that we were able to make such historic gains that we probably never conjured, especially here in Texas," said Johnny Garcia, a sheriff's deputy who won a newly created House district in the San Antonio area where Trump won by 10 percentage points in 2024. "The only way we did that is by going after the issues that were meaning the most to people." Republicans lost the gains Trump made with Hispanic voters in 2024 About one-third of Hispanic voters said they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. The shift was especially pronounced in Texas, where voters flipped a Senate seat and the governor's office to Democrats along with every statewide office on the ballot. Roughly 7 in 10 Hispanic voters supported Democrat James Talarico in the U.S. Senate contest, while only about 3 in 10 voted for Republican Ken Paxton. The group was essentially split in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP VoteCast, an extensive survey of voters and nonvoters. Younger Hispanics' shift was even more pronounced, with swings of around 20 percentage points toward Talarico among Hispanic voters in Texas under 65 years old. Cindy Candia, a 56-year-old lifelong Democrat, was thrilled to see her party find success for the first time in her 20 years living in Texas. She was especially excited about the incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, where Candia lives now. "She's a woman, she's Hispanic, she is from Brownsville, and I don't think anybody thought that Texas would vote for that, for that type of person," Candia said. Democrats won every House district that touches the U.S.-Mexico border — which includes seats in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California — for the first time since 2008. Even in the Senate race in Florida, where Republican Sen. Ashley Moody managed to narrowly win reelection, less than half of Hispanic voters supported Moody, while Trump definitively won this group two years earlier with 55% of Hispanics' support. In southwestern Kansas, three Hispanic-majority counties that voted overwhelmingly for Trump flipped to backing Adam Hamilton, who became the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a U.S. Senate contest in the state. Turnout also surged 27% over 2022 in the three counties, Finney, Ford and Seward. Fourteen Hispanic Democrats were newly elected on Tuesday, 10 of them in districts that are currently represented by Republicans or were redrawn to favor the GOP. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus will have more members than ever before, said Rep. Linda Sanchez of California, chair of the caucus' campaign arm, CHC BOLD PAC. Latino voters want someone who is "understanding of their issues" to represent them on Capitol Hill, said Leticia Gutierrez, a Democrat who won a Houston-area House district that Texas Republicans redrew in a failed attempt to pick up five more seats in the state. "I'm gonna carry all of those things with me to Washington to be able to have that lens," Gutierrez said. Manny Rutinel, a Democrat who defeated Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado, said voters responded to his life story, trusting that he understands their economic concerns after growing up in a family that sometimes struggled to make ends meet. "I think that they elected me because they know that for me it's deeply personal," Rutinel said. Democrats can't take Latino voters for granted In House districts where at least a quarter of the citizen voting-age population is Hispanic, the Democratic share in Tuesday's midterms averaged about 11 percentage points higher than Harris' 2024 performance. By contrast, other House districts saw a 7-percentage-point gain on average. In majority-Hispanic counties, Democratic Senate candidates exceeded their party's 2024 results by more than 15 percentage points. Latinos have been especially affected by Trump's immigration crackdown, which was a prominent issue alongside economic concerns in some of the most heavily Latino districts. d92dfc223175.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/3-charged-in-129-million-ai-scheme-targeting-thousands-of-companies Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 3 charged in $129 million AI scheme targeting thousands of companies Nation Nov 6, 2026 1:59 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday. Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York. Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents. The defendants, from Spain, the UK, Israel and United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment. Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It was not clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York did not immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press. The three were arrested between June and September. In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. The trio, who have nicknames that include "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy," often targeted the companies' accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents. They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment. The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents. Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the UK and had a "handwritten script titled 'Lawyer Call' that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims," according to the U.S. attorney's office. The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents. FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud. "As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate, and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities," he said in a statement. If convicted, each of the charges have a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which is two years, according to the attorney's office. Kennedy Jr. , said he resigned from the Trump administration over alleged internal corruption from a "concentrated group of people." a13cd264a097.text: By — Ted Anthony, Associated Press Ted Anthony, Associated Press By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/online-magazine-salon-announces-it-is-shutting-down Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Online magazine Salon announces it is shutting down Arts Nov 6, 2026 1:46 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Salon, one of the early internet's most influential websites that featured sharp voices and political and cultural journalism with a liberal sensibility, announced Thursday it would shut down after 31 years of publication. "It has been an extraordinary privilege," the outlet said in a farewell note. The announcement, seen as a surprise, cited the fact that "the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years." It did not immediately indicate what would become of its employees, though some reported they had lost their jobs. A spokesperson for the outlet said 19 full-time employees had been affected, as well as a handful of private contractors. "Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own," the unsigned farewell note said. "Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives." It began shortly after the internet went big Salon began its life in the mid-1990s, barely three years after the internet itself went mainstream and a time when the "World Wide Web" was still written out in that fashion. It launched a decade before the newspaper and print magazine markets imploded — and a decade, too, before the rise of social media fragmented the journalism world. As its name suggested, Salon was initially styled as an online magazine and meeting place, a site where more provocative opinions and stories that might not be at home in daily newspapers or even then-dominant newsweeklies like Time or Newsweek could surface and generate discussion. It quickly became a place where writers wanted their work to appear. "The timing was right — readers were tired of bland, market-tested media products, and the internet allowed us to launch something original, something with a strong voice," founder David Talbot said on the outlet's five-year anniversary in 2000. It drew a cadre of high-profile writers and people who would become famous, including Jake Tapper and Glenn Greenwald. Two of its editors-in-chief, Talbot and Joan Walsh, went on to become prominent progressive political voices as well. As the internet grew, so did Salon's competition. Slate emerged the following year, and soon after, online magazines became the order of the day. Eventually, older print publications like The Atlantic began putting more content online and the marketplace of online ideas grew. Salon used Princess Diana's death in 1997 to go beyond its culture-and-criticism roots and wade into breaking-news coverage. Salon's archives will remain online for now Salon told The Associated Press that it had no immediate plans to take down its online archives, which include three decades of stories from across the world and across topics and genres. In its statement, Salon also made a point of thanking its readers. "You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered," it said. "You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 69d8b9db53bf.text: Democratic House members and members-elect are being bombarded with phone calls and emails urging them not to elect Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker, more than a dozen lawmakers and aides tell Axios. Why it matters: The calls point to a fundamental disconnect between House Democrats — most of whom are likely to vote for Jeffries — and at least a portion of their grassroots base. An incoming House Democrat told Axios they are "getting inundated" and have received "about 150" calls since the election urging them not to vote for Jeffries. A senior House Democrat said they received "over 500" calls in the last two days, telling Axios they also got asked about it in-person at a Chamber of Commerce meeting in their district. "I think our numbers are higher" than 500, said another House Democrat. "It's our No. 1 issue, and it's not close." State of play: Jeffries is in pole position to become speaker of the House after Democrats' landslide victory Tuesday, which is set to give them a massive majority of more than 250 seats. He has enjoyed the unanimous support of his caucus since becoming Democratic leader in 2022 and has never had a single House Democrat defect from him in a speaker vote. But the last speaker ballot was in January 2025, right before Democrats' grassroots base began railing against party leadership for what they perceived as insufficient resistance to the Trump administration. "Democrats in both chambers can't go back to business-as-usual politics. People want leadership that's ready to join the rest of us in this new era of politics," Ezra Levin, co-executive director of the progressive group Indivisible, said in a statement to Axios on Friday. A Democratic chief of staff who said their office got "about 300" calls told Axios: "Lots of people are saying make Jamie Raskin speaker." Raskin (D-Md.) has often been floated as a more progressive alternative to Jeffries, whose associations with pro-Israel groups and corporate PACs have long been a sore spot for the left. The top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, Raskin became a superstar among the party's grassroots after serving on the Jan. 6 committee. Raskin has expressed no interest in mounting a bid. A spokesperson for his office declined to comment. The intrigue: A third House Democrat, who said they've "gotten between 300-400" calls, told Axios that actor Mark Ruffalo's post on X calling for "a new speaker" has been driving much of the outreach. The post links to a Change.org petition that says Jeffries "is simply not the right choice." The petition had nearly 900,000 signatures as of Friday. The webpage includes a disclosure that the person who started the petition "receives compensation" as part of the " Change Ambassadors " program, which has raised eyebrows on Capitol Hill. Reality check: Jeffries remains the overwhelming favorite to become speaker, House Democrats say. Nobody has offered even a hint of a whisper that they would be willing to run against him. A fourth House Democrat, who said their office has gotten around 50 calls urging them not to vote for Jeffries, told Axios the odds of anyone else becoming speaker are "none." A fifth — a senior progressive who said they, too, have gotten a lot of calls — told Axios there is a "0.0%" chance of Jeffries not securing the gavel. Democrats' leadership elections are scheduled for Nov. 18-19, and a floor vote for speaker will occur when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3. Between the lines: The volume of calls also varies, some members said, with progressives tending to receive more than moderates. "That's ridiculous. I haven't gotten one," Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.) told Axios, adding, "Jeffries absolutely will be speaker." Said Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.): "I'll be supporting Hakeem Jeffries, and anybody talking about a challenger is just selling tickets to a circus with no tent." Yes, but: Jeffries faces persistent skepticism and hesitance from incoming members — and not just from the progressive "Bloc." Axios interviewed nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him. Don Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who won a seat President Trump carried by 10 percentage points, told a local outlet that he will be "shopping for a new leader" if Jeffries doesn't commit to changing his pro-Israel position. The bottom line: There was an expectation that the roughly dozen members of the "Bloc" would use a small majority to extract concessions from Jeffries. With a massive majority of dozens of seats, however, he has significantly more room to maneuver. His allies are confident they'll get enough Democrats to a "yes" to get him across the finish line — even if he doesn't get the unanimous vote he has enjoyed in the past.

2b041c43ffe3.text: By — Marc Levy, Associated Press Marc Levy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/opposition-to-ai-data-centers-in-the-midterms-foreshadows-tougher-regulations-ahead Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead Nation Nov 6, 2026 1:30 PM EST HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown. Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots. Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices, often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats. In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies. "You know, there's an old saying around here that 'whiskey's for drinking and water's for fighting,'" Tucker told The Associated Press. "And that's exactly what happened." Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio. Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors' offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan. Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium. Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said. During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers. In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he's having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office. In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said. The industry sees a need to build trust AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write "clear rules for how the industry builds." "Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared," the post said. An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium. "We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that," Diorio said in an interview. Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said. Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom. On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it's getting costlier to borrow money. AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth, and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect. In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could "split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without." It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the "most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she'd block a permit for a data center if it wasn't a good deal for Texans or residents hadn't gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development" before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign. Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor "creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state."

Meet Fu Shuang and Ping Ping: New giant pandas in Atlanta
Two 6-year-old pandas made their public debut at Zoo Atlanta in Georgia. Ping Ping and Fu Shuang arrived in late September but spent their first few weeks in quarantine adjusting to their new habitat. Zoo Atlanta is now one of three US zoos with giant pandas, alongside San Diego and the National Zoo in Washington DC. Giant pandas have been a symbol of US-China relations since Beijing gave a pair to the National Zoo in Washington DC in 1972.

0459a9efa976.text: By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/eu-accuses-tiktok-of-violating-its-digital-rules Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter EU accuses TikTok of violating its digital rules World Nov 6, 2026 1:07 PM EST LONDON (AP) — The European Union accused TikTok of breaching the bloc's digital rules because its algorithm recommends a nonstop stream of personalized videos to users including those that it says could hurt mental health and body image. The short-video sharing platform must change the design of its "For You" feed so that users have more control over opting out of seeing certain content, the 27-nation bloc's executive arm said Friday. The platform failed to assess how its recommendation systems could lead people into "rabbit holes" that threaten their well-being, regulators said, by feeding them similar video clips based on what they've previously viewed or liked even if they are "triggering" such as clips about weight loss and mental health struggles. TikTok said the European Commission's findings are "fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform's architecture and our commitment to user safety." "We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience," the company said in a statement. The company will have a chance to respond before the European Commission issues its final decision, which could include a fine of up to 6% of TikTok's total annual revenue. "Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same, leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from," European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, who oversees tech sovereignty, said in a statement. "Today's preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users' well-being, including those of minors." TikTok has added some measures, such as a "not interested" button to reduce the "rabbit hole effect," but the commission said they're ineffective in reducing how often harmful content is recommended. European regulators said they want TikTok to make changes to its "For You" feed, including giving more weight to 'explicit preferences' of people using the platform, stopping reliance on viewing time as a metric for recommending content, and making user controls more accessible. It's the latest in a series of enforcement actions targeting TikTok by EU regulators using the bloc's Digital Services Act, a wide-ranging rule book that requires tech companies to adhere to a framework under threat of hefty financial penalties. The commission opened its investigation into whether TikTok violated the DSA more than two years ago. This year, it has already issued two other sets of preliminary findings, accusing the platform of breaching the rules with " addictive design " features that lead to compulsive use by children and charging it with failing to adequately protect children's privacy rights. 'Permanent, serious' dialogue needed with China on AI: tech-focused lawmaker
“The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do,” Rep. James Walkinshaw, D-Va., said Thursday.
Rep. James Walkinshaw’s vision for artificial intelligence regulation includes maintaining “permanent, serious” dialogue with China to mitigate the risk that powerful AI models pose.
That won’t be easy, but if the U.S. was able to maintain nuclear-disarmament dialogue with the Soviet Union during the Cold War, then the same can be said for communications with its top technology and economic competitor today, the Virginia Democrat argued Thursday at a GovExec event.
Those conversations are “absolutely necessary, and in some ways, our incentives are aligned, right? The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t want rogue AI agents hacking their systems and their water authorities any more than we do, so we have to have that permanent dialogue and reach some agreements,” he said.
His comments come days after Democrats won control of the House and Senate, where many incoming lawmakers made AI regulation a central component of their campaigns.
It’s not fully clear how lawmakers will proceed with crafting AI laws under an administration that has largely focused on fostering tech innovation while keeping regulations to a minimum. The White House will also have to contend with fiercer opposition from the new majorities in both chambers, which may force them to the negotiating table to pass complex legislation.
Walkinshaw is hardly the first member of Congress to advocate for U.S.-China AI dialogue, though his position gives the comments added weight. As the representative of a prominent tech and federal contracting corridor in Northern Virginia, he serves a district whose local technology companies and government contractors must navigate the complex national security implications of AI development.
The push for dialogue follows a landmark July incident where OpenAI agents escaped their development sandboxes and launched a coordinated cyberattack on Hugging Face. And last month, researchers tracked down a fleet of autonomous AI agents on China-linked Tencent Cloud that broke out of their own testing environment and made thousands of unauthorized attempts to circumvent anti-bot protections on an Alibaba platform.
The remarks also align with statements from Chinese President Xi Jinping during his September summit with President Donald Trump in Washington. Acknowledging that both superpowers share a “responsibility” to manage the technology, Xi agreed to establish the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue and a crisis “hotline” for severe AI incidents.
Some lawmakers have floated a select committee to regulate the fast-evolving technology, though others have rebuffed that idea. Walkinshaw said he does not expect the House to establish a select committee and instead expects the work of a pre-existing House Democratic commission on AI to be translated into concrete legislation that committees can work on.
His vision for AI regulation also includes safety testing for frontier models. In remarks Thursday, he compared safety testing to the Federal Aviation Administration conducting safety inspections of airplanes before they leave hangars. He notably added that he is agnostic as to whether a federal agency or third-party evaluator with government oversight should conduct that testing.

European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds, external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close SÃ¡nchez ally Ãscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that SÃ¡nchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.
The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
How to spot the Leonids
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
What is the forecast on Saturday and Sunday evenings?
This weekend's forecast will not necessarily be great news for those hoping to catch the start of the shower.
While the weather will often be dry, large amounts of cloud are expected to fill the sky in many areas with the chance of a few spots of rain or drizzle.
At the moment the best opportunities for clear skies appear to be in southern and western areas of England and Wales on Friday and Saturday nights, with more cloud in northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
By Sunday night it is likely that more parts of the UK will be clear.
However, fog could be an additional issue, forming in any areas where skies remain clear for any length of time, obscuring the view.
Overnight temperatures will drop into single figures with the chance of a touch of frost in a few locations so if you are looking at the night sky for any length of time you will want to wrap up warmly.
You can always check the hour-by-hour cloud, fog and temperature forecast for your area by checking BBC Weather online or the app.
And if you miss them this weekend then take heart that viewing conditions look particularly good around their peak in the middle of November. This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma entered the U.S. Senate to fill a vacancy in March with a clear priority: pass permitting reform that he argued was necessary based on his experience leading a major natural gas pipeline company.
Now, as he prepares to leave office, that goal is within reach—with big potential benefits for the company and him personally.
The bipartisan permitting bill slated for a vote next week would overhaul regulations for building all kinds of projects. But it also includes provisions Armstrong promoted that could push through a disputed pipeline that the Williams Companies, his former employer, has tried to build through New York for more than a decade.
When state regulators denied a water quality permit for the Constitution pipeline in 2016, it was a rare rebuke for an industry unaccustomed to having government officials block its projects. Provisions in the new bill would limit New York’s authority to deny it again.
Williams is now asking federal regulators to revive their approval of the pipeline from more than a decade ago.
Armstrong continued to hold at least tens of millions of dollars in Williams stock as of Oct. 22, according to his most recent financial disclosures. He also hired three former Williams colleagues to his staff, one of whom maintained his role as senior vice president and general counsel at the company while temporarily serving as Armstrong’s chief of staff in the Senate.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would greatly restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to deny or place conditions on water quality certifications. The bill would also make other changes to accelerate approval of Constitution and other pipelines, including restricting judicial review and scaling back certain environmental reviews.
Environmental lawyers say changes to what’s known as a Section 401 certification of the federal Clean Water Act appear tailored to help a small number of gas pipeline projects. One of the companies that would benefit most is Williams, where Armstrong served as chief executive and chairman for 15 years until his appointment in March by Oklahoma’s governor to fill a vacated U.S. Senate seat.
Williams has already received extraordinary support from the Trump administration.
President Donald Trump claimed he made a deal with New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to get the Constitution pipeline built, which she denies. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin has pledged support for the pipeline, and his agency is finalizing a rule change that would restrict states’ and tribes’ ability to condition permits in order to safeguard water quality, similar to the permitting bill.
In October, the U.S. Department of Energy said it would devote up to $42 million under the Defense Production Act to pay permitting costs for the project.
Armstrong’s office did not respond to questions for this article, though he has frequently criticized what he calls a broken regulatory system that drives up costs.
“When every pipeline, transmission line, power plant and industrial project is treated as something to stop rather than something to build responsibly, the costs do not disappear,” Armstrong said in a Senate speech in July. “They accumulate slowly, until families are paying more, reliability is deteriorating, and investment is moving elsewhere.”
Williams spokesperson Blake Jackson said the company supports the permitting bill “and all its provisions to provide a tech-neutral and level-playing field for all energy infrastructure.”
Some residents of upstate New York see things differently.
A Threat to State Waters
Anne Marie Garti, a lawyer who owns a home near the Constitution pipeline route, fought the project the first time around. From the start, “there was a huge amount of opposition,” Garti said, “and skepticism.”
The Constitution project would run 125 miles from the Pennsylvania shale gas fields across upstate New York, eventually connecting to other interstate pipelines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, also known as FERC, oversees interstate gas pipelines. But states retain authority under the Clean Water Act, which requires energy companies like Williams to apply for water quality certifications.
Garti called these permits the “weak link” in the regulatory process. Taking inspiration from an earlier permit denial in Connecticut, she and other residents focused their fight on the pipeline’s potential effects on 251 streams along its route. State regulators said 87 of those streams provided trout habitat.
Building the pipeline would require digging trenches across streams, diverting their flow and clearing trees and brush along their banks. The work would send sediment into clear waters, raise temperatures and temporarily damage habitat for trout and other species, according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation’s 2016 denial.
State regulators rarely reject water quality permits, which are needed not only for pipelines but many federally regulated projects. In a recent survey of 24 states by the Association of Clean Water Administrators, no state reported a denial rate higher than 3.5 percent—most said they’d never denied a permit.
New York denied the certification for Constitution in 2016, saying the company had failed to address the project’s water quality impacts and had not provided sufficient proof that Williams would comply with state standards. The denial kicked off years of legal wrangling. In 2020, Williams said it would not pursue the pipeline and a federal appeals court ruling later vacated the federal permit.
Another permit denial followed in 2019 for a second Williams project: the Northeast Supply Enhancement (NESE) pipeline that would have run from New Jersey across the New York harbor. A few other pipeline proposals in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic faced similar fates, while in some cases regulators imposed conditions to protect waterways.

f4d70379f40b.text: In our news wrap Friday, Trump’s plans to build a massive triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery have been put on hold, two more top officials resigned from the Justice Department, residents along the Georgia-Tennessee border are returning home after record floodwaters receded, Pope Leo started his 12-day tour of Latin America, and Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck. Geoff Bennett: And we start today's other headlines in Washington, D.C. President Trump's plans to build a massive Triumphal Arch near Arlington National Cemetery are on hold, at least for now. Late yesterday, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the monument for two weeks, citing concerns about disruptions to traffic and emergency services. The ruling came just hours after a federal panel, including several Trump appointees, gave final approval to the project. Despite the setback, the administration launched a new Web site today promoting the proposed monument. Some veterans have objected to its placement near Arlington National Cemetery, arguing that it detracts from the solemnity of the site. Two more top officials have resigned from the Justice Department just days after Democrats won back control of Congress. John Eisenberg led the DOJ's National Security Division, where he oversaw cases involving terrorism, leak investigations, and espionage. And Jason Reding Quinones helped lead the so-called grand conspiracy investigation into President Trump's political opponents. Attorney General Todd Blanche thanked both men for their service, but did not provide additional details on their departures. Just a day earlier, Harmeet Dhillon left her post as head of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division. Along the Georgia-Tennessee border, waters have receded and residents are returning home after record flooding submerged local towns. As much as 10 inches of rain fell in just six hours Thursday, turning the Toccoa River into raging rapids. Floodwaters surged through roads, rising as high as street signs and reaching the rooftops of some homes. First responders deployed helicopters, drones, and swift water boats to conduct dozens of rescues. In McCaysville, Georgia, businesses were swamped by mud and debris. One owner said he likely suffered hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost inventory, but said others were even worse off. Hugh Rogers, Business Owner: It's a little bit heartbreaking, but there's a lot of people that's lost their homes and everything they have, so it's -- we're not in such bad shape here. And I would a lot rather be doing this than lose a home. So... Geoff Bennett: Both McCaysville and neighboring Copperhill, Tennessee, had just recently finished cleaning up from a separate flood back in August. Senator Chris Murphy says he will miss several weeks of votes on Capitol Hill while he recovers from a recent stroke. The Democrat from Connecticut says he was released from the hospital today and will spend the coming weeks at a rehabilitation center. His doctor says Murphy suffered a small stroke last weekend and that he's shown tremendous improvement. Murphy is expected to make a full recovery. The longtime manager of the late country music legend Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew. The suit accused Bryan Seaver, who once served as Parton's bodyguard and announced her death on social media, of threatening to damage her business empire in an effort to extract money from her estate. Seaver denied the allegations, saying he was simply seeking payments owed to his security company. Parton died back in August after a brief battle with cancer. The reason for the lawsuit's dismissal was not disclosed. Pope Leo touched down in Uruguay today to kick off a three-country tour of Latin America. The 71-year-old pontiff was welcomed by the nation's president in Montevideo this afternoon. His 12-day tour comes just three weeks after he underwent lung cancer surgery, which put the entire trip in doubt. After Uruguay, Leo will head to Argentina and then Peru, where he will enjoy a homecoming of sorts. He served as a missionary and bishop there for more than two decades and even became a naturalized citizen before being elected pope last year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk says the company will wind down production of its Cybertruck by the middle of next year. Musk says the Texas factory that produces the electric pickup will shift its focus to Tesla's new Cybercab Robotaxi. The Cybertruck has struggled to gain traction since its 2023 debut. Sales fell short of expectations. The vehicle faced multiple recalls. And Musk's political activities also alienated some potential buyers. Tesla shares closed more than 4 percent higher today following yesterday's sell-off. Elsewhere on Wall Street today, stocks steadied a bit to close out the week. The Dow Jones industrial average slipped nearly 240 points, but the Nasdaq managed a gain of more than 1 percent. The S&P 500 also ended in positive territory.

3db1c09ba17b.text: Employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, according to a new government report. Job gains for August and September were revised upward as well, by a combined 84,000 jobs. That makes the last three months of the job market look better than expected, but it comes as questions grow about the sustainability of the AI boom. Amna Nawaz speaks with Diane Swonk, chief economist for KPMG, for more. Amna Nawaz: Well, hiring was much stronger than expected last month. Employers added 165,000 new jobs, according to a new government report out today. Job gains for August and September were revised upward as well by a combined 84,000 jobs. That makes the last three months of the job market look better than we thought, an average of 137,000 new jobs per month. But it all comes during a week when questions grew about the sustainability of the AI boom and its impact on the economy. Markets had a wild ride, losing more than $2.5 trillion in value yesterday before rebounding today. For some insight, I'm joined now by Diane Swonk. She's chief economist for KPMG. That's one of the world's largest firms for professional and tax services. Diane, welcome back. Thanks for joining us. Diane Swonk, Chief Economist, KPMG: Good to be here. Amna Nawaz: So, stronger-than-expected jobs report, upward revisions for August and September, what does all of this tell you about the labor market right now? Diane Swonk: Well, it tells us that we're generating a lot more paychecks, which is great. That is what's helping to keep aggregate consumer spending afloat, along with wealth effects tied to AI. The downside is, of course, that even though the unemployment rate fell to 4.1 percent, average hourly earnings rose only 3.1 percent from a year ago. That's yet another month it will fall short of overall inflation. That's why it's not resonating to most individuals, because they're actually losing purchasing power out there. And I think that's important. We also know the underemployment rate, which includes discouraged workers, those unemployed for a very long time, over 27 weeks, and those forced to take on part-time, instead of full-time work, when they were looking for a full-time job, that rose to 7.9 percent in the unemployment rate. That's the highest since July and well above anything we saw pre-pandemic. One more notable issue is that the New York Fed updated the unemployment rate for new college grads, which fell over the summer, but, again, for not the best reasons. And that is underemployment for new college grads is at its highest level since 2020, during the pandemic. Amna Nawaz: That's concerning news there. But we also saw that big drop in the markets yesterday that I mentioned, part of a massive tech- and AI-driven sell-off. We saw the president kind of refer to that drop today. He attributed to the midterm elections on Tuesday. Is that what you saw? Tell us more about that. Diane Swonk: Well, what we saw is, first of all, we have been tracking the backlash to AI since the beginning of the year, which has really grown to a crescendo. It crosses every age, income strata, and party affiliation. There's just nothing more galvanizing than the fears of job loss due to AI, along with the concerns that people have about a data center in their backyard, their higher electricity costs. So it collides with the concerns about inflation out there. And we had already seen market jitters in the month of October, which is why we started modeling both bear case, a bear market scenario, along with a base case where we're able to sort of muddle through and keep the wealth effects going. But when you're sitting on something that's a one-legged stool, which is the AI boom and the wealth that it generates propelling the economy forward and adding to inflation, that's precarious at best. At worst, it can tip over fairly easily. Amna Nawaz: So what kind of concerns are investors expressing with those kinds of sell-offs? How real are the concerns that we're hearing about an AI bubble? Everyone arguing that, like, housing and, like, the Internet, the investments and spending into AI, are -- gotten way ahead now of profit expectations. What if it bursts? What are you hearing? Diane Swonk: Well, that's exactly -- it is. This is not uncommon with the technological innovation. Innovation requires technology. Productivity requires trust. There isn't trust out there. And the returns on those investments are far in the future. It takes a long time to scale these innovations to make them as powerful and tap the productivity growth. But you have also got to make sure that you include human beings and people's lives and livelihoods in the center of that innovation. People have to see a place for themselves where their fortunes rise with the tide, instead of recede with the shoreline. Amna Nawaz: All right, that is Diane Swonk, chief economist for KPMG, joining us tonight. Diane, thank you. It's always great to talk to you. Diane Swonk: Thank you.

8d89932a8268.text: Democrats’ midterm wins have reached red states across the country, including Kansas, which has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932. That will soon change after Rev. Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist church in the country, defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall Tuesday night. Amna Nawaz speaks with Sen.-elect Hamilton for more. Amna Nawaz: Democrats' midterm election wins have reached red states throughout the country. That includes Kansas, a state that hadn't sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932. That will soon change after Reverend Adam Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist Church in the country, defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall on Tuesday night. And Senator-Elect Hamilton joins us now. Congratulations, Reverend. Thanks so much for joining us. Adam Hamilton: Oh, it's a joy to be with you today. Thank you. Amna Nawaz: So, 94 years since Kansans have sent a Democrat to the Senate. Why do you think they chose to do so this year? Adam Hamilton: I think there was a lot of frustration with what's happening in Washington. Across the state of Kansas, there were people who had voted Republican all their lives and yet looked at what was happening in Washington and felt like things were happening there that were -- that were not kind, they were cruel, they were immoral, they were corrupt, and policies that were hurting people in our state. And I think there was a lot of folks who said, this is not OK. This is not who we are. Amna Nawaz: You put messages of decency, of morality right at the center of your campaign. You said that those are rooted in your faith. How does your time at the pulpit translate to how you talk to voters in this campaign? Adam Hamilton: Sure. Well, first of all, I have spent my life communicating with people. That is what I do. And so every Sunday you're asking the question, how does this -- how does our sacred text, the old New Testament, how does it speak to people's daily lives? And part of that is trying to understand where are people, what are they struggling with, what's happening in their lives. So, when you go out, and, as a pastor, I will just tell you I deeply care about people. I tell folks I don't have very many remarkable gifts. My superpowers are that I listen carefully, I care deeply, and I fight for people. And so, when I traveled across the state, listening to people, hearing their stories, hearing their pain, their frustrations, their disappointments, and then imagining with them what a better future looks like comes naturally as a pastor. And then communicating on the campaign trail is a lot of fun for me. And -- but the biggest thing is, I have spent 38 years trying to ask, what should the world look like? And Jesus talks about this in the Sermon on the Mount in the Lord's Prayer. He asks us to pray, thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. And I tell people who have no particular religious faith, I say, if you think about that, this is like, what is the world supposed to look like? And we're hoping to see that happen. And as a -- as somebody who's running for office, you're imagining what that world should look like, and then you are willing to go fight to see it happen. Amna Nawaz: One of the first big decisions you're going to have to make is what you want your leadership to look like when you get to the Senate. You said you're not going to support Chuck Schumer to be majority leader. So who do you think should lead the party in the Senate at this point in time? Adam Hamilton: Sure. And I mean no disrespect by saying that about Chuck Schumer. He's had a long and distinguished career. I just -- I think we need leaders who are going to bring people together, Republicans and Democrats together, centrists, moderates, and progressives bringing people together, conservatives. And I would like to see... (CROSSTALK) Amna Nawaz: And you don't think Chuck Schumer can do that? Adam Hamilton: I'm not saying he can't. I'm just saying, in my mind, I don't know Chuck very well. a3f0e277cdf9.text: Georgia voters made history this week, electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as the state’s first Democratic senator in more than two decades and the first-ever Black woman governor in the country. The former Atlanta mayor campaigned on lowering costs, expanding healthcare access and pushing back against the Trump administration. Geoff Bennett speaks with Gov.-elect Bottoms for more. Geoff Bennett: Georgia voters made history this week, electing Keisha Lance Bottoms as the state's first Democratic governor in more than two decades and the first Black woman ever elected governor in the country. The former Atlanta mayor campaigned on lowering costs, expanding access to health care, and pushing back against the Trump administration. But she will face the challenge of advancing that agenda in a state where Republicans still control the Senate. I spoke with the governor-elect earlier today. Governor-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, welcome to the "News Hour." Keisha Lance Bottoms: Oh, thank you for having me. Geoff Bennett: You have, of course, made history as the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history. What does this moment mean to you personally? And what message did Georgia voters send with your victory? Keisha Lance Bottoms: It's deeply personal for me. My family goes back at least five generations in Georgia. We are able to trace our roots to a plantation in Crawfordville, Georgia, where my great-great-grandparents were once enslaved. So just on a personal level, to have come from people who had to toil the soul of Georgia, and to now be elected governor has exceeded every dream that I ever had for my life. So I'm grateful for that. And just for the people of Georgia, for us to have had the blue wave, or the blue tsunami, as it's being described in this state, really represents a shift in Georgia, throughout the South, I believe, that's going to reshape who we are as a party, as a state for many years to come. Geoff Bennett: I wonder, have you spoken with Stacey Abrams since your victory? As our viewers will know, she ran for governor herself and spent years rebuilding the political infrastructure that allowed for Georgia to be competitive for Democrats. What do you think this moment means for the movement that she helped build? Keisha Lance Bottoms: Yes, I haven't spoken with her, but for so many of us across the state, it's been about building on progress that's been made. And we take all the lessons from elections passed, we keep all the great things that were done, and then we make corrections where necessary. And this has been decades of work in Georgia. We haven't had a governor, a Democrat governor, elected since 1998. And there have been so many elections since then, so much work that's been done, not just from groups that Stacey has worked with, but a lot of groups across the state, names who never get called on national news, but people who've been deeply committed to building a true grassroots movement in this state. And it's finally all come together in the way that we have hoped that it would for a very long time. Geoff Bennett: What lessons should the national Democratic Party take from your winning campaign? Keisha Lance Bottoms: I think, across America, hopefully, everyone realizes that you have got to listen to people and those issues that matter to them and focus on those things that impact their daily lives. Throughout the course of this campaign, it's been about the cost of living and people asking me directly, what can you do, what will you do as governor to address these issues, and then going back and delivering plans to do just that? And, hopefully, Democrats across the nation -- and just based on the results, it appears that we all had the same takeaways, that we needed to focus on the things that mattered to people and not get distracted and not get pulled into fights that weren't productive for us to be able to deliver. Geoff Bennett: Affordability, as you mentioned, was central to your campaign. You have promised to raise the minimum wage. How do you plan to deliver on promises like that, given that Republicans still control the state Senate? How quickly can Georgians realistically expect to see your agenda put into action? Keisha Lance Bottoms: Well, we were able to take the House this time, and we are really one seat away from controlling the Senate. So we're going to try and find those things that we can get bipartisan agreement on, those things we can get done immediately. And if minimum wage, for example, is one of those things, then we're going to move forward with it. But it may be something that we have to wait until we have control of the Senate. But I do believe things like health care and education funding are things that we can cross party lines to find consensus on immediately. Geoff Bennett: Finally, there is enormous symbolism in your election, especially for the Black women who have been so central to the Democratic Party's success over the years. Symbolism also creates enormous expectation. I wonder, do you feel additional responsibility to deliver, knowing how many people see themselves in your victory? Keisha Lance Bottoms: You know, for me, it is just the responsibility to deliver. I moved around this state, and I asked people to support our campaign and to believe in the vision that I was setting forth for the state of Georgia. And I want to make sure that I'm true to my word. So it is -- it's beyond who I am and the symbolism, representation of who I am. It is just about being an effective leader on behalf of all Georgians. Geoff Bennett: Georgia's Governor-Elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, thanks again for your time. We appreciate it. And congratulations. Keisha Lance Bottoms: Thank you. Thank you.

Texas Democrats Swept Statewide Races. Now Comes the Hard Part of Solving Healthcare Angst.
Texas Democrats spent three decades trying to regain control of the governor’s mansion and other top state leadership positions. This Election Day, they pulled off a decisive upset, taking statewide offices and the state House, partly due to voter anger over healthcare costs and the difficulty of getting care.
Now the state’s newly elected leaders have two months before the next legislative session to figure out how to deliver on their promises on healthcare affordability and other thorny issues, such as abortion. And they need to do it in the face of bruising political opposition over a frenetic 140-day legislative session that begins Jan. 12.
“Democrats are still putting together something of an agenda in essentially what is a ‘dog catches car’ scenario,” said James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project, a polling and political analysis group at the University of Texas-Austin.
Texas was at the crest of the nationwide blue wave that flipped control of Congress. The traditionally deep-red state elected James Talarico to the U.S. Senate, and Democrats picked up a seat in the U.S. House, despite efforts by Republicans to draw districts in their favor and at least $225 million spent by Elon Musk to elect Texas GOP candidates.
But the biggest changes for Texans could come from the state-level elections that Democrats also dominated on Nov. 3. And the stakes are high: Texas routinely ranks among the lowest in the nation in health outcomes and has the most uninsured people in the country.
Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa and Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin, both state lawmakers, are scheduled to be sworn in on Jan. 19, a week after the legislative session opens. Hinojosa will become the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since Ann Richards moved out in 1995. Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, a popular, well-funded incumbent who had never lost an election before this one.
For three terms, Abbott, along with Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, fought against expanding Medicaid, contested the Affordable Care Act, oversaw the gutting of abortion rights, and weakened vaccine mandates.
While campaigning, Hinojosa and Goodwin said their top health priorities were expanding coverage, bringing down healthcare costs, and improving women’s health. Goodwin has proposed creating a state health insurance plan, funded through Texas’ $24 billion “rainy day fund.”
As state House members, Goodwin filed bills to expand Medicaid and restore abortion rights and Hinojosa filed or signed on to bills to broaden exemptions to abortion bans and add doulas to the state’s maternal mortality review committee. Few of those bills got floor votes.
Political watchers and lobbyists in Austin, Texas’ capital, say it’s too early to tell how Hinojosa, Goodwin, and other newly elected top Democrats will shape legislation for the upcoming session, whom they will appoint to top agency leadership positions, and how they will maneuver around opposition from Republicans who will still hold the majority in the state Senate.
This may be the new leaders’ best shot to figure things out. After the legislative session is over at the end of May, Texas’ legislative schedule doesn’t call for another regular session until 2029 — following the 2028 presidential election, when the entire state House will again be up for reelection.
The State of the State’s Health
About 5 million of Texas’ nearly 32 million residents lack health coverage. That includes 1 million children without insurance. Texas is one of 10 states that didn’t expand Medicaid to cover more low-income adults. New moms in Texas continue to die at higher rates than they do nationally. And healthcare costs topped lists of voter concerns in the state, according to polls in recent months.
On the federal level, Congress didn’t renew enhanced subsidies for Affordable Care Act premiums last year, passed a budget bill with new restrictions on food and healthcare assistance, and cut the federal health budget.
Because of rising costs and enrollment glitches, hundreds of thousands of Texans recently lost health coverage, said Lynn Cowles, director of health and food justice at the policy group Every Texan.
Rachel Elsberry, an insurance broker in Austin who has clients in more than a dozen states, witnessed the challenges people faced with affordability.
“Whether you voted red or blue, every client I talk to, regardless of where they are on the political spectrum, says healthcare costs are too high,” she said. She said she routinely turns away Texas clients who don’t qualify for subsidies on ACA plans or low-cost or free federal health programs.
“It’s heartbreaking,” she said.
Cowles has already met with Hinojosa’s staffers, who she said were receptive to more than a dozen steps her group suggested the governor take to make it easier for people to sign up and stay covered under state health programs.
“It’s an incredibly different world,” Cowles said. “It’s amazing to say these things out loud.”
About 1 million Texans would be newly eligible for Medicaid coverage if state leaders expanded the program. Even though the federal government would foot 90% of the bill for those enrollees, Democratic state leadership still faces steep odds.
“To thread that needle even after dramatic changes like last night is going to be challenging,” John Henderson, president and CEO of the Texas Organization of Rural & Community Hospitals, said the day after the election.
Legislators have a very narrow window to pass bills in the Texas Statehouse, said Charles Miller, director of health and economic mobility at Texas 2036, a nonpartisan policy research and advocacy group. And few measures succeed: During the state’s last regular session, in 2025, of 11,503 bills filed, 3,534 went into effect.
“The clock is ticking,” Miller said.

Here with us now is former Arizona Senator Jeff Flake, one of the most outspoken Republican critics of President Donald Trump during his first term and the author of the 2017 book "Conscience of a Conservative." Senator Flake, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake (R-AZ): Thanks for having me on. Amna Nawaz: I want to begin with that piece of news today that President Trump has elevated Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff. This is the man who's the architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, so many other policies. What does that decision, just days after huge Republican losses in the midterms, say to you? Fmr. Sen. Jeff Flake: Well, it suggests that the president is doubling down. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: And we end it with President Trump announcing that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.
On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.
Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.
"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.
One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.
"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."
Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.
He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.
He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.
Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.
He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.
Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.
The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.
Miller's hardline views sets up clash with Congress
While Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.
It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats â and some Republicans.
"Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."
Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".
The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.
Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.
On Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-president JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement- by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance".
That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.
Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".
Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises.
"Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.
At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.
Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

0dcc6baa3a46.text: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and longtime U.S. senator, has died at age 89. Born into one of America's wealthiest and most prominent families, Rockefeller forged his own path in politics and became a leading voice on healthcare, education and the needs of working families. Rockefeller IV, known As jay, dedicated his career to one of the nation's poorest states. Rockefeller was born in New York in 1937, a month after the death of his great grandfather of the same name, who co-founded the Standard Oil Company. His great-grandson charted a maverick path. His early jobs were at the Peace Corps' offices in Washington, but Rockefeller wanted a more hands-on position tackling poverty. That drive took him to rural Emmons, West Virginia, where he worked to improve the lives of young people in the community. From there, Rockefeller quickly decided to enter politics. He switched from Republican to Democrat, breaking from his family's longstanding affiliation with the Republican Party. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Since 1960, I have really felt myself to be a Democrat, although I realized that public image would probably be different. Kennedy, Rockefeller's uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller, offered him the then vacant Senate seat if he would become a Republican again. Rockefeller said no. Over the next decade, he instead rose up the West Virginia political ladder. He also met and married his wife, Sharon Percy. Their wedding was featured on the cover of "LIFE" magazine. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: I run for governor. Lisa Desjardins: The '70s brought one setback, a defeat for governor in 1972, and then a comeback in 1976. Fmr. Sen. Jay Rockefeller: Today, we leave behind the defeatism of the past. Starting here, starting now, you and I together step out into the rising sun of a new day for West Virginia. Jay Rockefeller: I have a tremendous sense of what our future can be and how I can help as your United States senator.
