From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering with U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman.
Congressional committees originate legislation and oversight investigations, and under the seniority system—as Democrats take control and their senior members presumably become chairs—many House committees have broad subpoena powers.
U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman has represented northern California’s second district since 2013 and is an environmental lawyer in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
STEVE CURWOOD: Representative Huffman, what can we expect to be a top priority from you and your committee when it comes to energy?
JARED HUFFMAN: On all of the subjects before our committee within our jurisdiction, it’s going to be a two-part agenda. We’re going to have to do oversight and investigations to make up for the fact that we haven’t really had a Congress for the last two years. There haven’t been checks and balances. So we will be digging into and investigating so many different things on energy and other subjects that we oversee.
But then we’ve got to move an affirmative policy agenda as well. And we can’t, in my opinion, constrain ourselves to just what Donald Trump might sign into law. I think we’ve got to advance an agenda that reflects our values and our priorities, even if we draw some vetoes from this president. There’s enormous value in drawing that contrast.
JENNI DOERING: Just how important do you think energy and access to affordable energy was in these midterm elections?
HUFFMAN: It was part of the affordability backlash that I think helped shape this blue wave, for sure. The fact that electricity bills, utility bills have been skyrocketing as Donald Trump pays offshore wind developers to walk away from projects that could bring cheap, reliable, clean energy onto the grid, as he does everything he can to strangle clean energy—the cheapest, fastest form of energy that can help lower utility bills.
I think people connected those dots, and they also put together the connection with the corruption, with just the fact that the fossil fuel industry was so programmed with Donald Trump on all of this and was making money hand over fist, war profiteering. Donald Trump boasted, in his words, “We are making a killing on the war in Iran” while people were struggling to afford fuel. All of that helped shape the election in a big way.
CURWOOD: I think it’s fair to say that in many campaigns we didn’t hear the words “climate change” or “climate emergency,” and yet, to what extent do you think the concern about the climate is part of this blue wave?
HUFFMAN: Climate is part of it, even if it wasn’t articulated with that specific phrase. When you look at the inability to get [home] insurance or the inability to afford insurance. When you look at skyrocketing food costs. When you look at the fact that American consumers found themselves stuck on the fossil fuel roller coaster once again because Donald Trump had burned the bridge to clean electric vehicles—or at least tried to do so—while the rest of the world is moving forward in a way that will liberate them from that fossil fuel roller coaster. These were significant elements, and climate was on the agenda, whether folks realized it or talked about it as such or not.
DOERING: How is the climate crisis affecting your district and your constituents? What are you hearing from them?
HUFFMAN: I’m hearing them kind of stunned that in the middle of sunny days, at high tide, we have coastal areas underwater because of what’s called a Kelvin wave—this pulse of warm water that’s moving up the West Coast due to El Niño, which is more intense because of human-caused climate change. The reality really comes home when you’re in the middle of a sunny day, there’s been no storm and you have roads and bike paths and trails and coastal buildings underwater.
CURWOOD: You’ll become chair, in a few weeks, of the House Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Looking at your newfound power, what’s at the very top of your list to get done while you have this opportunity to influence things?
HUFFMAN: We need to do a permitting reform bill on our terms. That’s going to be high on my priority list, if I’m allowed to do it. When we get back to Washington, everybody’s going to be consumed with this fight over the Senate permitting reform deal, a deal that was cut behind closed doors by four people—two of whom are coal-state Republicans—a deal that was written largely by the oil and gas industry. I think waking up after that profoundly huge blue-wave statement by the American people, people—I hope—are going to question why we would constrain our permitting reform ambition to this, which was negotiated with zero leverage for Democrats.
Why wouldn’t we give Democrats a chance to use this newfound power to cut a better deal that doesn’t throw the Endangered Species Act and Native American tribes and the Clean Water Act and all of these other core values under the bus, and a deal that ends the war on clean energy, so that we can give the next president a chance to lead on climate action instead of tying his hands, which is one of the things that this bill would do.
CURWOOD: To what extent is that going to move ahead, though, in a lame duck session?
HUFFMAN: They’re going to try to jam it [through]. That’s very clear. This deal is premised on a very rapid, no-hearings push through the Senate and the House. A lot of the votes have already been lined up, and it is just a good old-fashioned jam job that is going to hit us as soon as we get back to town next week.
DOERING: Part of this permitting bill fight that you’re referring to is public lands. When it comes to the lands that all Americans hold as a public trust, what are your priorities with the Natural Resources Committee?
HUFFMAN: Our public lands are an intergenerational trust.

As global climate negotiators and government officials convene for the annual United Nations climate summit, the scientific organization they rely on to guide their decisions is mired in gridlock and short on funds.
Since 1990, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has produced influential global reports in cycles. Its 2013 and 2014 reports provided the scientific foundation for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, which continues to shape international climate policy. But the IPCC suspended its mid-October meeting without approving a budget for next year or agreeing on a timetable for publishing upcoming reports.
The political disputes that derailed the meeting rattled many of the scientists who devote hundreds of hours, often without pay, to assess the latest climate research across dozens of disciplines, from ice sheets and glaciers to forests and agriculture. Their work not only tracks the science of a changing climate, it also identifies ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions and helps communities adapt to increasingly severe climate impacts.
More than 100 IPCC scientists expressed their concern about the future of the panel in an Oct. 19 open letter, asking political leaders to provide it with adequate resources. The scientists reaffirmed their commitment to the work, but warned that, as climate impacts intensify, governments must ensure the panel can produce timely assessments of climate risks and potential solutions when they are needed. They also called for a process that gives all countries an equitable voice, rather than allowing wealthy, industrialized nations to dominate.
The IPCC will resume its session online in December, after the annual COP, the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year’s event, COP31, begins next week in Antalya, Turkey. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change continually informs the negotiations with science updates, but political tensions have affected its budget and timelines for upcoming reports.
Governments decide voluntarily each year how much to contribute to the panel’s annual budget of $9.7 million, about the cost of producing a major movie. That pays to keep the meetings running, covering travel, scientific support and workshops, especially for developing countries.
Next year’s budget remains uncertain, but a concerted push by nations to increase funding at the upcoming climate summit in Turkey could be effective, history shows. In 1999, at COP5, an urgent funding appeal in the meeting’s final decision document helped the IPCC maintain momentum for its third and fourth cycles of updated climate reports.
Repeated reminders from the annual climate COPs helped sustain funding through the early 2010s, leading up to the landmark Fifth Assessment Report that is the scientific basis of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit human-caused warming as close to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5C) as possible.
Scientists Speak
The United States has, at times, contributed as much as one-third of the IPCC’s annual budget. The Trump administration’s withdrawal of funding over the last two years, along with the U.S. government’s withdrawal from the panel, likely contributed to stalling the IPCC process, said Bob Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University, who signed the Oct. 19 letter and has worked on several of the panel’s reports.
Despite the loss of federal support, the United States still has a significant scientific presence in the current assessment cycle, Kopp said. The U.S. Academic Alliance for the IPCC was formed in 2025 by the American Geophysical Union, bringing together colleges and universities to help ensure continued U.S. scientist participation without federal support. He said the U.S. has the largest percentage of contributing authors of any country, about 7.5 percent, and that the alliance nominated more authors for the current cycle than the U.S. government did for the previous one.
“I’m very pleased that civil society in the U.S. has managed to fill some of this gap,” he said. “But we can also see from what’s happening among the governments and the IPCC budget that there’s only so much civil society can do on its own.”
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Key IPCC reports are scheduled to track whether countries are living up to what they promised in the Paris Agreement, said Carl Schleussner, a climate scientist with Climate Analytics and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. Without a timeline for those reports, scientists can’t plan their IPCC-related work schedule, he said.
The delay in the IPCC’s process reflects a range of complex factors, against a backdrop of deteriorating international cooperation. Among them are concerns raised by a group known as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, including India and China. They are questioning whether the panel’s scenarios fairly represent the range of possible climate pathways for all countries, according to reports by observers with the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s Earth Negotiations Bulletin.
Weaponized Science?
Davide Faranda, another IPCC author who signed the letter, said he’s concerned that a breakdown of international collaboration could lead to climate information being weaponized.
If the IPCC fails to provide that timely, widely available knowledge, major powers like the United States or Russia could try to keep climate assessments private to gain strategic advantages through knowledge of climate impacts on agriculture, natural resources, national security and other sectors, he said.

The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.
The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.
"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."
There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.
"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.
Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.
Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.
He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."
He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."
In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."
"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.
Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.
Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.
Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.
He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , external
Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.
The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.
Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.
Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.
The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

PeÃ±a was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

Restoration work has begun at the site of a devastating wildfire in a national park.
More than 1 sq km (247 acres) of the New Forest was destroyed after a fire spread from a blazing van on 9 August.
The fire caused damage to rare heathland and an ancient woodland, as well as burning through a surface layer of peat in some of the boggy areas, reducing their ability to store carbon.
Forestry England said it had begun a long-term project to help nature return to the affected area, with specialist teams starting work to protect the most vulnerable areas ahead of winter and helping to reseed areas of heather.
The agency, which is responsible for managing publicly owned forests in England, said the blaze spread across the heathland, removing all the plants on the surface before travelling underground to destroy layers of roots and seed banks.
At its height, the fire closed the A31 - a major tourist and commuter route between Hampshire and Dorset - for nearly two weeks.
It came during an exceptionally busy summer for Hampshire and Isle of Wight firefighters, and is estimated to have cost the fire service Â£600,000.
Forestry England's Dave Morris said: "The scene immediately after the fire had gone through this part of the forest is something I will never forget."
Morris added: "Large areas were reduced to piles of charcoal, burnt soils and torched trees. At that time, it was difficult to imagine it would ever fully return to a place where nature could thrive.
"Undeterred, our specialist staff immediately got to work to see how we could help the area recover."
Heather full of seed was harvested from nearby parts of the forest and has been spread across the worst-affected parts of the fire site to form a "protective mat" and encourage new plants to grow.
Forestry England used the same technique after part of the New Forest was destroyed by a previous wildfire in 1989.
"Almost 40 years later, this area is now thriving and has been fully restored," it said.
Teams are also looking at ways to protect the vulnerable roots of ancient beech and oak trees damaged in this summer's fire.
The boggy areas of the fire site sustained the least damage, acting as a barrier to help slow the blaze from moving more widely across forest, and have recovered the quickest.
"The fire has reminded us that nature is remarkably resilient and in the boggy parts of the fire area we can already see plants and wildlife returning," said Morris.
"It will take many decades for the area burnt by the fire to recover completely but, with the right help at the right time, we can give it the helping hand it needs."

Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.
The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.
The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.
"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.
"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.
On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.
In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".
He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.
He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral.
Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.
On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.
The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.
Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.
Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.
The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.
Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.
The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.
This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.
"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.
We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.
He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.
But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.
Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.
It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place,"

As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia

There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

65e9cbe23818.text: Stephen Miller is no Susie Wiles: He believes in almost limitless presidential power, considers the Democratic Party an extremist organization, and dreams of ruthless crackdowns on immigration and foreign adversaries. Why it matters: Miller, the new White House chief of staff, isn't just unlike anyone who's had the job under Trump — he's unlike any to occupy the powerful position in the modern era. He puts the hard in hard-liner and understands how to pull the levers of power to get his way and make the U.S. government a MAGA machine. Miller's appointment sets the stage for two years of partisan warfare with the new Democratic-led Congress, which is likely to launch investigations of Trump's administration, political committees and allies. "Stephen is Trump's wartime consigliere," Roger Stone, one of the president's oldest friends and advisers, told Axios. The big picture: Despite his post-midterm comments about finding ways to work with Democrats, Trump's choice of Miller signals that he's not looking for truces. He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints. Trump's MAGA brain for a decade, the 41-year-old has detailed his Miller Doctrine in speeches, policies and press conferences: Presidential power is "very substantial and will not be questioned." Miller said those words about Trump's Muslim travel ban in 2017 on CBS's "Face the Nation," but to him they broadly apply to other areas of the executive's authority. Court authority is limited. In May 2025, when courts blocked aspects of Trump's deportation policies, Miller said the rulings were the work of "radical rogue judges" who were "at war" with the executive and legislative branches. The political opposition is a threat to America. "The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization," Miller told Sean Hannity in August 2025. He also warned that if Democrats won Congress, "it's game over." They just won it. Homeland security is the nation's spine. A key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies, Miller said in a March speech: "Our national security, our homeland security, the safety and well-being of our people begins at home, begins in our neighborhood, begins in our home region." America should use "hard power" in the Western Hemisphere. "The cartels that operate in this hemisphere are the ISIS and the al-Qaeda of the Western Hemisphere, and should be treated just as brutally and just as ruthlessly as we treat those organizations," Miller said in the same speech, to foreign leaders at the Shield of the Americas conference. Behind the scenes: Miller's Shield of the Americas speech indicated the depth of his involvement in Trump's Latin America policy. He has a keen interest in Mexico and was a driving force in the military action leading up to and including the deposing of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro. Miller has a close working relationship with Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, and he has friendly relations with El Salvador leader Nayib Bukele, a crucial Trump ally in extending U.S. power. "Stephen makes Marco more aggressive on policy, in a good way. When Stephen isn't around, Marco defaults back to being more of the politician," said one White House official who worked with the two. "If people thought regime change in Cuba was going to fall by the wayside, Stephen Miller should make them think twice," the source said. "Today is a bad day for the Cuban regime." Go deeper: Trump advisers see Miller's elevation as a way to reenergize the president's populist base, which failed to turn out in sufficient numbers for the midterms — and in some cases voted for Democrats. Advisers point to Trump's handling of the Epstein files and his decision to attack Iran — which in turn escalated fuel prices — as reasons he lost support among those voters. Without winning them back, Republicans say, they'll have no chance in the 2028 elections. Critics also fault the harsh immigration enforcement championed by Miller, as well as voters' perceptions of corruption in Trump's administration, as additional drags on Republicans. Miller's allies dismiss questions about his management experience, noting that he has overseen the Department of Homeland Security and regularly runs morning meetings with the White House staff focused on immigration policy. They also point to the size of his White House policy team, one of the administration's largest. With Trump's legislative agenda effectively stalled, Miller's allies argue he is particularly well suited to a White House that will increasingly rely on executive orders and legal battles — areas in which Miller has extensive experience. Yes, but: Some critics worry that Miller's elevation could mean Trump turns Miller's hard-line immigration agenda into a centerpiece of his final two years in office — something that could continue to alienate independent and moderate voters, as it appeared to do in the midterms. Trump's administration and supporters expect the criticism and are unfazed. "It's Miller Time," said another Trump adviser. "Buckle up."

Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

The warming of Nepal’s mountains is dramatically transforming some of the grandest landscapes on Earth, leading melting glaciers to collapse, thawing permafrost that can slide from steep peaks and crumbling ice dams to release vast lakes. But other impacts are barely the length of a fingernail.
As the alpine cold recedes, disease-bearing mosquitoes are taking its place. Over the past decade, researchers have documented Aedes aegypti—the primary mosquito species responsible for transmitting the dengue virus—at elevations up to 2,500 meters (8,200 feet). Its expansion into Nepal’s mid-hill and high-altitude regions is driving a major shift in the geographic footprint of insect-borne diseases in the Himalayas.
“In Nepal, Dengue used to be the problem of lower altitude regions, mainly the disease of Terai (the lowlands of Nepal and India),” says Sunita Baral, a research associate at Nepal Health Research Council. “When we were younger we used to hear and even experience the mosquito bite in Terai and we used to ignore going there during the monsoon and post-monsoon. But after a few years, a dengue outbreak occurred in hilly regions like Kathmandu and mosquitoes began to appear here.”
According to a literature review published in January in the journal Clinical Infection in Practice, dengue transmission in Nepal has escalated over the past two decades from localized outbreaks to major nationwide epidemics.
First reported in the country in 2004, the virus caused major public health crises in 2019, 2022 and 2023. Transmission is no longer restricted to the lowland Terai region along the border with India; sustained outbreaks now occur routinely in densely-populated areas at higher elevations. Recent health data reported by local Nepalese media shows the virus has reached 76 out of the country’s 77 districts, with roughly 9,000 recorded infections and at least six deaths in 2025 alone.
“Climate change has a huge impact on geographical distribution and establishment of these vectors in a new area,” explained Ishan Gautam, an associate professor at Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu. “Years ago they were only found in the tropical regions, but they have migrated thousands of meters up to Kathmandu Valley.”
The expansion is driven by a combination of changing climatic patterns, population mobility and unplanned urbanization. Higher average minimum temperatures allow Aedes mosquitoes to survive and reproduce at altitudes that previously acted as natural thermal barriers.
At the same time, rapid urban growth in cities like Kathmandu has created severe water infrastructure challenges. Chronic shortages lead residents to store water in open drums, buckets and construction cisterns, providing optimal breeding conditions for both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Flash floods from unusually strong monsoons have overwhelmed municipal drainage systems and washed out water pipelines in cities like Kathmandu, leaving more standing water for breeding mosquitoes.
“They lay eggs in different types of building habitats, so as they disperse and continue to lay eggs in varying places, the population continues to increase,” Gautam continued. “Dengue vectors are rapidly increasing.”
Beyond climate conditions and urban density, specific biological characteristics of a given vector can accelerate the speed of disease transmission. According to Gautam, infected mosquitoes frequently bite seven to eight individuals before reaching repletion–the state of being fully engorged with a blood meal.
This high feeding frequency means a single infected vector can transmit the virus to multiple hosts within a short time frame, creating a transmission chain driven by a mix of biological compulsion and favorable climate conditions.
Despite these growing risks, public health response efforts are constrained by a widespread lack of community preparedness.
“Many of the communities who are at risk are not aware of dengue vectors and their likelihood of contracting dengue disease,” Gautam noted. “They don’t know about all of the potential breeding sites, so they aren’t able to eliminate them.”
The presence of multiple distinct strains of the virus circulating in Nepal further heightens the risk to public health. A secondary infection with a different strain significantly increases the likelihood of severe dengue, which can cause plasma leakage, severe bleeding and organ impairment.
Additionally, both Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus serve as vectors for other insect-borne diseases. Chikungunya is already documented in Nepal, and health officials warn that established vector populations create a serious risk for local Zika virus transmission.
“Due to the news of dengue outbreaks, communities are becoming more aware of dengue, but still they do not recognize mosquito breeding sites around their houses,” said Baral. “In newly affected mountain communities, dengue is still relatively unfamiliar, which can delay recognition and response.”
Because dengue-carrying mosquitoes bite during early morning and late afternoon hours, when most residents in the affected communities are awake and active, relying on bed nets while sleeping provides a false sense of security.
The implications extend beyond the emergence of individual diseases. Together, the presence of two competent vector species and multiple dengue serotypes suggests that Nepal’s mountain regions are becoming increasingly suitable for forms of transmission once associated primarily with warmer lowlands.
The warming trends unfolding in the Himalayas mirror shifts happening across tropical highlands globally, from the Colombian Andes to communities in Costa Rica’s central valley. Historically, these high-altitude regions were shielded from vector-borne illness because lower temperatures slowed mosquito development and virus transmission.

452e690ba866.text: Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced Saturday that he will task Gadi Eisenkot , leader of the opposition Yashar party, with forming a new government, dealing a major setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Why it matters: Eisenkot will have 28 days to establish a new government. This is the closest Netanyahu has been to losing power since 2021, but deep divisions could still prevent them from forming a government. Driving the news: Netanyahu's Likud party won the most seats in the Oct. 27 election, but his coalition lost its majority, winning just 53 of the 120 seats in parliament. Eisenkot's bloc won 48 seats, but the two Arab parties, which won 19 seats, backed his bid to form a government. During consultations held earlier this week, 67 members of the Knesset recommended Eisenkot to form the new government, while only 46 recommended Netanyahu. United Torah Judaism, an ultra-Orthodox ally of Netanyahu, declined to endorse him and signaled it could join an Eisenkot-led coalition. This is a breaking news story. Check back for updates

e7877f48abd2.text: By — Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-president-taps-opposition-candidate-eisenkot-to-form-a-government-in-setback-for-netanyahu Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's president taps opposition candidate Eisenkot to form a government, in setback for Netanyahu World Updated on Nov 7, 2026 3:45 PM EST — Published on Nov 7, 2026 3:39 PM EST JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27. Eisenkot, a former military chief who ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is now a step closer to ousting Israel's longest-serving premier. He has up to six weeks to form a coalition, a challenging task in a deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond. READ MORE: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results In discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel's main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government, but putting together the parliamentary majority needed remains fraught. Netanyahu and his allies lost their majority in parliament in last month's elections. But the bloc led by Eisenkot also didn't win a majority. That left Arab-led parties, which made historic gains, as potential but politically fraught kingmakers. An Arab party has been part of a governing coalition just once in Israel's history. Forming such an alliance could be especially divisive for Eisenkot after more than three years of war in Gaza. Netanyahu has been on a campaign to head off any alliance between Eisenkot and the Arab-led parties, including unsubstantiated claims that Arab parties "stole" the elections. Shortly before Herzog's announcement, he called for a "national unity government" in a video statement and warned against "hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters" — language he uses to refer to the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security, while Eisenkot has indicated a willingness to partner with them under certain conditions, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed. Eisenkot and Netanyahu, whose Likud is the single largest party in parliament, could seek to create a broad unity government with major Jewish parties. However, the men have deep differences over many issues that will be difficult to bridge. That includes Netanyahu's reliance on religious parties that demand draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men, as well as Netanyahu's opposition to a formal investigation into the failures surrounding the Oct. 7 attacks. Eisenkot could also seek to create a "minority" government — shored up by external support from Arab parties that are not formal members of his coalition. However, other members of his bloc have said they would reject such an alliance. Eisenkot's party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister's video with a statement posted on X and urged members of his party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with "radical parties," in an apparent reference to the far-right parties in his religious-nationalist base. The statement argued that Eisenkot would only include parties and parliament members who support its principles. Associated Press writer Julia Frankel contributed from Jerusalem. At least six people have been killed and several others injured after a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland. Here's everything we know so far.
How did the attack unfold?
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.
A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, is being checked for possible explosive devices, police say. Residents of nearby buildings are being evacuated while the operation is under way.
How many people have died and been injured?
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a foreign national.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker.
One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.
What do we know about the suspect and motive?
Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier.
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police.
How did witnesses describe the attack?
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Krakow and is expected to give an address later on Saturday.
Earlier, he said he was being kept informed by the interior minister and that police were investigating "the background and all the circumstances".
Krakow Mayor Åukasz GibaÅa has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, November 11.
President Karol Nawrocki said he was "deeply concerned" and was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events".
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post.
"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"
It's unclear whether the president's public job offer is genuine. The BBC has asked the White House and TKO Holdings, the parent company of UFC, for comment.
The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia exited after just a few days on the job.
Trump's post comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.
In Saturday afternoon's post, Trump called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country".
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters.
Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the podium in the White House press briefing room.
"On to the next chapter," White's post said, though it was unclear if the post was tongue-in-cheek.
Famously combative, White has at times clashed with journalists covering the sport during news conferences.
In 2020, he released a video targeting reporters who had questioned the UFC's decision to hold fights early in the pandemic.
In 2009, he released an expletive-laden video tirade using an anti-gay slur while rebutting a journalist's story about changes to backstage credentialing rules at UFC events.
White is a longtime ally - and friend - of Trump.
When White and his business partners bought the then-struggling UFC organisation for $2m in 2001, the sport was facing intense bipartisan backlash.
Just five years earlier, Republican Senator John McCain had famously labelled mixed martial arts "human cockfighting", sparking bans in 36 US states.
"None of the venues wanted [the UFC]," White told CBS, the BBC's US partner, in 2025. "They didn't believe in it. They didn't like it, and they were worried about the type of crowd that would show up for this type of event."
With mainstream arenas shutting them out, White credits Trump with saving the organisation by hosting two UFC events at the Trump Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 2001.
This summer, the UFC held a cage match on the White House lawn.
White became a speaker for Trump's White House campaigns at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

The first lady later planned to attend the football game between LSU and Alabama, which also is participating in the initiative. "As adults, we have a moral obligation to our children, especially those in foster care. But, as you know, we must act to truly make a difference. The foster care community doesn't need words," she added, before concluding her brief remarks by saying, "Now, let's go and enjoy the game." There are 14 scholars under the program at LSU and nine at Alabama, she said, part of a group of 100 students supported across 26 schools this semester. The foster care program was being featured across the campus as well as on the field at Tiger Stadium just before kickoff, the White House said. WATCH: First lady Melania Trump announces Fostering the Future partnership with IndyCar and Fox Rousse presented her with an LSU helmet with the "Be Best" logo and an LSU jersey with the "Be Best" patch that he said every player would wear in the game. The broader "Fostering the Future" initiative is an offshoot of the "Be Best" campaign that was her signature issue during President Donald Trump's first term. "At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said. "That is why access is one of our highest priorities. Students who have experienced foster care have already demonstrated resilience, determination and potential. Our responsibility, our responsibility is to make sure circumstances beyond their control do not stand between them and a life-changing higher educational experience." The first lady started working on foster care issues after the Republican president's first term ended in 2021, and created "Fostering the Future" to provide resources and support, including scholarships. LSU is among more than 20 colleges and universities nationwide that participate in the program. Earlier this year, Melania Trump was on Capitol Hill to push Congress to pass a legislative package that would broaden access to services for young people in foster care by updating a decades-old program. The measures cleared the House and are pending in the Senate. WATCH: First lady Melania Trump announces new investment accounts for foster youth During the appearance, she told members of the House Ways and Means Committee that young people in foster care face barriers to housing, transportation and other challenges outside of the classroom that affect their performance in school along with their future financial independence. "We can close this gap," she said in April. "New legislation for the foster care community is a moral imperative." Last November, the first lady spearheaded an executive order signed by the president linking the federal government, colleges and universities, the private sector and charitable groups to create educational and employment opportunities for those in foster care. She also created "Fostering the Future Together," a global version of the program with more than 45 participating countries. Alabama and LSU, meanwhile, are historical regional rivals and both teams entered the week in contention for a College Football Playoff berth. Thousands of people, many of them tailgating before the game, filmed the first lady's motorcade as it drove through campus. Donald Trump has attended two prior LSU games as president: one at Alabama in 2019 and one in New Orleans in January 2020, when LSU defeated Clemson for the national championship. Melania Trump accompanied him to the second game. The president was not scheduled to attend Saturday's game. AP Sports Writer Brett Martel in Baton Rouge, La., contributed to this report. d7987518bc58.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-wants-former-u-s-attorney-to-investigate-whether-the-government-misled-her-in-trump-golf-case Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge wants former U.S. attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case Politics Nov 7, 2026 1:34 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" of the course while the lawsuit is active. Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled. READ MORE: Trump's Washington projects are a likely casualty as Democrats claim Congress Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys. As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers' group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP. READ MORE: Trump's triumphal arch is blocked for now, but a new website highlights the plans David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial's participants "can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court." Super said it also is a reflection "of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn't have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues." Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on. The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real. Bedayn reported from Austin, Texas.
