Why it matters: Texas is suddenly — and unexpectedly — the American story. It's the battleground and proving ground for immigration policy, AI, data center growth, Hispanic voting patterns, and the direction of the Democratic Party. Put simply, it seems nearly impossible for Republicans to retain the presidency in 2028 without the Lone Star State. And it seems nearly impossible for AI to keep growing so fast if Texas rejects or dramatically slows it. Texas is so populous, so wealthy, so Hispanic, so energy-rich — and now so top-to-bottom blue — that both parties see it as a de facto nation-state capable of reordering ... everything. "Texas is everything," Steve Bannon, one of the top voices of MAGA, told us. Bannon has been so Texas-obsessed all year that he took his influential podcast, " War Room, " on the road to the " forward lines " of Texas for months at a time. Bannon said Texas needs to be an early focus for Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff. Houston Mayor John Whitmire on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with ICE, saying : "Elections matter." Bannon said he expects many more such actions, with Texas becoming a sanctuary state "quickly unless dramatic action is taken." "Trump is going to be forced to federalize the border," Bannon said, either with National Guard troops or federal law-enforcement agents. The big picture: Texas was red as blood on Nov. 2, the day before midterms. Now it'll have a Democratic governor ... lieutenant governor ... attorney general ... comptroller ... land commissioner ... agriculture commissioner ... Texas House ... and U.S. senator, 37-year-old James Talarico. Talarico won by double digits over state Attorney General Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa — who'll be Texas' first Latina governor — upset three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats won all four state Supreme Court seats on the ballot and are set to flip Texas' Board of Education. The new Texas House speaker is likely to be an 87-year-old Black woman, Senfronia Thompson , a Houston Democrat first elected during the Watergate era. Everything's bigger in Texas , especially in politics going forward: 1. South Texas' border counties broke the GOP's thesis. Republicans built their Texas future on South Texas Hispanics, based on President Trump's performance there in 2024. Talarico won Hidalgo by 46 points, Cameron by 38 and Webb by 47. Trump had narrowly carried all three! The lesson: The Valley didn't realign. It swung — or came home to Democrats, as many South Texans would say. 2. Immigration came home, too . Republicans' border-security argument was undermined as President Trump's ICE, cheered on by Abbott, hit South Texas' rural counties and then moved hard-line enforcement into cities across the state. Hidalgo voters were driven by a sluggish economy and the historic immigration crackdown. In Harris County (Houston), voters cited immigration, corruption and GOP leaders' policies as motivating their votes — and 72% of voters in Hispanic precincts in Harris County backed Hinojosa. The takeaway: Voters wanted a secure border and undocumented criminals removed. They didn't sign up for enforcement in their own neighborhoods. 3. Texas is now ground zero for the AI wars. Elon Musk, the world's richest person , moved to business-friendly Texas from California along with other tech elites , and brought along Tesla's headquarters . Musk posted a reminder Saturday to incoming leaders: "SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government. ... As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas." Musk made himself a midterm issue , spending $225 million on races in Texas — about half of his national total . Talarico ran straight at him : "This Senate seat doesn't belong to Elon Musk." After the rout, Musk said on X that data centers in space were looking "pretty appealing." Texas was on track to become home to one of the world's largest concentrations of data centers, but that buildout is now at risk . In August, 57% of Texan registered voters in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll opposed a data center in their own community, including 43% of Republicans, 60% of suburbanites and 60% of rural voters. Gov. Greg Abbott (R) tried to pivot from his bullishness on data centers but still lost reelection . On Aug. 3, he paused new data center grid connections. Hinojosa called data centers a physical manifestation of a governor doing the bidding of monied interests. Sid Miller, the Republican ag commissioner, said he didn't vote for Abbott and blamed him for not listening to Texans on data centers: "He needs to go." 4. All-of-the-above energy now has a Democratic landlord. Texas pumps the oil, drills the gas, harnesses the wind, runs its own grid — and powers the AI boom. Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on new data center approvals until the Legislature passes protections in 2027. One energy lawyer called it "a brand-new day in Texas" for policy once considered settled. The challenge: Wage war on oil and gas, and Texas snaps back red. Govern like Texans have through much of the state's history, and Democrats could get a lease measured in decades. 5. The Hispanic vote is America's biggest swing bloc . Texas had a record-setting surge in Latino turnout, and Talarico won 68% of them . Two years ago, that same bloc gave Trump the Valley. This time, the more heavily Hispanic the county, the heavier the leftward shift . 6. Republicans suddenly have a 2028 math problem. Texas has the second-most electoral votes, after California. Three ways the new Congress can stop Trump’s war
The “Blue Wave” that swept Democrats to victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections was powered by public opposition to President Trump’s disastrous war of choice with Iran. In exit polls, 74 percent of voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote.
Seven in 10 voters want Congress to prioritize ending that war, which it never authorized.
Even with healthy majorities in both chambers, making good on that mandate won’t be easy. After all, a congressional majority has already voted to stop this war: in June, both houses directed the president to withdraw U.S. troops from hostilities, yet here we are.
Even so, the incoming Congress has several constitutional tools to push Trump toward ending the war. Let me name just three.
First, Congress can refuse to fund the war. The most effective leverage Congress has capitalizes on what it usually does best: nothing. It doesn’t take a supermajority to defund a war; all it takes is for one chamber of Congress to refuse to pay.
The Trump administration has spent nearly $50 billion on “Operation Epic Fury” so far, even though Congress has yet to pass specific appropriations for it. But in a conflict this expensive, creative accounting only goes so far. Facing “an urgent budget shortfall” this summer, the administration requested Iran war funds; that request now sits with the Senate, which can tighten the squeeze just by letting it sit.
The power of the purse has historically been Congress’s “most effective way” to force presidents to change course, the Congressional Research Service notes. But maximizing that leverage requires more than simply standing pat.
During the Nixon administration, a resurgent Congress used appropriations riders to help wind down the Vietnam War, imposing a hard cutoff on combat operations in Southeast Asia after Aug. 15, 1973. Twenty years later, after Black Hawk Down, similar tactics helped end our nation-building excursion in Somalia.
The 120th Congress can follow the same playbook: conditioning funding on withdrawal by a date certain.
Second, Congress can impeach Trump’s Defense secretary, reinvigorating a constitutional weapon dulled by the Trump era. In mid-September, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) rushed the House to early recess to avoid a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The articles, drawn up by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), are coming right back: the Republican gadfly intends to force a vote this week when the House returns.
Four of the eight articles in Massie’s bill of particulars center on Iran: that he is carrying out an illegal war in violation of the Constitution’s Declare War clause and multiple provisions of the 1973 War Powers Resolution.
Amid a deeply unpopular war, constitutional censure by the House could really leave a mark. True, Trump could moot the effort by firing Hegseth. But either way, the goal shouldn’t be simply getting a scalp, but imposing costs for continuing an unnecessary, unconstitutional war.
Third, the new majority can bring in the courts. The first branch can enlist the help of the third, the federal judiciary.
In July, after Trump blew past the War Powers Resolution’s time limits and the resolution directing him to withdraw, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) moved to enforce the law in court. Under Meeks’s bill, the House would sue the president, with Johnson dragooned into the role of lead plaintiff (no doubt apologizing to Trump the whole way).
Article III courts are ordinarily loath to intervene in war powers fights between the political branches. Past attempts by House members to sue presidents over unauthorized warmaking have been bounced for lack of standing.
But when the House as an institution files suit, the case has a much better shot at getting heard. In 2020, when the House sued Trump for illegally diverting funds to his border-wall project, the D.C. Circuit granted standing because Trump’s gambit had effectively “snatched the House’s key out of its hands.”
Johnson may be able to put off the suit, but in January, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) gets the Speaker’s gavel and the House can take Trump to court.
Would a federal court declare the war illegal? That’s unlikely. But, win or lose, both Meeks’s lawsuit and Massie’s impeachment drive will keep the war and the constitutional arguments against it in the front of the public mind.
Survey experiments by political scientist Douglas L. Kriner indicate that congressional opposition to war framed in constitutional terms is especially persuasive because “most Americans, like the Framers, still desire collective judgment in questions of war and peace.”
Meanwhile, Congress can keep the pressure on by wielding its most powerful weapon: the power of the purse.
Congress doesn’t need new powers or bigger majorities to fulfill its constitutional responsibilities and bring an end to an illegal war, it needs to start using the powers it has.
Gene Healy is a senior scholar at the Reason Foundation and author of “The Cult of the Presidency.”

Tough choices, uncertainty, and scrutiny may lay ahead for defense contractors
With a new Congress in 2027, companies could see more anti-corruption probes.
New and existing defense programs may face funding delays or challenges, and companies could see a flurry of Congressional anti-corruption inquiries when the new Democrat-majority Congress takes office next year, experts say. Until then, industry can expect a push for funding by the current majority.
“There'll be a lot of pressure on the Republicans to get something passed during the lame duck [session] because they know how hard it will be after that. And defense hawks will be pushing very hard,” said Mark Cancian, a government budget expert and senior adviser with the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
While Republicans being able to amass enough support to pass $350 billion in reconciliation funding for defense “looks iffy,” he said, passing the base budget of around $1.1 trillion is “quite doable.”
But that reduced funding ceiling—along with the possibility of another continuing resolution—means the Pentagon will need to choose what gets funded.
“At $1.5 trillion, [the Pentagon] could do everything. In other words, they could fund a lot of legacy systems, but also fund a lot of new systems. And a $1.1 trillion dollar budget will require them to make some trade-offs—which [ones] get protected will be an important question,” Cancian said.
Defense spending, overall, typically garners bipartisan support. But this year, the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has been a source of political contention—from the Trump administration starting it without Congressional approval to the downstream economic effects.
Also, the administration has, again, tethered funding for several prominent national security programs to a supplemental funding bill instead of the regular defense budget. Those programs include the White House’s massive missile defense effort dubbed Golden Dome, some shipbuilding, and munitions production.
A failure to secure that extra funding could constrain some of the Pentagon’s modernization programs, said Shaun McDougall, lead defense analyst for Forecast International, a sister brand of Defense One.
If Congress passes a long-term continuing resolution instead of a new budget for 2027, the Army would not be able to start building its MV-75 program, to replace the UH-60 Black Hawk, or its Bradley replacement, XM-30.
“They're wanting to start production on those using FY27 funds,” McDougall said.
Navy shipbuilding programs that would take a hit include “new submarine tenders [and] work on the new frigate,” while the “Air Force has several missile programs, and…the collaborative combat aircraft.”
And, when that potential stopgap funding expires, it may be replaced by another continuing resolution—or result in a government shutdown.
“You have the possibility of a government shutdown if there's disagreements over using the Iran War as a bargaining chip or something like that. So there's a lot of potential for budget disruptions, and that's been one of the big struggles for the Pentagon in general,” McDougall said.
However, Democrats could opt to pass the more-than-trillion-dollar defense budget to cover big expenses like munitions.
And in that case, “the war funding is essentially covered” if the base budget includes “a little flexibility to move money around,” CSIS’s Cancian said. “The biggest piece is munitions,” though it likely would also include other operational costs of the Iran war.
Plus, even as polarizing as the Iran war is, stockpiles of the exquisite munitions that were used must be replenished.
“Democrats obviously aren't happy with the war and how it's going, but replacing all those munitions, it has to be done, whether you support how those munitions were used up in the first place,” McDougall said.
Under the microscope
A Democrat-led Congress will likely focus on anti-corruption, with probes into companies that have close ties to the White House and broader Trump administration, said Kristina Moore, a partner with Womble Bond Dickinson law firm in Washington, D.C.
The “first wave of investigations” would likely explore “where there is evidence that a family member close to the president or the administration had an unfair advantage, or somehow benefited directly financially because of a transaction—an acquisition, a merger, a government loan or a contract,” Moore said. “Was a contribution made, say to the White House ballroom, and—close in time—a policy outcome or a contracting decision, right?”
Then, Congressional oversight and defense committees may examine individual policies for potential wrongdoing.
Venezuela, Iran, drones, AI use: “What is that oversight angle there? Was there a no-bid contract awarded in one of those scenarios? What influenced the administration's policy? Who benefited from a change in the administration policy? And then there's just simply who holds information,” which could be interesting to investigators, said Moore, who was previously a Congressional investigator and has advised clients undergoing such probes.
“You kind of get there either because you were involved in a transaction that looks suspicious, or you were involved in a policy area that is of interest and under scrutiny.”
That means companies must know how to navigate public opinion, and the risks that arise because Congress is investigating.
“They operate in the court of public opinion. Who are those third parties that might be amplifying this? What is that specific risk that exists because Congress cares about us? And what's our fact pattern…our narrative?” she said. “Is there any alignment between what the Congress is looking for in our actions or activities?” and is there “internal awareness of what people were saying to the administration?”

b2c29abf32ef.text: House Republican leaders are bracing for enough GOP defections to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the measure comes to a vote this week. Why it matters : Republicans who were defeated in Tuesday's election-night bloodbath have little left to lose and could be more willing to back impeaching Hegseth, whose overall support has eroded since the start of the Iran war. Hegseth doesn't have "a lot of love" on Capitol Hill, retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Fox News. Bacon told Axios he's undecided on this week's vote. Driving the news: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is planning to force a vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth for allegedly defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Republican leaders avoided the measure before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early. Johnson has denied his decision to send members home was related to the impeachment vote, but it would have been a politically difficult vote for Republicans just weeks before the midterms. The political calculus has now shifted dramatically since Tuesday, with the GOP's crushing defeat fueling anger within the conference and increasing the number of Republicans willing to back impeachment. The big picture: The blame game is already in full swing among House Republicans, with the Iran war emerging as a top target of their ire. "Iran, Iran, Iran ... We should have never done the war before the midterms," a GOP lawmaker told Axios. Hegseth is the face of the war for many on Capitol Hill, putting him in the crosshairs of frustrated Republicans. Another GOP lawmaker told Axios that Hegseth's tone and rhetoric have been "very damaging to our ability to get the facts out to the American people on why the strikes targeting Iran's nuclear facilities, and the additional military actions, were necessary." Zoom in: Hegseth is also on "thin ice" with the Trump administration, with some officials pushing for his ouster, Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt reported . Trump defended Hegseth on Wednesday, telling reporters he has every intention to "keep him" in his post. If Hegseth is still around come January, the new Democratic majority will have the power to pursue investigations and impeachment proceedings. The other side: Hegseth is fighting back, calling the impeachment effort a "sham" led by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" in a video posted on X Thursday. Massie, who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, fired back, urging Trump to replace Hegseth while Republicans still control the Senate. "There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie wrote . Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to Axios: "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law, and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America." "We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office." Reality check: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a threshold that would be difficult to achieve, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Habitat work and a monitoring scheme have helped hazel dormice thrive at a National Trust site, despite declines elsewhere, experts have said.
Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon. Rangers weigh and record details of each mouse between April and October.
The trust said the animals "continue to thrive" in the area - a sign it was "doing something right" by creating a "healthy, diverse and well-connected habitat for wildlife".
The People's Trust for Endangered Species said populations had declined by over two thirds in the UK since 2000. Experts said the decline was largely down to "habitat fragmentation".
The trust hopes the mammals, which typically weigh between 20g and 40g, will have gained enough weight to begin hibernating in the coming weeks and survive the winter ahead.
Fi Hailstone, senior ranger for the National Trust at the Killerton estate, said: "When we have warmer weather, it wakes them up and when we have wet springs, that affects their ability to forage when they do wake up.
"So having a resilient ecosystem with lots of shelter for them, lots of scrub, lots of things for them to eat [is important]."
"They love bramble, and I know that bramble has a bit of a bad reputation with a lot of gardeners," Hailstone said.
"But bramble is the life source, really. It has flowers in the spring, it has berries on it. â©It's also protective in terms of cover from other predators, so it's a really great place for them to nest."
When they are not hibernating, they are shy and nocturnal.
Hailstone said Devon was "a bit of a stronghold for dormice" because "there is such a strong hedge network".
"We've been monitoring our dormouse population at Killerton since 2018, and during that time, we've noticed that they are fairly stable, which does buck national trends."
Hailstone said: "We are finding them in new areas which indicates them spreading across the estate.
"We think this is because we're planting a lot more hedges, a lot more trees."
"We might be planting lots of woodland now, which is great, but we won't see the effects of that for dormice for another 100 or so years," Hailstone added.
"It's really important to manage the woodlands that we already have in a positive way."
Anyone who finds a dormouse in the winter is urged not to pick it up but to alert the RSPCA or local animal shelter.

Second of two stories about the effort to support Lahaina fire survivors’ health in the long, hard aftermath. Read the first story, about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, here.
LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—As Mikey Burke walked into her acupuncture appointment on a Wednesday morning in May, she felt the energy shift, just as she always does.
Noelani Ahia, 51, an acupuncturist and Hawaiian healer, greeted Burke, 42, with a smile and a hug, and led her away from the sunlit, open-air courtyard of the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center and into a dark room, walled in with dividers and empty except for a single bed, a chair and a few small tables. As they settled in, they spoke about Lahaina.
Burke, a mother of four, has been going to the local health center since her home burned down three years ago in the deadliest U.S. wildfires in more than a century. Sometimes, it feels like these appointments are the only time she can truly breathe.
“I don’t think people realize how hard a time people are still having,” said Ahia, who directs Maui Medic Healers Hui, a community organization that operates out of the state-run center. “Pretty much no one is fine.”
“And we’re almost worse off now than we were right after the fires,” Burke replied.
“Can you say a little bit more about that,” Ahia asked, softly.
Burke’s appointment was one day before a construction crew would pour the cement foundation of her family’s future home, and the same week that the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study might be shutting down for good.
As she started to speak, Burke fought back tears.
“The fire was a point in time,” she began, her voice breaking as she laid out a chronology that disaster survivors know all too well.
In the immediate aftermath, the first, most acute trauma was that everything was gone, she explained. But now there’s a slower, unrelenting ordeal of all that has fallen apart since.
It’s not just about the destruction of her family’s house, which she’d fought for years to find and secure. It’s her family’s mental health, the loss of friends and neighbors who were priced out and moved away, the fights to address water access, regain local control of land rights, advocate for her children’s Hawaiian immersion school and protect her people’s ability to be Hawaiian in this place that has been taken over by colonizers and corporate interests again and again. She and her neighbors have to be strong for every battle. Everything feels too important; nothing can fall through the cracks.
It was in this building that Burke found out about the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, a University of Hawai‘i research project both quantifying the health impacts of the wildfires and helping survivors navigate them. Burke participated in MauiWES with her husband and four boys, and it was through the study that she learned that her twins, then just 10, were showing signs of post-traumatic stress disorder. It was also how she’d enrolled them in therapy.
But keeping the study funded had been an ongoing struggle, and a few days before Burke’s acupuncture appointment, organizers held a weekend-long event to collect survivors’ health information for what they feared could be the last time.
It made Burke angry. She’d seen what the study had done for her boys. She felt how deeply her community was still struggling. If no one tracked her community’s health, then how would they know, years from now, how the fires changed them? How would they know how to heal?
“There’s always something that we have to fight,” she continued, her tears now falling fast. “We can’t even just be in our own grief.”
The Maui wildfires on Aug. 8, 2023, destroyed more than 2,200 buildings and killed more than 100 people. The Burkes were among the nearly 13,000 displaced.
For months after the fires, Mikey, her husband, Rob, their four sons and four dogs were shuttled between family and friends’ homes, hotel rooms and finally to the two-bedroom, one-bathroom rental where they’re now living, another waystation in the long wait for a new home.
Three years out, she was still meeting people who hadn’t heard about the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center or MauiWES, who had been so swept up in surviving, day-to-day, they hadn’t had time to seek support. It was clear to her there was a pressing need for these health resources.
In the dimly lit room at the health center, the magnitude of it all rose and took over. She fell into Ahia’s arms, shaking, and the older woman stroked her back with strong, fluid movements.
“I’ve got you,” Ahia said. “You’re carrying so much.”
Burke took a deep breath through her tears.
“Just for today, just for this little bit of time, we’re gonna set it down,” Ahia continued, her voice low and calm. “We’re going to take the pōhaku out, even though the pōhaku is your kuleana.”
Her worldly responsibilities, her kuleana, are like pōhaku, stones, weighing her down every day, Ahia explained. But for now, she could set them aside.
Burke’s shoulders softened, the tension of the morning dissipating.
This is a central part of Ahia’s work. Her clients come in with a lifetime of wounds, small and large, their nervous systems shot by unending, compounding traumas. She refers to it as colonial inflammation, how years of layered injustices pile on and manifest in a physiological response to stress. A Native Hawaiian diaspora kid who grew up on the continent and returned to Hawai‘i as a young adult, Ahia blends teachings from Hawaiian healing and traditional Chinese medicine into her practice.
She co-founded what grew into Maui Medic Healers Hui in 2019 to care for protesters opposing an observatory on Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawai‘i island considered sacred by many Native Hawaiians. After the 2023 fires, the organization mobilized to support survivors. Now, many of Ahia’s patients are still feeling the disaster’s aftershocks.
“Can I share a thought?” Ahia asked cautiously, and Burke nodded, her breathing slowing down.

First of two stories about the effort to support Lahaina fire survivors’ health in the disaster’s long, hard aftermath.
LAHAINA, Hawaiʻi—Early on a Saturday morning in May, Ruben Juarez took the 45-minute flight from Oʻahu to Maui, just like he’d done dozens of times over the past three years.
This one felt different.
Juarez landed in Kahului Airport with his partner, Alika Maunakea, and drove on a long winding highway beside the piercing blue ocean until they reached the Lahaina Comprehensive Health Center.
A cool breeze wafted in from the Pacific less than half a mile below as they set up stations for blood collection, lung function tests and mental health check-ins, directing a team of Ph.D. students and local healthcare providers. Then they waited for the fire survivors to arrive.
On Aug. 8, 2023, Maui was hit with the deadliest wildfires the U.S. has seen in over a century. They killed at least 102 people, displaced nearly 13,000 residents and destroyed more than 2,200 buildings. Three years later, just 15 percent have been rebuilt.
Juarez, an economist, and Maunakea, a biomedical scientist, never expected to focus on disaster recovery. But after the fires, they were thrust into the space by the overwhelming scale of need. The two University of Hawaiʻi professors dreamed up the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study, or MauiWES, as a form of rapid response: an effort to track the impacts of the fires on survivors’ health.
Three years and 2,500 participants later, the study has blossomed into a combination of research and intervention, a web of community organizations working together to give participants not just free testing but also therapy, food assistance, cash support and help connecting with doctors and insurance. Some even say the study saved their lives.
The researchers hope MauiWES could become a national blueprint for public health response after disasters. Experts across the country are paying attention. One longtime disaster researcher, David Eisenman at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the study’s holistic approach is “singular.”
But critical federal support to keep the effort going for at least a decade was running out, and its renewal was uncertain—grant applications had been met with silence for months. And just two weeks before Juarez and Maunakea landed on Maui, state funding they were counting on fell through.
Now, here they were at what might be their last big event to understand how survivors were doing and what help they needed.
Juarez was distraught: It felt like the end. But Maunakea, usually the pessimist of the pair, refused to believe it. He felt the study had to continue. The need was too great. They would find a way.
At the health center that Saturday morning, Maunakea greeted Lisa and Nilsson Panis, a pair of siblings born and raised in Lahaina. As he checked them into the study, he explained what they’d do that day. Urine samples to track environmental exposures. Saliva collection for biomarkers of stress and aging. Blood tests for metabolic function. Two assessments of lung health. Recordings of blood pressure, height and weight. A mental health screener.
At the end of it all, they’d meet with a volunteer physician who would help them understand their test results, and they’d each walk away with $100, compensation for their time.
“We’re trying to do this every year,” Maunakea told the Panises.
He was determined to make that happen.
A Different Kind of Research Study
The lobby of the health center had a dark stain on its ceiling where water had leaked in just a month before.
The building—run by the state’s Department of Health and loaned to MauiWES for the weekend—sits near the base of the sprawling West Maui mountains. That weekend, the foothills above the center were covered in dry, yellowing grass that was nonetheless much greener than usual, courtesy of recent Kona low storms.
The storms swept water damage into construction sites and homes that had just been rebuilt. They busted up highways and caused torrential flooding, triggering millions of dollars in damage across the county. They also kicked off an unusually verdant spring, with flowers blooming on the trees outside the center and along the highway below. Wetness that early can heighten the fire risk later in the year, fueling grass and brush growth that dries out and becomes plentiful tinder, susceptible to heat and strong winds.
Lisa Panis had an appointment with MauiWES that day, but she was hoping they’d have room for her older brother, too. In a fluorescently lit room just beside the center’s main lobby, she introduced Nilsson to Maunakea and explained that he had been a first responder after the wildfires, cleaning up debris in the burn zone. Maunakea immediately instructed the Ph.D. students working the check-in desk to sign him up, along with Nilsson’s girlfriend, another survivor.
MauiWES had limited resources, especially with funding so up in the air. But on an island already suffering from a severe healthcare provider shortage, Maunakea and Juarez didn’t like turning anyone away.
Maunakea listened to Nilsson explain what his life looked like in the months after the fires: 12-hour days, seven days a week, clearing the burn zone for a construction company. He wore full-body gear to keep as much of the dust out as possible, but he still ended each day coated in grime. Though he’d never been tested, Nilsson felt confident the constant inhalation of ash and the debris that covered his body as he worked had impacted his health.

“Are you still doing that, or pau?” Maunakea asked.
“Pau,” Nilsson replied. Finished. Now he was working as a mason, bringing his sister on whenever he could. It wasn’t steady. He hoped jobs would pick up in the summer.

How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded
Six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second largest city, on Saturday.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows about a dozen people running inside two buildings before a black car with its front window open passes, followed by a police car.
Another video shows the moment that gunshots were heard in the city's main market square.
Poland's interior minister described the suspect - a 25-year-old Polish citizen - as being inspired by "far-right ideologies"; police said he used "military weapons" in the attack.
Hours after the attack, Polish PM Donald Tusk said three other bodies were found at the suspect's home, which is still being searched.

Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-UniversitÃ¤t (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

The lawmaker in pole position to lead the US House of Representatives after Democrats take control of Congress in January has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".
Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. The BBC asked the Pentagon for comment.
Congress returns to session this week after the Democrats' midterm elections landslide.
Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 for America's role in the war with Iran.
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday.
"Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued.
Jeffries, who is favourite to be next House Speaker, the most powerful member in the lower chamber of Congress, has vowed that the newly empowered Democrats will serve as a check and balance on the Trump administration.
But he said after the midterms results that House Democrats were not currently focused on impeaching President Trump.

08428c515246.text: By — Amanda Becker, The 19th Amanda Becker, The 19th Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-midterms-energized-a-powerful-political-constituency-abuse-survivors Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The midterms energized a powerful political constituency: abuse survivors Politics Nov 8, 2026 1:41 PM EST This story was originally published by The 19th. When Leanna Rocheleau saw the ad that Ohio gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy created, weaponizing his opponent Dr. Amy Acton's childhood sexual abuse, the Columbus-area mother and small business owner felt "triggered." Rocheleau, like nearly half of all U.S. women, is a survivor of sexual violence, and the ad hit at a gut level. In it, Acton's long-estranged mother suggested her daughter had lied about the well-documented abuse and neglect that Acton had discussed during her campaign. Court records confirmed Acton's account. Ramaswamy spent $4 million airing the ad anyway. Then Acton, a Democrat, won by 8 points in a state where her party hasn't been elected to the governor's mansion in nearly 20 years. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on the deeply personal attack ad in Ohio "I was disturbed by the ad — but also fueled to jump back into the fight," said Rocheleau, who has become an activist at the Ohio Statehouse pushing for legislation to protect survivors. "Being able to have a woman survivor as governor of Ohio? I have high hopes that we're going to be able to move some of this legislation into law," she added. Rocheleau has been in the fight for about five years now, since her own sexual assault by a massage therapist and the series of obstacles she confronted as she sought justice. She reported the alleged assault to the owners of the facility where it occurred — nothing happened. She went to the local police department — it took them a year to take her official report. A prosecutor told her they would not bring charges due to lack of evidence. She went to the state medical board. Attorneys advised her to wait for the medical board's findings to bring a civil lawsuit. By the time the board's investigation concluded, the statute of limitations had run out. The massage therapist received a six-month suspension after the board's investigation. "I needed somewhere to put that energy and anger, so I started talking to [state] legislators about changing all of the barriers that I faced," she said. Rocheleau started talking about her assault during Statehouse hearings and in meetings with lawmakers, urging them to pass legislation protecting survivors. Along the way, she met Chris Graham, a survivor of childhood sexual abuse who has become a well-known advocate in the halls of the Ohio Capitol, organizing fellow survivors and coaching them on how to engage in citizen advocacy. READ MORE: After a flurry of ethics cases, sexual harassment rules for Congress are under review Graham and Rocheleau are part of a growing movement of survivors of sexual abuse and gender-based violence who are showing up at statehouses, lobbying the U.S. Congress and coming forward to share their experiences with political candidates — and they're getting results. Sheerine Alemzadeh, the founder of Healing to Action, a grassroots organization focused on ending gender-based violence through survivor leadership, said she thinks of the movement as "a political constituency." She has a book on the subject out next month. In Ohio, Ramaswamy's ad was seen largely as a desperate attempt to regain momentum in the waning days of a losing campaign. In northern Ohio, U.S. Rep. Max Miller lost a seat that Republicans have held since World War II amid allegations of spousal abuse during a contentious divorce. Nationally, Graham Platner, a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Maine, was pushed out of the race after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. U.S. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a four-term Democrat in California, lost to a Democratic challenger amid a House investigation into potential sexual misconduct. In Arizona, Democrat Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who said she was raped during her House campaign, was trailing her opponent by less than 3 points on Thursday in a district Republicans won by 13 points in 2024. Survivors of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein toured the country this year calling for the release of investigatory files related to the disgraced financier and urging voters to demand accountability. In a Wednesday morning note, Liz Roberts, the chief executive of Safe Horizon, the country's largest nonprofit services agency for survivors of abuse and violent crime, called the midterms results "a win for survivors, period." "We saw candidates accused of sexual assault and abuse withdraw from their campaigns, we saw candidates accused of violence lose their race. A survivor of child abuse, who speaks openly and without shame about her experiences, was called a liar by her opponent in a message backed by millions of dollars and still won. She was believed, not just by the survivor community, but by her constituents, voters, and the public across the nation," Roberts wrote. READ MORE: House Ethics Committee opens investigation into domestic abuse allegations against Ohio Rep. Max Miller Graham, who was raped by a priest when he was 14, said the Ramaswamy ad was particularly disturbing because it used Acton's mother against her. Many children who experience sexual abuse do not tell their parents due to fear or shame. "Amy Acton faced that monster in a way that a lot of people in Ohio, and across the world right now, are thinking to themselves: 'The plan was to never tell anybody about what happened to me but what if I did the opposite? What would that look like?' And they're inspired," Graham said. One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague"undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six and injuring 15.
The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.
On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.
Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies".
A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.
Professor Michal PÄdziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reported.
"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," PÄdziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.
PÄdziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.
"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who," he added.
Once the shooting stopped, PÄdziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the perpetrator, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.
"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.
"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance."
Meanwhile, PÄdziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.
"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.
According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states PÄdziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.
The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur MoraÅski.
The attacker has not yet been named by authorities.
When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.
The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.
Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.
James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square, external when the shooting happened.
The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".
Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.
Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there were multiple - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
He continued: "I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away."
The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.
The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.
Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.
The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.
The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

6a8bccaaa4b4.text: By — Garance Burke, Associated Press Garance Burke, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/staff-at-u-s-center-for-ai-safety-are-reporting-to-the-white-house-raising-independence-concerns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP sources: Staff at U.S. center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns Politics Nov 8, 2026 1:05 PM EST SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research. Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That's according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers. The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center's findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself. Please check your inbox to confirm. "These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public," said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists. Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding. The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That's about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies. READ MORE: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force In April, the division's director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director. In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division. The White House didn't respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president's preferred term for artificial intelligence. Trump has commissioned a report on risks from his Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, and will ensure "continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people," the White House said. An industry that polices itself The federal government often takes an active role in deciding what is safe for the public. Take the automobile industry, for example. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration sits crash test dummies in cars and then runs them into walls to measure how human bodies are affected by vehicle collisions. Government researchers then analyze the crash test data, share it with the public and prescribe national standards to improve vehicle safety, all with the mission of saving lives and lowering economic costs from crashes. With AI models, safety testing looks very different. Under then-President Joe Biden, leading AI companies voluntarily agreed to promote "safe, secure, and transparent development" of their models by sharing details with the newly created division of the Commerce Department and following the administration's guidelines for tests and transparency reports. WATCH: Trump announces accord signed by top AI companies to 'self-police' development In September, following alarming reports of AI systems eluding their makers' control, Trump asked leading AI companies to undertake "tremendous self-policing" as part of a voluntary safety pact, but his administration hasn't said how it will monitor the AI companies' implementation. The technology is advancing so rapidly that many models are now deployed instead as AI agents that work without human prompting and can plan out myriad steps in real-world environments, such as in a recent case in which an AI agent sent a false tip to Philadelphia police about an unsolved homicide case. As AI capabilities have grown, the government's capacity to independently check these systems hasn't kept pace. There still is no standard process for testing how safely AI agents are acting in the real world, even in simple cases such as when AI agents book a flight, said Sayash Kapoor, an incoming assistant professor at the University of California, Berkeley School of Information. "Our previous methods would just look at the final answer, the final check, whether the flight was correctly booked. And in this case, it might seem as if the task was solved correctly," said Kapoor, the co-author of a new paper examining agent evaluations. "But unless you're looking at the entire set of steps that an agent took, you won't be able to tell t

452250771f5c.text: President Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call Thursday that he wants him to take steps to implement his Gaza peace plan , according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: The roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. The Trump administration did not want implementation of the plan to become a politically explosive issue during the Israeli election campaign. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election. Now that it's over, the president wants to forge ahead with his Gaza plan, regardless of whether Netanyahu or his opposition forms a new government. Catch up quick: A year ago, Israel and Hamas agreed to the first phase of Trump's 20-point plan, which led to a ceasefire in the Gaza war and the release of the last 20 living hostages taken during the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. Trump's Board of Peace, which was established as part of the Gaza agreement, has been working for months on an implementation plan that includes the establishment of a Palestinian technocratic government and an International Stabilization Force. Last July, the Board of Peace reached an agreement with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm the armed groups in Gaza and transfer civilian and security control to the new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it, mostly for domestic political reasons. In an August visit to Israel, Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner told Netanyahu that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm. He urged the Israeli prime minister to take steps to test whether that commitment was real. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas will ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Zoom in: Over the past three months, Trump's Board of Peace has been working with the Israeli government and military to refine details of the plan and address Israeli concerns about demilitarization in Gaza. A U.S. official said the process would be gradual. Reconstruction would only begin after progress in disarming Hamas had been verified. Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a six-month, $2.45 billion initial recovery plan for Gaza during the U.N. General Assembly in September. The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war recovery and governance in Gaza would look like. But for the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. A source with knowledge of the details said the Trump administration, Board of Peace and Israel agree that the plan remains the best way forward and that there is no credible alternative. Behind the scenes: Secretary of State Marco Rubio as well as Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff also participated in the call between the president and Netanyahu. A source with knowledge of the details described the call, which Netanyahu initiated, as constructive. It also addressed the war in Iran. The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. State of play: A day after the call, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is a member of the Board of Peace, visited Israel. He met with Netanyahu and his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who's been tasked with trying to form a new government to replace Netanyahu's. A source with knowledge of the visit said Blair urged Netanyahu and other Israeli political leaders to give the plan a chance. What they're saying: "The implementation will be difficult but we believe it is a good plan for Israel. Nevertheless we can't do it with one hand tied behind our back," the U.S. official said. "We want to move forward collaboratively and we need full cooperation and partnership from the Israeli government," the person added.

45aac469a793.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/collision-between-2-trains-in-egypt-kills-7-and-injures-more-than-100 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Collision between 2 trains in Egypt kills 7 and injures more than 100 World Nov 8, 2026 12:40 PM EST CAIRO (AP) — Seven people were killed and over 100 others injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the Chief Prosecutor's office said in a statement. It also said the train's conductor was among those killed. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. WATCH: Shock, anger and mourning in Spain after 2nd major train crash this year The Chief Prosecutor's office said late Sunday its investigators had arrived at the site. An inspection indicated that the crash took place when the Giza-Fayyoum train collided with the last carriage of the Cairo-Aswan train, that was stationary on the same track and traveling in the same direction, officials said. Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system which has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years, the government announced modernization initiatives to improve its railways. Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people living nearby rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances, Gamal said that he saw around 80 of the injured were taken by ambulances to nearby hospitals. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash. Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said. Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district. Egypt's deadliest train crash was in 2002, when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt. - Published
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

71f298312da2.text: By — Wufei Yu, Associated Press Wufei Yu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/floods-bring-rare-relief-to-u-s-southwest-reservoirs-as-lake-powell-rises-20-feet Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Floods bring rare relief to U.S. Southwest reservoirs as Lake Powell rises 20 feet Nation Nov 8, 2026 12:31 PM EST PHOENIX (AP) — Recent flooding across the U.S. Southwest is providing rare relief to thirsty reservoirs that had fallen to record lows amid a yearslong megadrought. WATCH: How the West is preparing for a drier future as water supplies hit lows Storms in late October and early November sent torrents of water through normally small or dry creeks that overflowed their banks and flooded local communities. Hundreds of people were told to evacuate, and the flooding cut off access to some areas. Yet most of that water will end up feeding depleted lakes and underground aquifers, said Martin Hoerling, a climate scientist and hydrologist at the University of Colorado, Boulder. "That's somewhat of an unexpected boost from Mother Nature," Hoerling said. Last winter's lackluster snowfall did little to recharge water bodies when it melted in the spring and summer, when they typically get their biggest bump of the year. Then came the chaotic climate phenomenon, El Niño, that has intensified heavy rain and floods. Experts say its impacts will last several more months, potentially further boosting water supplies across the West where water primarily is stored in lakes, aquifers and snowpack. READ MORE: Colorado River plan to cut water amid drought brings uncertainty for cities and farmers Lake Powell, the second-largest reservoir in the U.S., rose more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) from its mid-September low — dwarfing its gains from this year's snowmelt, Hoerling said. Still, the lake remained just over a quarter full, and 15 of its 17 boat launches remained unusable as of Friday. The floodwaters and additional rain could raise the lake along the Arizona-Utah border further, for a total of over 1.2 million acre-feet — enough to support around 4 million average families for a year, Hoerling estimated. Rain brings temporary relief to regional and local water supplies Cities in the region reported some of their wettest weather in decades. Before storms began dumping about 7 inches (17.78 centimeters) of rain around Pagosa Springs, Colorado, in October, more than 10,000 people in the town and surrounding communities were under water restrictions. Restaurants were encouraged to serve water only on request, town manager David Harris said. Those restrictions are now lifted. "While the storm was destructive, I think there is a silver lining," Harris said. "You're getting a good start to the winter snowpack in the higher elevations." WATCH: Tipping Point — The Colorado River Reimagined | A PBS News Special Upper Lake Mary, which captures spring snowmelt in Northern Arizona and supplies Flagstaff, Arizona, with up to 40% of its water, received more than 3 billion gallons of water since early October, said Flagstaff water production manager Brian Huntzinger. Storms last weekend dumped the equivalent of more than two years of water into the town's surface water supply and provided a buffer for an operation that depends heavily on underground aquifers, Huntzinger said. "It's just a great, great thing to see," Huntzinger said. "We might be overflowing at this rate before we see any snow fly." In central Arizona, heavy floodwaters that trapped people in their homes gushed into streams that feed the Verde River. That prompted water officials to release water from two nearly full dams into the Verde's normally dry stretch in metro Phoenix, said Bo Svoma, the principal meteorologist at the Salt River Project that manages reservoirs on the Salt and Verde rivers. Wet weather is unlikely to change decisions on the Colorado River The region remains in drought despite the intense rains. And decisions already have been made to divvy up water in the Colorado River basin. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which manages reservoirs in the West, is unlikely to change its water releases from Lake Powell or other areas until it knows when snowpack has peaked, typically around April, said Jack Schmidt, a Utah State University professor who studies the Colorado River. READ MORE: Lake Powell hits record low, threatening key water and electricity supply for millions Reclamation spokesperson Mary Carlson acknowledged conditions have improved but added "considerable uncertainty remains." Under the federal plan for managing the Colorado River's Lower Basin, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet (about 1.54 billion cubic meters) annually in the next two years. That is enough to fill over 600,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions. Nevada and Arizona are challenging the plan in court. Some Arizona cities have agreed to fund preliminary work to reduce reliance on the Colorado River by expanding an existing dam on the Verde River to capture runoff from storms, Svoma said. "We need to figure out how to be resilient in a drier future. And we're not quite there yet," Hoerling said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
