A charity wants to raise Â£70,000 for a project aimed at boosting wildlife populations on farmland in the Thames Valley.
The Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust (BBOWT) said the money would form part of its Nature Recovery Fund and would be used to tackle falling numbers of birds, bees and butterflies.
The trust said farmland bird populations had fallen by 63% since 1970, while half of the UK's 27 bumblebee species were in decline.
It said measures to help wildlife could include using fewer chemicals in farming to create healthier soil and less polluted waterways, as well as setting aside corners of grassland for animals.
BBOWT's chief executive Estelle Bailey said: "Farmland makes up 68% of our three counties, so to truly have an impact on nature's recovery, our work must expand far beyond our precious nature reserves."
In 2023, a report produced by government agencies, environmental groups and universities found one in six species in the UK were at risk of extinction.
Bailey added: "I want future generations to experience the joy of countryside filled with life - swallows darting above fields, butterflies and bumblebees feeding on abundant wildflowers, hedgerows alive with the sound of birdsong, and to eat locally grown food that supports a healthy, resilient landscape."

Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence
Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.
It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.
"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.
The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.
One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.
What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.
Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.
Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.
The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.
While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.
After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.
We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.
We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.
The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.
DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.
The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.
Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.
In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.
France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.
The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates â¬7bn (Â£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.
Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.
DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.
We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.
They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.
And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.
Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.
Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.
But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.
"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."
Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."
Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.
That area was Quartier Nord.
Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.
Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.
Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.
"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.
It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.

Pope Leo XIV has said Argentina's economy must benefit everyone including the poor, in a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures.
The Pope was speaking as he arrived in Buenos Aires, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
In response, right-wing leader Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today".
This leg of the Pope's journey was expected be the most politically sensitive, with the president's agenda of slashing public spending having been denounced by the Catholic Church for hitting the poorest hardest.
"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," Pope Leo said.
He stressed the plight of those who, "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs", and urged that "particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability" - a veiled reference to the government's controversial cuts to disability assistance.
In what appeared to be a rebuke of Milei's combative style and language, the Pope said strengthening democracy required a "willingness to listen" and the "careful use of words".
Milei had been particularly outspoken about Leo's predecessor Pope Francis, whom he called "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor.
On Sunday, however, Milei struck a conciliatory tone, calling Francis an "exceptional figure" and "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history".
He was also keen to welcome the current Pope earlier, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy".
Pope Leo urged Argentina to safeguard its democracy. "Those who exercise authority have a duty to act with prudence, to acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them, and to direct their decisions toward the good of the entire community," he said.
In his own address welcoming Leo to Argentina, Milei defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of Argentina's constitution and of Western democracies.
The Argentine leader, who has said he will seek re-election next year, is a strong supporter of US President Donald Trump, who has criticised Pope Leo for his opposition to the Iran war.
Pope Leo's trip to Argentina has been described as a homage to Francis, who did not return to his homeland during his own papacy.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

1a633932fb44.text:
Thereâs little precedent in US corporate history for the crisis facing Nvidia after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese âhoneytrapâ operation. The national security implications of the allegation, the chipmakerâs founder-CEOâs centrality to his companyâs growth story, and Nvidiaâs pivotal place in the AI ecosystem all mean the fallout is likely to stretch further than other cases of executive infidelity.
Nvidiaâs board on Sunday announced an independent investigation, but expressed confidence in Huang. In his own statement admitting that he had been unfaithful to his wife, Huang said he remained âfully committedâ to the company.
Nvidia is, at the time of writing, the worldâs second-most valuable company after Apple, with a market capitalization of $4.5 trillion â almost 12% of the Nasdaq 100 index. And no public company has been more important to the AI revolution or its impact on stock markets: The ravenous appetite from hyperscalers such as Amazon and Google for Nvidiaâs chips propelled its annual revenue from under $11 billion to more than $130 billion between 2020 and 2025. The most bullish analysts think its sales will hit $1 trillion in 2029.
Huangâs personal indiscretions do not change Nvidiaâs order book. But he has been inseparable from its commercial success story, helming its new product presentations, negotiating the loans to customers that have made Nvidia âthe central bank of AI,â and dealing directly with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a moment when access to the worldâs most advanced AI chips has been called âthe defining strategic questionâ facing the two superpowers. On Sunday, Sequoiaâs Shaun Maguire, a Huang supporter, called him âirreplaceable for Americaâs AI leadership.â
The nod to earlier US intelligence warnings that China is targeting US tech leaders will serve as a cautionary tale for many of Huangâs peers in Silicon Valley. Meanwhile, any challenge to investorsâ confidence in Huangâs leadership, or any allegation that his personal relationship influenced Nvidiaâs lobbying in Washington, could have serious implications for his position and his companyâs valuation. Nvidiaâs stock already took a beating from a wider reversal in chip stocks as US votersâ protests against data centers shook confidence in the marketâs AI trade.
Extramarital affairs and relationships that were not disclosed to board members have felled CEOs at companies as prominent as Boeing and McDonaldâs in the past. In many cases, boards and investors focused on ethical breaches, such as executives using company funds inappropriately or advancing the careers of romantic partners who reported to them.
The allegations about Huang are more serious, but the reaction to those past peccadilloes offers some clues to what Nvidia can now expect. Directors will now face questions about when it knew of the allegations, and whether the earlier investigation it reportedly conducted was thorough enough. That could test a board that is short on corporate heavy-hitters â thereâs not one sitting CEO on the board other than Huang â or people with deep experience of national security or political crisis management.
The company can also expect litigation from shareholders, and possible regulatory action, if Huang or the board held back material information from investors (Nvidia previously denied the allegations of an affair to media outlets). And Huang is unlikely to avoid high-profile investigations from Congress, whose incoming Democratic-led majority is suspicious of Big Tech CEOs and is already preparing a rash of subpoenas for Trump allies.
Huang, unlike many other Silicon Valley founders, is not in control of his own fate: He has run Nvidia as if he fully controls it, but he lacks the dual-class stock that shields tech founders like Metaâs Mark Zuckerberg and Alphabet cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. While his near-4% stake gave him a net worth of $155 billion at Fridayâs close, it does not protect him should the board or investors try to oust him.
For now, that outcome looks unlikely. There is no obvious successor waiting in the wings, lawmakers are fully aware of Nvidiaâs strategic significance to the US, and Wall Street knows Huang as a brilliant founder who has made fortunes for his shareholders. Bill Ackman, the hedge fund manager, was among the investors urging support for Huang on Sunday.
Huang has promised to cooperate with the investigation his board has launched. He has no choice. Investors who struggle to imagine Nvidia without him have $4.5 trillion reasons to hope and expect that he rides out this crisis. But his serious lapse in judgment will dent confidence in one of the worldâs most consequential companies, at the very moment when investors have shown that their faith in the marketâs AI growth story has limits.

A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El NiÃ±o year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

The News
Opponents of AI-powered cars have been using artificial intelligence to get their message out in the news media.
Theyâve been waging a kitchen sink campaign, placing op-eds in local news outlets arguing the autonomous taxi company Waymo could cost jobs, endanger riders, deprive the government of information, and block fire trucks. The AI detection service Pangram found that many of the pieces were written with a significant amount of AI input, but none contain labels disclosing AI use.
Several op-eds were drafted by a PR firm, said Ira Goldstein, the former head of New Yorkâs Black Car Fund and the author of an op-ed in the New York Daily News.
âA first draft of this OpEd was prepared by our PR firm at the time, which is standard procedure when working with a PR firm. I reviewed the OpEd, and made some edits. The PR firm then handled placement in the Daily News,â Goldstein told Semafor in a statement.
âWith all that said, I stand by every word in this OpEd and believe that AI being used without my knowledge, to write a first draft of a 700-word opinion piece pales in comparison to the economic and public safety damage that thousands of AI powered robotaxis will inflict on New York City.â
(In the same statement, Goldstein said the PR firm in question later last year also dropped the campaign to work for â¦ Waymo.)
The campaign also included series of op-eds for the Dallas Morning News on autonomous vehicle accidents by local lawyer Amy Witherite, which registered as 95% AI-written and 71% AI written, respectively, on Pangram; a San Francisco Chronicle article warning about how autonomous vehicles could go dormant in public streets during power outages, whose text Pangram reported was 88% generated by AI; another Daily News piece that Pangram said the piece was 68% AI-written; a San Diego Union-Tribune piece arguing that autonomous vehicles would likely displace jobs that registered as 95% likely AI-generated text; and a Times of San Diego piece about how the city should track Waymoâs rollout, 87% of which was likely written with AI assistance.
âLike many, many writers, I use AI tools for research, to sometimes test my arguments, help organize my thinking, and make my writing as clear as possible. These tools are a fact of modern life and modern writing,â said Michael Redmond, the San Francisco Chronicle author. Chronicle editor Matt Fleischer told Semafor that the news organizationâs policies were to ask opinion writers to disclose whether they had used AI.
David Margulies, a spokesperson for Amy Witherite, the author of the Dallas Morning News article, said the firm that runs her communications helps develop, draft, edit and place these pieces, and âsometimes use AI tools to monitor media coverage, develop press lists and to prepare initial drafts, which are then reviewed, edited by our staff, fact-checked and reviewed with Amy or other attorneys in the firm before she gives her comments and final approval.â
âAI is just being used as a shiny object to try to change the subject. It wonât work. Every piece published under Amyâs name reflects her views. They are personally reviewed and approved by her before submission,â he said.
âLimited use of AI for research or polishing doesnât automatically disqualify a submission, but we donât accept pieces generated entirely by AI,â Dallas Morning News commentary editor Ryan Sanders said in an email.
Andrew Julien, executive editor at the Daily News, said in an email the organization aims to create stricter guardrails against AI on the site, given the publicationâs ongoing litigation against Microsoft and OpenAI.
The paper feels âstrongly that our readers deserve original opinions â certainly not machine-generated content created by companies we are suing over billions of dollars they owe us for stealing our content.â
The tokens burned spitting out anti-Waymo opinions are part of a monthslong battle between Waymo and its rivals over whether the autonomous driving company can operate commercially on the streets of several major cities.
The Washington Post reported this month that the Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety, a group of Waymo opponents, spent more than $2.6 million on ads in the DC area in 2026, a greater sum than the winning mayoral candidate spent in the same year. Waymo operates commercially in 15 US cities, but has faced opposition from labor unions, ride-hailing giants such as Uber and Lyft, and various AI-skeptical groups and pedestrian safety advocates.
Maxâs view
AI writing has become a fact of life for billions of people around the world, raising questions within the media and academia about the value of and standards for human-written text.
The realm of authorship in the opinion section has also always been a bit dubious. As Semafor tech reporter JD Capeluto wrote earlier this year: âNewspaper op-eds from big names have long been ghostwritten by junior staffers or outside PR firms â no disclosure necessary, and often watered down and hyper-optimized to be as palatable as possible. In that sense, outsourcing to AI is just replacing one form of slop with another. Just look at LinkedIn, where many cringe human-generated posts have been replaced by AI.â
All that may be true. But for media organizations, allowing the proliferation of AI seems more likely to dilute, rather than enrich, the ultimate product. In a world where chatbots and agents easily answer most generic questions for free, the value of news organizations seeking payment from readers could be to provide a perspective that audiences know has been verified by a human being.
Room for Disagreement
To certain journalists, thereâs little point in distinguishing between AI and human authorship now that many people use AI to research and draft. In a precedent-setting move earlier this year, The Wall Street Journalâs opinion editor declared that AI-generated submissions from notable figures were fine, and didnât need disclosure, so long as they were newsworthy,

The longtime executive producer of 60 Minutes said heâs unimpressed with his successors and disappointed that the show had missed an opportunity to press Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the Iran war.
Bill Owens, who resigned last April in protest of what he saw as editorial overreach that was tilting the show in favor of President Donald Trumpâs administration, argued an interview at Semaforâs New Media & Marketing Playbook event in New York that while 60 Minutes may look and feel the same to many viewers, the quality of the show has declined.
When asked what he thinks now of the show he used to oversee, Owens succinctly replied: âNot a lot.â
âThey own the company, they can do whatever they want,â he said of CBS parent company Skydanceâs new leadership. âBut the ratings are telling.â
âThereâs no doubt that linear television is in decline. But the numbers the other day were less than 6 million people. Itâs like the evening news. 60 Minutes? That would have freaked me out,â he said.
Semafor editor-in-chief Ben Smith noted that the new iteration of 60 Minutes had aired segments on alleged corruption in the Trump administration, and to many viewers the show was nearly indistinguishable from the old version. Owens singled out the news organizationâs recent interview with Hegseth, arguing that what the networkâs journalists didnât ask was notable.
âSome of it is subjective. But other things are just questions that need to be asked,â he said, adding: âThey didnât ask how the war was going. â¦ I would have turned to the producing team and screamed bloody murder.â
Owens, who starts in March as executive producer of the YouTube-native outlet Newpress, acknowledged that his resignation in 2025 hadnât had the intended impact, and may have actually prompted a broader network realignment that has seen many on-air personalities and top producers leave.
âWhen I left, I really hoped that I was going to cause enough of a commotion that they would kind of back off. And the people, my senior team, the correspondents, theyâve tried their best,â he said. âBut itâs just a really difficult circumstance.â

cc9325cd4a4e.text:
The News
By January 2025, Paulina Mangubat knew the Democratic National Committee needed to change its digital communications approach dramatically.
The organization had been shattered by a second loss to Donald Trump, in which the party had been strategically outmaneuvered by a new alternative media ecosystem that had helped Republicans circumvent traditional gatekeepers. The DNC didnât have an online creator strategy beyond one Signal group chat with about 20 left-leaning creators, where it occasionally shared messaging. Its brand had never quite recovered from the 2016 campaign, when it was thought to have tipped the scales against then-presidential candidate Bernie Sanders.
Voters saw the national party as overly invested in outreach tactics of the past, as exemplified by a widely-mocked February 2025 post in which its official X account shared a long, hard-to-read list of Democratic accomplishments.
That spring, staff met at a weeklong offsite to regroup, and Mangubat, the head of content and creative, opened with a presentation of comments the DNC was getting on social media.
âOur team took a lot of the online criticism to heart,â she recalled Friday.
The committee decided to make a few key changes. Most visibly, it took a more combative and at times personal tone, an approach mirroring the national mood of Democratic voters. It changed the Republican party logo to one labeled âpedo protectors,â invoking Trumpâs connections to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. And after White House senior aide Stephen Miller wrote on X that Texas Democrat James Talarico was the partyâs âfirst transgender Senate candidate,â the DNCâs account replied, âshut up you ugly f*ck.â
The DNC started posting faster, shortening a previously labored back-and-forth approval process to just 15 minutes between drafting and publishing. DNC senior strategist Tim Hogan told Semafor that the committee reoriented its internal leadership structure, empowering its most online staff to make decisions with less oversight from skittish traditional political operatives.
âPut the posters in charge,â Hogan said.
But it also decided to take a more behind-the-scenes approach. The DNCâs toxic brand among some audiences was hampering the reach of its posts. In early 2025, the organization relaunched its rapid response online efforts under a new brand, @FactPostNews, an account intentionally designed to look like an independent news aggregator, not a messaging arm of the party.
âIf you talked to the admins of some accounts, they wouldnât even realize that they were essentially pushing DNC messaging to their audiences who were not explicitly political,â Mangubat said of some users sharing their content.
Mangubat noted that the DNC had hired researchers to monitor and dig up negative material on Republicans, largely in the form of video clips from little-noticed interviews on podcasts or public channels. It needed a better way, though, to seed that information to its audiences and voters online.
So the committee created a clip library, and began to grow its group of unpaid influencers. The DNC would distribute what it saw as embarrassing or damaging clips of Trump or other administration officials to its one-way Signal group chat, which by October had swelled to more than 700 creators. Instead of sharing talking points or bland DNC messaging, the national partyâs communications team decided to simply share clips and let the creators decide whether or how to use them.
Once the primaries were over, the party set up group chats with Democratic campaignsâ digital directors to help them share negative and positive video clips. Jon Ossoffâs campaign, for example, quickly shared highly-produced clips from his rallies to the Signal chat and the partyâs unpaid creators, who helped the Georgia senator become a viral sensation and elevated his profile significantly.
âWe were not really concerned with being credited or receiving attribution,â Mangubat said. âWe were mostly interested in increasing the surface area of our messaging on every single part of the internet.â
While much of its focus was on X, TikTok, and Instagram Reels, the national party also began ramping up production of original longform content for YouTube. Mangubat said the DNC sent its video team out into the country to find farmers and others impacted by Trump administration decisions and created mini documentaries for YouTube, which it then chopped up into clips and distributed across other social platforms.
Maxâs view
A decade of politics that began with Michelle Obamaâs 2016 mantra, âWhen they go low, we go high,â has concluded with âshut up you ugly f*ck.â
For years, the party had struggled to push back against Trumpâs messaging; his bluntness, sensationalism, aggression, and comedic looseness were perfectly suited for the algorithmic-driven online communications environment. Rudeness, when in the spirit of resistance to the partyâs opponents, has clearly proven popular with its base.
But the DNCâs approach may carry more lasting lessons. Clearly, it worked: The clips it distributed to its creator network frequently went viral. The FactPostNews accounts gained millions of new followers and billions of impressions across platforms, and the organization largely avoided becoming a story itself after fumbling the release of its 2024 autopsy report. The party had success whipping up engagement around posts related to food safety issues, which it noticed were performing well, and tried to tie them to Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The DNCâs ability to also distance itself from its work by seeding content to seemingly independent creators and accounts is yet another sign that what we see on social media isnât as organic as it may appear at first glance. With 2028 around the corner, expect more political actors to find sneakily creative ways of getting their messaging out.

- Published
Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.
The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.
However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.
Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.
That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.
But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.
The only species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.
The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.
It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.
More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.
The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.
Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".
But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."
The hazel dormouse is famous for spending much of the year asleep. It hibernates from around October to May, spending the winter in a nest on the ground.
Even during spring and summer, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep, known as torpor, when the weather is cold and wet, or food is scarce. This helps the small rodent conserve energy.
Researchers believe warmer summers may be reducing the need for torpor, leaving dormice with more energy for feeding and breeding.
They say more research is needed to understand what longer-term impacts climate change could have on the species.
Dr Charlotte Armitage, an ecologist who worked on the survey, said significant uncertainties remain, including how dormice will respond to warmer, wetter winters.
However, she said warmer summer conditions are likely to give the animals more energy to reproduce and raise additional litters.
"This is good news, but we can't be complacent," she told BBC News.
"We still need to protect their habitat, do more research into the effects of climate change and carry out effective woodland management for the benefit of dormice."

bbfb5a98aa5d.text: President Trump defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday night, even as the company's board launched an investigation into his affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Why it matters: The blowback to Huang's relationship is only getting more intense by the hour, with multiple members of Congress calling for probes and investors saying the news could put a cloud over the entire AI trade. What they're saying: Trump was asked Sunday night if he's taking Huang with him on an Asia trip next week. "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him," the president told reporters. "I haven't heard that he's done anything wrong," Trump added. "He dealt with somebody but, you know, so does everybody else." The intrigue: The New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed earlier this year about Huang's relationship with the potential spy but chose not to act. Huang has been one of Trump's favorite corporate executives since his return to office, frequently appearing at White House events. He also traveled with Trump to China earlier this year, even after the reported memo warning the president of Huang's relationship. What's next: A group of House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to agree by Nov. 11 to a date for a briefing on his relationship and Nvidia's national security controls.

The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.
A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.
The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.
Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.
The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.
The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.
It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.
Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.
Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.
An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.
Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

5f581f7c6af7.text: By — Susie Blann, Associated Press Susie Blann, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/russia-and-ukraine-exchange-strikes-a-day-before-u-s-brokered-talks-are-scheduled-to-begin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes a day before U.S.-brokered talks are scheduled to begin World Nov 9, 2026 12:19 PM EST KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia battered Ukraine's power grid again and Ukrainian forces hit another of Russia's biggest oil refineries, officials said Monday, hours before delegations from Moscow and Kyiv were due to meet for new U.S.-brokered talks on how to end the fighting. READ MORE: Russian strikes on Ukrainian aid site kill at least 31 people, with dozens still missing Nearly five years after Russia invaded its neighbor, the two countries remain locked in battle with no sign that either side is ready to budge from their demands. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say. Talks aim to build momentum for settlement, U.S. envoy says The three-way talks between envoys from the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are due to start in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and last for two days. The previous round of talks was in February. U.S. President Donald Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv are "very close" to a deal, despite the "tremendous hatred" between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said that Ukraine would have "a little bit different shape" under the settlement, but he didn't elaborate. Trump has previously made statements about developments in the war which haven't materialized. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who will mediate in the talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, said that the priorities will be ending the conflict, finding ways to stop the war reigniting, reviving Ukraine's postwar economy and preparing humanitarian aid. "We hope these discussions will identify areas of common ground, advance practical solutions, and build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations," Kushner said on X Monday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday that Trump's team has placed "collective security," covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda. Moscow insists that Europe won't be in the 3-way talks The last three-way talks, in Geneva nine months ago, also took place amid continuing attacks. They delivered no significant progress in ending the war, but some circumstances have changed. Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, has to reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections. They could demand more support for Ukraine. Russian state finances are under heavy strain because of the war, and Ukraine's economy is being choked by the relentless attacks. In Abu Dhabi, the talks will look at what security guarantees would satisfy Russia, which sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine, which wants to prevent future Russian invasions. Putin has sought to sideline European countries and negotiate Ukraine's future directly with Trump. However, European leaders and Ukraine have insisted that they be included. Moscow says that European representatives won't be directly involved in the Abu Dhabi discussions, but European officials said that representatives will be in the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said that European officials will hold "separate coordination" with the delegation from Kyiv. READ MORE: Zelenskyy pushes for 'clear' postwar security guarantees in Ukraine Kushner said that before the talks in Abu Dhabi begin, he and Witkoff will consult with officials from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that the meeting would focus on trilateral negotiations, with the United States mediating between Russia and Ukraine. "You are aware that the Americans have their own channels of communication with the Europeans, as do the Ukrainians, and it appears they are already establishing their own methods of coordination," Peskov said. "But, to reiterate, this is a matter of trilateral negotiations." Russia hits electrical substations, Ukraine targets a refinery Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine's Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia's Defense Ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia's campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday that the European Union had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russia launched 317 drones of various types including 105 jet-powered drones at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said. Russian aerial attacks have pummeled Ukraine throughout the war, with gruesome consequences. A Russian glide bomb attack last week near the front line in the southern Zaporizhzhia region killed at least 55 people at an aid distribution center. On Monday, Russian forces hit a warehouse in Odesa in southwestern Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said. Meanwhile, an attack by long-range drones developed by Ukraine during the war started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia's largest, close to St. Petersburg and more than 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from the Ukrainian border, Leningrad Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said Monday. Ukraine said in early October that its long-range strikes had neutralized more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow's ability to supply its forces. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant

AI safety advocates are counting the midterms as a major win while sketching out their plans for the fight ahead, according to a memo from Anthropic-linked Public First Action and its affiliated super PACs that was shared first with Semafor.
Public First, which gets significant funding from Anthropic and backs AI guardrails, wrote that Leading the Future â the top pro-AI super PAC â had a âcrash out,â but warned: âIt would be a mistake to read this cycle and Leading the Futureâs decline as the end of Big Techâs AI political project. â¦ It is paramount that a pro-safety organization be prepared to counter, toxify, and ultimately overcome such an industry-backed opposition campaign.â
Its 2027 goals include getting Congress to pass AI laws that donât preempt state legislation, supporting pro-AI safety candidates, and rebutting pro-AI messaging by Leading the Future, which has $30 million currently in the bank: âBetween now and 2028, we will make sure that AI is a top-tier issue in the presidential race, in every House and Senate race, and in gubernatorial, attorney general, and state legislative races.â
Burgess Everett contributed.

US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses - days after saying he would accept the outcome.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.
He has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races.
The outcome has been clear since election night and Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."
He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.
Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.
In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.
He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.
The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.
Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.
Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

a577f6a2e513.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-house-returns-to-washington-after-blowout-election-for-democrats Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: House returns to Washington after blowout election for Democrats Politics Nov 9, 2026 12:00 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Congress returns Monday to a changed Washington, the Democrats having trounced Republicans in the midterm elections, but with President Donald Trump doubling down on his political threats despite the landmark GOP losses. The House convenes at 12 p.m. EDT. Watch the House floor live in the video player above. Newly elected lawmakers arrived on Capitol Hill over the weekend, creating a jumble of split-screen moments reflective of the new political landscape. Dozens of jubilant Democrats, families and suitcases in tow for freshman orientation, appeared emboldened by the party's sweep of power. The trickle of Republicans coming in spoke soberly of the GOP's vast challenges ahead. WATCH: Hegseth speaks at the Naval War College as possible impeachment vote looms "This country sent a clear message from coast to coast, and that message is they've had enough of what's gone on," said Rep.-elect Daniel Biss, D-Ill. "They've had enough of Donald Trump. They've had enough of MAGA. And critically, they are ready to transform who holds power, and what they do with it." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Republican Rep.-elect Chris Stigall of Missouri said it's clear that voters sent a loud message, "and I hope, as a new member, I can be on the ground level of figuring out how we can reconnect." WATCH: Rep. Garcia says voters gave Democrats a mandate to pursue accountability For starters, he said, the GOP needs to understand that the economy is not where it needs to be. "Six-dollar diesel, I will tell you, for the farmers in my district, that is a tough pill to swallow." But first, it's out with the old before the new Congress takes over in January. Hegseth impeachment vote tops lame-duck agenda The House and Senate are in session for just six short weeks of a lame-duck sprint to finish up the Republican agenda before the GOP majorities come to an end, making way for the change of power on Jan. 3, 2027. Leadership elections and a government funding package are all priorities ahead. READ MORE: After taking control of Congress, Democrats vow major probes into Trump's 'tentacles of corruption' One first order of business is expected to be a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his leadership at the Pentagon. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie pushed the impeachment resolution forward over the objections of House GOP leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the Iran war, which many Republicans blame for the party's midterm election wipeout. House Speaker Mike Johnson had tried to prevent a vote on Hegseth's impeachment in September and abruptly halted proceedings by sending lawmakers home early. But it's unclear Johnson, who remains close to Trump, will be able to slow the drive for impeachment now, unless he decides to adjourn the chamber again. Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night before he flew back to Washington after spending the weekend at his Florida home. "He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that." Democrats are expected to widely support the impeachment resolution and a number of Republicans have signaled they could join them. "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday on ABC. Jeffries said it's time for Hegseth to go, and that the secretary "has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran." New Congress arrives, as does Trump's new chief of staff The halls of the Capitol are expected to swell this week with the collision of incoming and outgoing lawmakers, as the newcomers attend orientation sessions while the retiring lawmakers start to clear out. At the same time, Trump has tapped top aide Stephen Miller, the hard-right architect of much of the White House's domestic policy agenda, as his new chief of staff. Miller takes the helm Monday in what is expected to be the start of a more direct confrontation with the Congress. Republicans in both the House and Senate are planning to hold their leadership elections this week in closed-door meetings that could end up being blame-casting sessions about what went wrong in the elections. House Republicans are bracing for a contentious leadership battle after Johnson decided to step aside, setting up a showdown between the No. 2 Republican, Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the brawling former wrestling coach allied with the hard-right conservatives. The two men had confronted one another when trying to become House speaker three years ago, but neither was able to win enough support from the Republican rank and file, leading to Johnson's rise. With the House Republican numbers now shrunken, lawmakers could seek wholesale change in leadership. In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune is expected to retain his job as Republican leader, though in the minority as Democrats flipped Republican-held seats, including milestone wins in Texas and Kansas. Democrats are expected to hold their elections later this month. Men recruited to French gang as children to kill give rare insight into drug underworld
A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.
Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.
One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.
He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".
"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jamsâ¦ it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
French Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.
He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack".
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.
Barrot said of the attack on France's supermarkets: "It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of CoopÃ©rative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others at a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom. READ MORE: Russell Brand convicted of rape and sexual assault Judge Joel Bennathan denounced Brand's "casual and arrogant disregard" for any woman who said no to him, and castigated him for the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated back to 2004. "About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator." Brand showed little emotion during the stinging rebuke. He turned to mouth the words "we'll be OK" to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers after the hearing. The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and provocative behavior on television and radio broadcasts, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual. But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Prosecutor: Brand used fame to carry out crimes The convictions — years after the #MeToo movement turned a spotlight on sexual abuse by the powerful and famous — raised questions about how Brand's behavior was tolerated by TV and radio stations he worked for, including the BBC, and those around him. "Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said. "He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity." Brand was supported by his wife, father and fans outside court Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand. Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand's good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that he had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse. He also asked the judge to consider the impact of the sentence on Brand's family, particularly his three young children. Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, and his father, Ron Brand. Laura entered the courthouse without Brand, who had been in since custody Thursday's verdict. A couple of Brand's supporters, reflecting his recent conversion to Christianity, held a banner bearing crosses with the words: "Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth." Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand. One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the trauma the crime caused. The others provided statements read by the prosecutor. A woman whom Brand groped during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like "damaged goods." "It was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke," she said. READ MORE: Russell Brand denies all charges as he testifies at his rape and sex assault trial Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke from behind a curtain that shielded her from public view to preserve her identity. Bennathan said Brand's entourage may have written off the sexual assault as "laddish," the boorish and obnoxious behavior for which Brand was known and with which he thought he could get away. "It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offense, and as it turns out you haven't got away with it," the judge said. Rape victim felt 'powerless' A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking. She said she spent months fearing that she might have contracted HIV and that it took years for her to speak up. She only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary. "I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed," she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. "His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless." Winter, the defense lawyer, argued that Brand should be "regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given" following consensual sex. The judge noted how disrespectfully Brand had treated the woman, including putting her in his phone contacts under "T" for "tart." A woman he was convicted of kissing and groping at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 said it had a lasting impact on her life. "Since the sexual assault ... Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget," she said. "Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump." At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.
The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.
The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.
Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.
Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.
Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.
Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.
Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.
President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.
In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.
"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.
The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.
Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.
Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.
Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.
Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.
More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.
This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.
Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.
The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.
Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.
Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.
The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.
In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.
In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.
Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.
Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.
For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.
Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.
Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.
The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.
The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.
With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

ad7fd6d85784.text: By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press By — Darlene Superville, Associated Press Darlene Superville, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-says-his-deportation-policy-might-have-been-too-tough-for-midterm-voters Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for midterm voters Politics Nov 9, 2026 10:56 AM EST President Donald Trump, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS's "60 Minutes" in an interview that aired on Sunday: "I think it might be too tough, yeah." He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. "The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview. Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff. "Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. "Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That's not a course correction. That's a promotion." The president's immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations. Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress. Trump said he believes that "killers" and "drug dealers" in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay "if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes." Trump says he may stay on the sidelines for the 2028 race On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral. WATCH: Midterm voters rebuke Trump, handing Democrats both chambers of Congress Asked whether he'd endorse a potential successor, the president said "probably, not necessarily." "We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with," Trump said in the interview. Asked about possible candidates other than Vice President JD Vance, Trump only named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is viewed as a possible 2028 contender. "I think Marco's great," Trump said. "But there are many others and I'd rather not mention their names. There's some senators that are excellent. I know 'em all, I like 'em a lot. "So I may or may not get involved. I don't know. Maybe I'm better off not getting involved," Trump said. Trump brushes aside questions about becoming wealthier while in office During the midterms, Democrats sought to make the president's personal wealth a campaign issue. About half of voters nationally said government corruption was "crucial" for their vote for Congress, according to the AP Voter Poll. Asked how his net worth went up by $3 billion since returning to the White House, Trump said he doesn't pay much attention to it and said his sons look after the family business. "I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make — I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," he said. Trump was asked whether he thinks people from foreign countries investing in the company he co-owns with his sons are trying to buy influence. "I don't know. But that's true — look, every president has a problem," he said. Trump, who survived an assassination attempt while campaigning for reelection in 2024 and has lashed out against his political foes, was asked whether he could forgive his enemies. He said it would be easy to say yes. But he added: "I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
