f86bf9105d99.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/deportation-flight-of-iranians-from-u-s-canceled-at-last-minute-attorney-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Deportation flight of Iranians from U.S. canceled at last minute, attorney says Politics Nov 9, 2026 10:07 AM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — A U.S. deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation. READ MORE: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, court documents show At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said. Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country. The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials. There were three deportation flights to Iran between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported. But the administration's confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees. Homeland Security refuses comment In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on "prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details," nor would the agency confirm future removal operations. "As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history," the statement said. The administration did not specify in the October court records when the deportations would be carried out. But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS. Advocacy group says detainees have been contacted by Iranian officials According to Rahnama, the eight detainees who boarded the flight on Sunday were visited by a senior official with the Iranian Interests Section — an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs — and were told that the Iranian government would transport them from Pakistan to Iran. In the litigation brought by the Iranian immigrant advocacy group, at least a dozen Iranian detainees have said they've been contacted by Iranian officials who had knowledge of sensitive information on their asylum claims. U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, a nominee of President Joe Biden, has not ruled on the claims but ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out. In a court filing Sunday, the defense fund laid out what it had learned about plans for a removal flight Sunday and argued that the administration may have violated the judge's directive to give advance notice of deportation plans. Later Sunday, the government filed court documents in the case, but they were sealed and inaccessible to the public. Group says individuals could face persecution The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund has called for a halt to the removal flights, saying in a news release that they would "reportedly mark the first deportation of Iranians to Iran since the U.S.-Iran war began." The group's executive director, Yasmin Chubin, said in a statement Sunday that it was difficult to comprehend why the U.S. would forcibly deport Iranians, including asylum seekers, to Iran, amid ongoing military hostilities. The consequences of removal, Chubin said, "could be irreversible and individuals may face persecution, torture, or death." At least one person who had been part of the scuttled flight volunteered to go back to Iran after nearly two years of detention, Rahnama said, out of desperation to leave what he described as inhumane imprisonment. It's not clear how many other of the deportees may have volunteered to leave. Associated Press reporter Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report. Resident birds have returned to Broughshane Waterfowl Park after an oil spill which caused the death of 13 of the flock.
The popular attraction in County Antrim was forced to close after a nearby home heating oil tank was vandalised, causing the oil spill into the pond.
In a post on social media, The Waterfowl Pond confirmed that work is still underway to address the oil contamination and that a number of pens remain out of bounds.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters for urgent specialist care following the incident.
The park, which was home to 120 birds, has since reopened.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said about 10-12 birds have returned including two black swans and Nenes.
Hayward said they are back safely in their pens and they are lucky to be healthy.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in removing the oil waste.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil or kerosene.
Police said about 44 gallons (200 litres) of oil had leaked from the tank which had been damaged at a business premise in the Main Street area of Broughshane.
Hayward said that there is very little evidence of the oil left as the NIEA have removed the majority of it.
"They have made problems a lot less than they could have been," he told BBC News NI.
He said there is still some oil around the edges, and once the oil leaves the pens the birds will be moved back into them.
The USPCA has also been a key part of the rescue operation.
They said that all of the birds, including geese, ducks and swans, needed bathed and treated due to the level of contamination they suffered.
Unfortunately some had already ingested too much and died as a result.
The Waterfowl Pond offered thanks to the USPCA for looking after the birds.
"We are truly grateful for everything you have done."
It also paid tribute to the support received from the public.
"It's another positive step forward for our park, and we couldn't have got here without you."
Police have said that enquiries into the incident are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to come forward.

68d97c03b26f.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press Almudena Calatrava, Associated Press By — Deborah Rey, Associated Press Deborah Rey, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-visits-care-home-in-argentina-for-people-with-disabilities-renewing-call-to-protect-the-vulnerable Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope visits care home in Argentina for people with disabilities, renewing call to protect the vulnerable World Nov 9, 2026 9:41 AM EST BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV renewed his call Monday for Argentina to protect its weakest and most vulnerable people as he visited a home for people with disabilities in a symbolically powerful rebuke of President Javier Milei's austerity measures. On his first full day in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre (50-hectare) grounds. READ MORE: Pope Leo arrives in Argentina and tells Milei that people, not the economy, should come first The center, known as the "city of charity," has been hit hard by Milei's austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina's estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net. Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He chatted with them and blessed them and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society. "You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life," Leo said in the center's chapel. He said he dreamed that Argentines would be inspired to replace the pursuit of economic success and the "cult of outward appearances" with "great works of charity" like the Cottolengo home. "A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said. Argentina's Congress overrode Milei's veto last year to pass a law increasing funding for disability care. But his administration has resisted implementing it, citing concerns that it would undermine his hard-won fiscal balance. Care homes such as Cottolengo are still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars. Leo's visit comes days before the Senate is due to consider legislation that would set aside money for disability benefits in next year's budget. Milei opposes the measure. Given the circumstances, it was deeply significant that Leo chose to start his visit to Argentina by meeting with the Cottolengo guests, said Kuyen Rolon Rey, a volunteer at the home. "The people here deserve this grace," Rolon Rey said. "Choosing such a small place, but big if measured with love, makes us very happy." A message to Argentine business and labor The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope, fulfilling the unfinished legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy. Upon arrival Sunday and with Milei at his side, Leo cited Francis' frequent refrain that money must serve and not rule: "The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy," Leo said in his first speech in Argentina. It's a message Leo is expected to repeat later Monday when he meets with business leaders, union representatives and leaders of popular movements at the Catholic University of Argentina. Among those invited are domestic manufacturers battered by cheap imports since Milei scrapped long-standing trade barriers, and members of Argentina's largest labor confederation, who took their worries over job losses and shrinking wages to the Vatican in September. Since Milei took office in late 2023, his austerity agenda has made him an icon of the global conservative backlash against the liberal establishment. Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts to disability programs as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy. First papal Mass in nearly 40 years For many Argentines, the day's highlight was to be Leo's late-morning Mass at the Monumento a los Españoles, which was expected to draw as many as 2 million people. The same site hosted the last papal Mass in Argentina, celebrated by St. John Paul II nearly 40 years ago. READ MORE: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru Thousands arrived at midnight to secure a good spot for Leo's first Mass in Argentina. Isabel Martín, 73, came with her parish group from San Andrés Avelino. She said she was praying for Leo to "touch the heart" of Milei, whose spending cuts have also hit pensioners hard. "The pope was very specific in his message yesterday," she said, referring to Leo's inaugural speech to Milei. "The weakest cannot be the ones carrying the burden of the adjustment, especially poor retirees. If anyone can make him reconsider, it's the pope." Argentina's minimum pension is approximately $300, about a quarter of what an older adult needs to cover medicine, housing and food. Leo's message was also resonating with younger Argentines, who have shown the sharpest decline in Catholic practice of any age group. Margarita Lanús celebrated her 16th birthday Monday while waiting for Leo's Mass, sharing a cake on the sidewalk with her large family. "I really like that he says things as they are; he goes straight to the point," she said. d3252d0510de.text:
Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.
A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.
Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.
We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.
Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.
The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.
It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.
And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

0497658c07b2.text:
Alexisâs view
Nigeriaâs Federal High Court invalidating the election candidacy of President Bola Tinubuâs leading challenger was unexpected â but not entirely surprising.
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, runner-up in the last election, has fewer than 100 days to secure a reversal on appeal ahead of the January vote. But the broader danger is that last weekâs legal curveball further erodes trust in Africaâs biggest democratic exercise.
The ruling is consistent with a recent pattern of late interventions ahead of Nigerian elections. In 2019, the countryâs then most senior judge was suspended weeks before the vote, prompting speculation that he was dismissed because he couldnât be relied upon to back the incumbent if courts weighed in on a close result. And Nigeriaâs central bank wreaked havoc four years ago when it issued new bank notes in a move widely seen as an attempt to disadvantage some politicians and favor others. Each intervention raised questions about the independence of key institutions.
Tinubu was already the frontrunner, even before Atikuâs legal headache. Peter Obi, the other main opponent, should not be underestimated. But the failure of the opposition to unify behind a single candidate has weakened the challenge to Tinubu, despite widespread anger over the rising cost of living, which many blame on the presidentâs removal of the countryâs fuel subsidy.
The smart money is on the ruling against Atiku being overturned before the election. The danger for Tinubu is that suspicion that the judiciary undermined a rival â one who vowed to restore the fuel subsidy â turns Atiku into a lightning rod for public frustration.
The more deep-rooted threat is apathy. Tinubu won in 2023 with just 27% voter turnout â the lowest since the return to civilian rule in 1999. Any sense that courts, rather than the ballot box, will sway the election could dampen interest further, handing the victor an even slimmer mandate to govern Africaâs most populous country. Under such circumstances, a Tinubu victory could soon feel Pyrrhic.
Notable
- South Africaâs biggest party, the ANC, faced intense campaigns ahead of the local elections, which involved politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and wading through giant-sized potholes.

An 80 cent âmaternal drapeâ is saving womenâs lives in Kano, Nigeria â the country where more women die in childbirth than anywhere else in the world. The drape measures blood loss during childbirth; once the level passes 300ml, midwives use massage, oxytocin, tranexamic acid, and IV fluids to encourage the uterus to contract.
Hadiza Galadanci, an obstetrics and gynecology professor at Bayero University, was initially skeptical that anything could reduce the mortality rate from postpartum hemorrhage â experienced by 10% of women who give birth and the biggest risk to new mothers â when she was approached by researchers. But the drastic reduction in deaths since the drapeâs implementation spurred her to persuade Nigeriaâs health minister to introduce it as a national standard of care. Suppliers in Kano now produce them for Nigeria and neighboring countries.

- Published
At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.
The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.
Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.
Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.
One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".
The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.
The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.
More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.
The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.
Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.
Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

The new investment would bring the long-stalled MabouniÃ© deposit, southeast of Libreville, into production. Abu Dhabi-based mining group New Energy Metals is developing the deposit with engineering support from Beijing-based ENFI, with construction expected to begin in 2027, the presidency said.

Africaâs biggest grocer Shoprite plans to team up with upmarket lender Investec to offer customers a debit card and expanded financial services, as competition in South Africaâs banking sector heats up.
Under the proposed tie-up, Shoprite, which built its retail empire by partly borrowing from Walmartâs mass market playbook, will use Investecâs banking backbone and regulatory framework to expand financial services to millions of its customers. The unusual pairing offers Investec, traditionally focused on wealthier clients, a way to âbroaden our access to retail deposits,â said Investec CEO Fani Titi. The deal is subject to regulatory approval.
The strategy takes Shoprite into an increasingly contested battle for South African wallets, where established banks are facing a growing crop of digital challengers. British fintech Revolut is targeting a 2028 launch in what would be its first African market.

African sovereigns are flooding back into global debt markets, accepting some of the worldâs highest borrowing costs and adding to the debate about how investors price risk just as the continentâs new credit agency begins operations.
External debt owed by low- and middle-income countries climbed 5.5% to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest pace since 2021, according to the World Bankâs International Debt Report. Africaâs poorest borrowers, which are eligible for the World Bankâs cheapest financing, paid 9.8% interest on new bonds in 2025, nearly double the 5.5% paid by middle-income borrowers, whose rates fell.
âAccess to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not,â World Bank Chief Statistician Haishan Fu said. The report comes almost a month after the launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency, the African Unionâs most concrete answer yet to longstanding complaints that global rating agencies unfairly attach risk premiums that eat up an estimated $75 billion in additional annual interest fees.

The African National Congress suffered its worst-ever result in local elections, potentially shifting the balance of power in South Africaâs coalition government.
The ANC, which led the country out of apartheid, won 31% of the vote nationwide, just over six percentage points ahead of the Democratic Alliance, a historically white-led movement. The performance extends the decline that cost the ANC its national parliamentary majority in 2024 and sets up a battle over the direction of economic policy as the once-dominant party prepares to choose a new leader next year. It also means the biggest cities, key drivers of growth in Africaâs largest economy, will mostly be governed by coalitions.
The DA emerged as the largest party in three metropolitan municipalities in Gauteng, the economic heartland, including in the commercial hub of Johannesburg. That outcome is likely to boost its bargaining power nationally and in talks to form municipal governments where no party won a majority. But some warned the new political reality has drawbacks: âUnstable coalitions with precarious leadership teams cannot deliver,â said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa.

c65ed8e83606.text: By — Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Huizhong Wu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-dismisses-claims-of-spy-plot-involving-nvidia-ceo-huang-as-a-smear-campaign Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China dismisses claims of spy plot involving Nvidia CEO Huang as a smear campaign World Nov 9, 2026 8:31 AM EST BANGKOK (AP) — China denied on Monday it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing. Huang has acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. He did not name the woman. READ MORE: Nvidia investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese spy when he had affair Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security," Huang said in his letter. In a routine news briefing Monday, a Chinese spokesperson rejected claims it used the woman as a spy. READ MORE: Nvidia announced a software tool to stop rogue AI. How would it work? "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China. Nvidia shares dropped roughly 5% in pre-market trading early Monday. The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. READ MORE: Taiwan charges 9 over illegal AI server exports to China, including Nvidia and Super Micro staffers Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology. "The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy. "Those questions require evidence rather than speculation," he added in a text message to reporters. Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning U.S. President Donald Trump's approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government. The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China. Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations. "Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows," the state-owned Global Times said. Associated Press Business Writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 699f2cc5c934.text:
Lizâs view
This feels like the beginning of the end of the AI trade. Itâs going to have wider consequences than we think.
The geyser of money is starting to sputter, affecting high-flying stocks and zapping debt deals. OpenAI set out to raise $30 billion, money it could have put together in its sleep a few months ago, and appears likely to fall far short. Lenders are treating SpaceX, an investment-grade giant, like a flier bet on a junk-rated startup.
Those companies will likely find the money somewhere. But the canât-lose trade powered by a combination of FOMO and the greater-fool theory of investing is evaporating, replaced by a tinder pile ready to ignite. The spark could come from almost anywhere. A data-center delay sets off a hyperscaler guarantee fight, a swarm of rogue agents hacking into a major cityâs electric grid, Nvidiaâs CEO admitting he slept with a Chinese spy, pick your poison.
The market is sobering up and going back to doing its job of separating winners from losers. Some of those losers are likely to be household names with 12-figure valuations.
And because the AI boom pulled in companies far outside Silicon Valley, the unwind will, too. Glassmaker Corningâs stock doubled in the first six months of the year after a $6 billion deal to outfit Metaâs data centers; it has now given up almost all of those gains. Modine, a maker of car radiators, is now trading lower than before it announced the spinoff of that business in January to become âa pure-play climate solutions company focused on the high-growth data centerâ market. Paint supplier Sherwin-Williams and HVAC-maker Carrier are in the middle of their own pivots to AI.
The boom reached far beyond Silicon Valley. So will the hangover.
Notable
- A Bloomberg analysis of corporate and regulatory filings and credit deals showed that marketsâ dependency on tech â which, these days, is mostly AI â has grown to record levels. Technology also now makes up more than 50% of the S&P 500âs market cap.

468510e660eb.text: By — Rio Yamat, Associated Press Rio Yamat, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nvidia-investigates-whether-ceo-jensen-huang-was-targeted-by-chinese-spy-when-he-had-affair Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Nvidia investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese spy when he had affair World Nov 9, 2026 8:08 AM EST Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors said Sunday. The announcement came after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing. READ MORE: Nvidia announced a software tool to stop rogue AI. How would it work? In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," Huang wrote. "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the board said. READ MORE: Taiwan charges 9 over illegal AI server exports to China, including Nvidia and Super Micro staffers Huang, 63, will remain CEO during the investigation. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Nvidia has become a central player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence, with its chips powering many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China's access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology. The Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The two are not related, according to the Times. Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times. The Nvidia CEO's letter to employees did not name Alice Huang or address her apparent ties to Beijing. He did, however, refer to the national security concerns raised in news reports and said he supported the board's investigation and would cooperate fully. "I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang said. "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security." President Donald Trump said Sunday he hasn't spoken to Huang about the latest development and praised him. "I hope everything's fine then. He's done such an incredible job," Trump said, speaking to reporters before returning to the White House. Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying, Trump again praised Huang: "I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He's done an amazing job for our country." As to whether he'd take the CEO with him on his trip to Asia next week, Trump said he was open to it. "I don't know, but I'd certainly take him," he said of Huang, who serves on the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday as he was departing the U.S. for a G7 meeting in Paris that he could not address the situation with Huang. "I just can't comment because of the nature of it," he told reporters. "And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia." Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August. Associated Press writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report from West Palm Beach, Florida. 2178bfc4756d.text:
The News
The Democratsâ historic sweep in US elections has been setting markets askew, as investors guess at what it could mean for economic policy or the billions of dollars being poured into AI infrastructure. One thing seems clear: All signs point to disinflation, according to Thierry Wizman, global rates and FX strategist at Macquarie Group.
For much of the last half of the year, the cost of capital has only been going up â yields on sovereign debt and corporate bonds alike have been rising, as hyperscalers loaded up on debt and the data center buildout faced pushback on the ground. The Fed raised rates. And the cost to buy insurance against hyperscalers defaulting on their debts has spiked.
But if President Donald Trump retreats from the Iran war and oil prices fall, or tariffs are rolled back, Wizman said, yields will come down. âUltimately the view on yields has to be linked to the view on inflation. So, most of whatâs happened overnight as a result of the election feels disinflationary.â
Q&A
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Ellen DiMauro: European sovereigns have been under pressure. At what point do those yields get interesting?
Thierry Wizman: Well, they are interesting. Because theyâve been very volatile.
If youâre thinking of jumping into France, Iâd be somewhat cautious. It really depends on how the events are going to transpire over the next few months. But if youâre not the gambling sort, you would want to wait until thereâs clarity on the election in France next year.
And if thereâs any clarity on any trajectory towards debt sustainability, the budget thatâs going to have to be passed by the end of the year is a part of that, but itâs not going to be the thing that determines ultimately what Franceâs long-term debt trajectory is. Thatâll be determined after the election. If thereâs an austerity program thatâs put in place, itâs not a question of what the yields are, itâs a question of, âwhat do I need to see happen?â The yields are already very high and theyâre already attractive.
Are the hyperscalers crowding out Treasuries and competing with governments for cash?
Theyâre definitely competing with governments for cash. Itâs one reason why the US Treasury is considering reducing the issuance of 20- and 30-year bonds. It doesnât want to crowd out the issuance of the bonds that are used to finance the expansion of the AI infrastructure economy.
Itâs one reason why bond yields have been higher all year. Itâs evident in the data on how much issuance thereâs been by corporations and itâs slated to continue potentially for another two years based on the CapEx intentions that the hyperscalers have divulged to investors already. So, thereâs no doubt there. The answer is yes.
Where are we seeing investors get scared?
Itâs not just that the hyperscalers may have over-invested, itâs also that the turn in the political atmosphere in the US is going to turn against the hyperscalers. Politically, not just economics. State and local legislatures [are turning] against data-center construction.
Are prediction markets a better way to play at rates and foreign exchange markets? Are they a way to hedge?
Not if youâre an institutional investor. Because thereâs just not that much liquidity in these prediction markets. There are people who are trying to bring liquidity to the prediction markets by entering them and making markets. But the amount of capital thatâs being devoted to them is not great enough yet for institutional-size bets.
Itâs difficult to look at the price of a prediction market and be assured that if you try to come into that market and buy or sell contracts that you wonât move the price. So, itâs not an easy way to hedge.
It looked like the US Treasuries rallied on news of the Blue Tsunami. Whatâs your take on that?
Well, there is the possibility that thereâll be less inflation in the US. So thereâs three ways that could happen. One way is if the data-center construction slows down. That would depress the economy somewhat because the economyâs been very dependent on data-center construction.
Bond yields could come down simply because the market thinks the economy will slow down a bit under a Democratic victory. Some of the tariffs might be rolled back and that would be disinflationary, something that helps bring down yields. And the final thing is the fact that oil prices are down on the premise that heâs not going to tempt the fates with an attack on Iran. Itâs globally disinflationary.
The unemployment rate has ticked up very slightly. How do you see that factoring into moves by the Fed and potential rate hikes?
Weâre still at a very low unemployment rate. The Fed is not really concerned about the labor market based on what theyâve said themselves. Theyâre much more concerned about inflation and inflation expectations right now.
What else are you looking out for post-midterms?
The Democratic agenda is going to be largely about reducing the cost of living. I donât think they will succeed, but there may be people in the market who think that they will. So if thereâs enough people who believe that and itâs in conjunction with maybe Trump reducing some tariffs here and there, the narrative around disinflation can continue.

A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow, and his parents and sister at their home, died in hospital early on Monday, Polish police have said.
The 24-year-old, who has been named as Michal Oksinski by local media, was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday, police said.
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
Officials initially reported the gunman had apparently been inspired by "far-right ideologies", but have since said they are still investigating any possible motivation.
After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man.
In the hours after the shooting, a minister said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
However, during a press briefing on Monday morning, PrzemysÅaw Nowak, a spokesperson for Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said investigations into his motive remain ongoing.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.
Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
Four firearms were found in the gunman's car, including two AR-15 rifles and two handguns, along with several hundred rounds of ammunition, Nowak said. Authorities also seized at least four phones from his car and person, and electronic equipment from his home.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.
Speaking on Sunday, one of two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.
The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers.
Professor Michal PÄdziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible."
"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."
PÄdziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.
On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.
Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded.
Ruby, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".
She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside.
Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".
"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.
In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.
After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in KrakÃ³w".
"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.
Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

- Published
Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents in central Gaza following heavy rain, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
Five injured people were also reportedly rescued after the incident on Sunday night at a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah.
Videos showed men using phone torches to search for survivors beneath boulders, sand and collapsed tents.
The Civil Defence service, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said the "humanitarian tragedy" should prompt urgent action by international organisations to provide safe shelters for displaced people and move tents away from sandy areas, slopes and locations at risk of collapse.
Torrential rain on Saturday reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, leaving many Palestinians without a dry place to sleep.
The Civil Defence said water levels reached up to 1.5m (4.9ft) in some places and that its first responders were able to respond to only 10% of the 2,100 distress calls they received.
"Protecting the lives of displaced people is an urgent humanitarian responsibility. Their tents must not become death traps beneath sand and rainwater," it warned.
The Civil Defence initially reported on Sunday that three children and two women were killed when the sand embankment collapsed. But the health ministry said on Monday morning that only one woman was among the dead.
She was identified as Tahrir Nabhan, while the children were named as Mariam Nabhan and her brother Salah, and Habiba al-Zein.
Mustafa al-Masri told the BBC that he and other rescuers had used their bare hands to dig the victims and survivors out of the sand and rubble.
"It was extremely difficult. This mound was huge and wide. It collapsed onto the tent, and we didn't know what to do," he said.
"When we got here, we, along with the young men from the camp, pulled them out with our own hands. We pulled out the children and the woman."
"Their father arrived shouting, 'My children, my children, my children, my children.' We pulled his children out, put them in the ambulance, and took them to the hospital."
Masri added that he had been displaced from the northern town of Beit Hanoun but had stayed in central Gaza because there was "nowhere for me to return to".
"We went out looking around, searching through the open areas and hills, but I couldn't find any place other than this area that felt suitable for me."
The International Organization for Migration's regional crisis co-ordinator, Karl Baker, told the BBC from Gaza that the territory's 2.1 million population was confined to only 30% of its total area and that many people were "unfortunately living in areas which would not be normal if we were not in this time of conflict".
He said the UN agency and its partners were trying to make sure there were enough tents and tarpaulins, as well as improved drainage in camps, to help them get through the winter.
However, he warned that aid currently getting into Gaza was not sufficient to meet the demands of the population, describing it as "the very smallest of Band-Aids [plasters]".
"We need more support, in-kind donations. We need funding in order to help the communities to help themselves," he said. "We need a lot more to happen."
UN agencies have called on Israeli authorities to allow in the specialist equipment and materials required to improve living conditions for displaced families.
Cogat, the Israeli military body tasked with co-ordinating deliveries, said on Sunday that more than 91,000 tents, 12 vacuum trucks for waste removal, and fuel and engine oil for pumping facilities have been delivered since the start of the "Gaza Winterization Plan".
But it added that Israel would not permit the entry of equipment that could be used for military purposes by Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups.
An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.
More than 1.9 million people have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.
The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed in October 2025, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,640 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Additional reporting by Malak Hassouneh

eea513d5cdd9.text: The potential for partnership between newly ascendant Democrats and the "Make America Healthy Again" movement is already threatened by their deep disagreements over Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Why it matters: Democrats want to convince health-conscious voters that they're the party that can deliver on food and pesticide use, but many view an alliance with Kennedy as a nonstarter. They're already threatening to investigate Kennedy, and they're clashing bitterly with him over vaccines and other issues — so any common ground with MAHA over nutrition and pesticides could take a back seat to those fights. State of play: Most MAHA-backed candidates lost at the polls last week. Some of the movement's leaders blame low turnout for the GOP's terrible election night, saying MAHA faithful stayed home because they were disappointed with the Trump administration and a lack of progress on food and environmental issues. Whatever they may think of the White House and federal health officials, the base remains intensely loyal to Kennedy, who created the movement during his 2024 presidential bid. "The voters sent a clear message to this administration and to all political parties, that we are not motivated to vote for people who have a lack of integrity. Promises were made, and promises were broken," said Zen Honeycutt, founder of Moms Across America. While she's open to working with Democrats going forward, "We want them to work with Kennedy, not against him," she added. "That's the red line for almost all of us. You cross that line and you go after Kennedy, you are never getting our vote," she said. "I'm not interested in working with people who are trying to get rid of our champion." The big picture: Some Democrats were making overtures to MAHA voters on key issues ahead of the midterms. Lawmakers like Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) have already said they're willing to work with Kennedy on issues like cleaning up the food supply, school lunches and banning the use of certain pesticides. Now, the movement's leaders are responding to those overtures. Driving the news: "There are good people across the political spectrum who want to be part of this, and we're going to find every last one of them and fight with them," MAHA Action president Tony Lyons said last week on the organization's weekly call. Lyons also rejected suggestions that the movement is dead, saying "we've won the hearts and minds of the American people." Yes, but: Democrats have drawn the line on vaccine issues, refusing to adopt Kennedy's medical freedom agenda or greater scrutiny of vaccine safety. Few seem willing to accommodate Kennedy, who's likely to be a top target for oversight and investigations once Democrats take power. And Kennedy remains committed to relitigating vaccine safety claims that mainstream scientists say have been thoroughly debunked. That's likely to kill any bridge-building before it starts. After Maryland Democratic Sen. Angela Alsobrooks called for Kennedy to resign or be fired, MAHA influencer Kelly Ryerson — known as "Glyphosate Girl" — said she didn't understand the strategy and warned it "will lose many future voters." "Food Babe" Vani Hari wrote to Democrats in response to the same post: "This is not how you win a coalition or work together. This is how you waste time while our children continue to get sicker than any developed nation." Honeycutt warned: "To get rid of him because you don't like the fact that he's trying to make vaccines safer is absolutely insane." The intrigue: Though MAHA hasn't secured major political wins or a raft of new laws, big portions of its platform remain popular with the electorate, with support cutting across party lines and including many independents. For the new Democratic majority, progress on certain MAHA-backed issues may be more important than the actual endorsement of MAHA leadership.

d165f8a14279.text: Elon Musk's sprawling empire — from rockets to robots, electric cars to AI — is facing a political onslaught with few parallels in modern corporate history. Why it matters: The world's richest man confronts a constellation of risks spanning the halls of Congress, his Texas industrial empire, Wall Street and his vision for AI supremacy. 💰 Political: To Democrats, Musk embodies corrosive forces of the MAGA era — extreme wealth, billionaire influence over government, the gutting of federal institutions, the poisoning of social media and the unchecked power of AI. Musk spent at least $475 million on the midterms, becoming the election's largest individual donor — only to see more than 99% of his traceable spending go to losing candidates, according to WIRED . Musk's most humiliating defeat came in Texas, where a $160 million bet on Ken Paxton ended in a Democratic sweep of the Senate seat, governorship and attorney general's office. In a hint of a possible détente, Sen.-elect James Talarico praised the billionaire as a "great business leader and entrepreneur," and offered to work with him on technology and innovation. Musk, who said last month that Talarico "hates Texas," responded : "Nice of him to say that." ⚖️ Congressional: Armed with subpoena power, Democrats are preparing to investigate Musk's DOGE operation, its access to sensitive government data and whether his companies benefited from his extraordinary influence over the Trump administration. Musk is already downplaying his dependence on Washington, claiming government contracts will account for less than 5% of SpaceX revenue a year from now. "Happy to cancel any that the government doesn't want," he posted Friday . The scrutiny also extends to national security: Lawmakers are demanding answers about Musk's reported communications with Vladimir Putin and his role in the October slowdown of Starshield that disrupted Ukraine's drone operations. Elon Musk responds to reporting about his vulnerabilities in Texas. Screenshot via X 🏭 Regulatory: Musk moved his home and the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas, betting on a safe haven for his expanding empire. Now, the Democratic takeover threatens to turn his political sanctuary into a regulatory minefield. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is suing to uncover 1,374 pages of largely redacted communications with Greg Abbott, while incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has pledged to scrutinize state broadband grants awarded to Starlink. Tesla's robotaxi ambitions also face new obstacles as Democrats threaten to derail federal legislation that eases state safety restrictions. Hinojosa herself urged Tesla last year to delay its Austin launch until stronger regulations took effect. 📉 Financial: Tesla and SpaceX shed roughly $460 billion in combined market value in the two days after the election, then rebounded Friday as investors raced to reassess the risks to Musk's business empire. Wall Street is especially concerned that Democratic scrutiny could complicate a potential Tesla-SpaceX merger , while new restrictions on AI data centers threaten a cornerstone of Musk's growth strategy. In a fitting coda to a brutal week, Musk announced Friday that Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production by mid-2027, pulling the plug on a pet project plagued by weak sales, recalls and quality problems. 🤖 Technological: The midterms have given the backlash against AI new political muscle, threatening both the massive data centers powering Musk's ambitions and the technology behind Grok itself. Democrats are preparing legislation that would require independent safety testing of advanced AI models and hold developers liable for harmful outputs. Lawmakers have already demanded SpaceX's AI safety records. Voters sided against data-center development in 44 of 45 local referendums , while incoming Democratic governors in Georgia and Ohio pledged tougher restrictions. Musk joked on X: "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." The bottom line: Democrats must find a way to separate Musk the political combatant from Musk the industrialist, whose companies are central to America's technological and military power.

35b8d63d921e.text: Efforts to fight climate change, conserve nature and build clean energy have long unfolded on competing tracks. Now, they're colliding — and exposing tough trade-offs for environmentalists. Why it matters: Congress' sweeping permitting debate is forcing those competing priorities into the same conversation, with major consequences for climate action and conservation. Driving the news: The Senate is set to hold an initial procedural vote Monday on a sprawling bipartisan bill that would make it easier to build power lines and energy projects of all kinds, including clean energy and fossil fuels. At the heart of the debate is how much public scrutiny projects should face before they're approved — and how much protection those approvals should receive afterward. Supporters say the current system takes too long, delaying clean energy and other infrastructure. Opponents warn that speeding things up could come at the expense of wildlife, public lands and tribal rights. Between the lines: The dilemma reflects a fundamental tension within the environmental movement: Building the infrastructure needed to combat climate change can threaten nature, while protecting nature can complicate efforts to build that infrastructure. Wind and solar farms, for example, can require large expanses of land, potentially disrupting wildlife habitats even as they help reduce greenhouse gas emissions. "The part of my organization that cares about climate sees great opportunity and the part that cares about nature sees some dangers," said a leader of one organization that focuses on both causes, speaking anonymously to discuss the proposal candidly. The big picture: Both parties broadly agree Washington needs to overhaul federal permitting, a perennial goal that has eluded Congress for years. The question is what reforms can attract enough support to pass both chambers. The bill's bipartisan sponsors and the White House want action before year's end. But some Democrats, emboldened by their midterm victories, argue they should wait until next year, when they'll have more power and time to scrutinize the legislation. Even if the Senate passes the bill, the House would still need to approve it before it could reach President Trump's desk. Zoom out: The legislation is confined to the United States, but the tensions it exposes are global — and are playing out at two major international gatherings. Representatives from more than 190 countries are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for annual United Nations climate talks beginning Monday. The host country is pushing to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035, which would require much of the same buildout under discussion in Washington. A separate, lower-profile UN gathering focused on protecting biodiversity concluded in Armenia late last month. Countries acknowledged they're falling short of their goal to halt and reverse nature loss by 2030, while agreeing on steps to accelerate progress. What they're saying: The fact that these two discussions take place separately is part of the problem, said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Within the U.S., the permitting debate is forcing these conversations to converge. "We want everyone to be more overt about this tension, rather than covert about it," said Dasgupta, a former World Bank official. "I don't think it helps to say we can't build anything today, and also that we need to take everyone's rights away to build stuff." Friction point: Three provisions of the Senate bill show what's at stake for conservationists. Public lands: Former Biden climate adviser John Podesta warned that an earlier version of the bill could make federal permits harder for agencies to reverse, potentially allowing the Trump administration to approve development on sensitive public lands that future administrations would struggle to undo. Federal reviews: The legislation would shorten and limit aspects of federal environmental reviews, including public input and opportunities to challenge project approvals in court. Conservationists and tribal organizations warn the changes could weaken protections for wildlife, public lands and culturally significant sites. Wildlife: The bill would allow states to take over certain federal responsibilities for assessing how projects affect endangered species. Environmental advocates warn the changes could weaken protections for vulnerable wildlife. Catch up quick: An updated version released Saturday revises rules on permit reversals and adds safeguards for wildlife and tribal consultation. But the changes haven't satisfied all conservationists. The Wilderness Society reaffirmed its opposition on Saturday, warning the bill still threatens public lands and weakens environmental protections. Zoom in: Carter Roberts, head of the World Wildlife Fund, which has not taken a public position on the bill, says environmentalists should seek solutions that address both climate change and nature loss. "The best solutions to climate change also conserve nature and prevent it from disappearing," Roberts said. The other side: Sponsors of the legislation and other proponents emphasize that no bill is perfect and trade-offs are inevitable. "There's no question that making the system more efficient diminishes certain aspects of access to project approval. That is the point of the legislation," said Jason Grumet, head of the American Clean Power Association. But he added: "We think the balance has been struck in a way that sustains meaningful access." What we're watching: Whether lawmakers can reconcile these competing priorities and pass the bill before the new Congress takes office remains uncertain. The bottom line: "The permitting bill debate is not a unique debate," said Dasgupta, who is in Turkey for the climate talks. "Everywhere in the world, we need to build stuff."

214e0df6be73.text: There is no Nvidia — nor an AI boom as we know it — without Jensen Huang. He has reassured jittery markets with his words, bankrolled a trillion-dollar buildout and put economies on his shoulders. Now, the world is wondering if he can save himself . Why it matters: Global markets must confront a terrifying reality: The AI ecosystem's first "too big to fail" executive is suddenly vulnerable, and there is no backup plan if he is forced to step down. Catch up quick : Huang apologized Sunday and Nvidia's board launched an independent probe after he admitted to having a relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese operative. Nvidia's board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. President Trump stood by Huang, calling him "an honorable guy." The big picture: Keeping his job is one thing. Maintaining the ability to steady markets, finance customers and shape government policy is another. These are the five questions that now loom over the AI boom : 1. What happens to Nvidia? Forged 33 years ago (initially using a Denny's as an impromptu office), Nvidia is a uniquely founder-driven company, making any potential leadership transition incredibly perilous. Investors have little precedent for valuing the company without him. "It's very hard to envision Nvidia run by anybody else," said Dan Gallagher, an analyst with Washington Post Intelligence and long a keen observer of the chip titan. Huang has more than 60 direct reports, eschews traditional corporate layers and hasn't been publicly grooming a successor. "I don't know if anyone's going to know how to value Nvidia" without him, Gallagher told Axios. 2. What happens to the market? Huang has repeatedly rescued the AI trade from bearish sentiment. On multiple occasions, he has offered backstops to shore up growth plans for companies across the AI landscape, from CoreWeave to OpenAI. In July, he argued that cheaper open models would boost demand for Nvidia's chips, pushing back against a market scare. Last month, he toured Europe pitching national AI projects as debt investors signaled their appetite for some AI financing was limited. 3. What happens to the companies that depend on him? The risks vary across an industry that relies on Nvidia for chips, capital and credibility. The AI giants : Anthropic and OpenAI have options. Anthropic plans to barrel ahead with an IPO this month and already uses chips from Google and Amazon. OpenAI is developing its own chips in-house and with Broadcom. Diversification is underway, but replacing Nvidia is not in the cards near-term The "neoclouds" : Companies such as CoreWeave and others that rent out computing power have less room to maneuver. CoreWeave suffered a prolonged stock-and-bond selloff last month as investors began to question how it would finance continued growth. Nvidia has provided crucial backstops to many neocloud companies. The "neolabs" and AI startups : Nvidia has supplied investment and offered access to computing for AI startups such as Thinking Machines Lab, as well as dozens of other startups providing a variety of services in the AI race. 4. Where does the investigation lead? Southeast Asia's data center boom puts the limits of U.S. chip restrictions in focus. The loophole: U.S. restrictions on shipping advanced chips to China generally haven't stopped Chinese companies from accessing them in overseas data centers, the New York Times reported . Nvidia told the Times that remote access is consistent with U.S. export controls because the chips remain outside restricted countries. That access is distinct from suspected smuggling. The Times reported that Megaspeed, the Nvidia customer where Alice Huang worked, was under investigation for steering advanced chips to China. 5. What happens to Huang's advocacy? His arguments for selling chips to China and embracing open AI models will face renewed scrutiny, with many of his comments potentially being seen in a new light due to the relationship. Huang has repeatedly, and stridently, pushed to loosen restrictions on sales to China , arguing that reliance on American technology serves U.S. interests. The bottom line: Huang has made himself the AI boom's indispensable man. The industry must now reckon with what happens when its fortunes depend so heavily on his.

c9b118d0395a.text: The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence. Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House. Trump stood by Huang on Sunday evening, telling reporters that the Nvidia CEO is "an honorable guy" and "probably has an excuse" for his infidelity. The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice. He has brushed aside fears of both a speculative bubble and technological catastrophe, joining forces with Trump to calm markets and the public as warnings of an AI apocalypse reached fever pitch. For almost any other CEO, an affair with a suspected foreign intelligence operative could be career-ending. Huang's grip on Nvidia — and the company's extraordinary importance to the AI economy — may insulate him from the same fate. Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation. U.S. officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was recruited by Beijing's top spy agency to gather information and potentially influence Nvidia's campaign to expand advanced chip sales to China. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised and expressed confidence in Jensen Huang, who intends to remain CEO during the investigation. Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO. The company portrayed their interactions as routine business dealings — an account now under scrutiny in the wake of Huang's admission that he was "unfaithful" to his wife. Trump defended Huang on Oct. 31 as a "great, brilliant person," but hedged when asked if he should remain a White House adviser: "I would like to say yes. I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary." The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public. Trump was briefed in 2025, according to the Times, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio personally oversaw a classified intelligence memo warning senior officials this spring. Yet Trump continued to embrace Huang as a trusted adviser, welcoming him to the White House as the Nvidia chief pressed to loosen restrictions on advanced chip exports to China. Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia. "Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," John Rizzo, head of public policy communications, said in a statement. What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight. A post-election rout wiped trillions from U.S. stocks on Thursday, deepening uncertainty over an AI boom that has powered much of the market's growth. Huang's admission is now poised to open an explosive new line of inquiry : Did the White House disregard intelligence warnings while advancing policies championed by one of Trump's closest corporate allies?

548f2d8379c3.text:
For 20 years, Roberta Kellam, a retired lawyer and longtime birder, has watched ospreys return to their nests and raise chicks from her home on Nassawadox Creek, on Virginia’s Eastern Shore.
She’s been monitoring around two dozen nests near her house. Kellam has also surveyed osprey populations with Bryan Watts, a longtime researcher at William & Mary’s Center for Conservation Biology and logs her observations on Osprey Watch, a citizen-science project the center runs.
Nassawadox Creek drains into the Chesapeake Bay, the nation’s largest estuary and home to the world’s largest breeding population of ospreys. The birds typically return from their wintering grounds in late February and early March to rebuild nests and raise chicks.
But about eight years ago, the situation turned from joy to dread.
“Once they hatched, they were disappearing,” Kellam recalled. By mid-to-late May, according to Kellam, the creek could shift from active osprey nests to “just silence” in recent years, with adults no longer feeding the young, signaling a worrying decline. The disturbing observations prompted her to report the situation to Watts, who she’d known for nearly two decades.
Early on, they considered possibilities such as predation. But nothing seemed to explain the losses. Watts, who’s studied Chesapeake Bay ospreys for about 40 years, said they decided to ramp up nest monitoring after residents and watermen raised concerns about poor osprey reproduction.
The first comprehensive survey of Kellam’s local osprey colony began in 2024, which she described as “very grim.” That was the first time she could “look inside the nest and see the dead chicks and the abandoned eggs.” Sometimes chicks were still alive, she said, but many did not survive.
The center’s 2026 osprey breeding performance survey found the bay’s osprey population in steep decline, especially in saltier regions of the estuary. The study linked the decline to severe food stress tied to the low availability of Atlantic menhaden for nesting ospreys.
Menhaden for decades have been considered a “keystone prey species for the osprey population” due to their abundance, high energy density and schooling behavior, the survey said. Nesting ospreys “require high fish abundance during April, May and June to successfully raise broods” and are not able to adjust when menhaden do not arrive in large numbers until late June or July.
The study described the 2026 breeding season as “the worst productivity year ever recorded for ospreys in the Chesapeake Bay,” raising fears that breeding rates are too low to sustain the population.
Watts said that on the lower Patuxent River, where ospreys depend more heavily on menhaden, pairs are raising too few young to replace the adults that die. Upriver, where birds have access to a different mix of fish, pairs are doing better.
The food shortage is visible in the nests, he said, and chicks were starving at older ages than historically observed. Watts estimated an 80 percent decline in menhaden deliveries and a 50 percent decline in food quality compared with the 1980s.
More than 30 percent of osprey females in some study areas were not laying eggs, Watts noted, compared with about 2 percent in the 1980s. Current productivity was about 0.26 chicks per pair, below the minimum break-even estimate of 0.8.
Watts said ospreys show strong fidelity to their nesting sites, but in saltier bay regions, where menhaden is the birds’ primary food source, many pairs now cannot bring home enough food to raise their young. “They need [menhaden] in mid-May to about mid-June. That’s a critical period, and they’re not available.”
Researchers have a much firmer grasp on what is happening in the nests than on why fewer menhaden are reaching ospreys. According to Watts, climate change is a contributing factor, shifting the fish’s distribution and arrival times. And while state and regional fisheries councils emphasize that localized menhaden depletion has not been empirically linked to commercial harvest, conservationists and researchers like Watts have field observations to raise questions about that.
Watts said researchers lack fisheries monitoring data, and industry-held commercial data is not available to the public, leading to data gaps about menhaden availability and older age classes of ospreys.
The American Small Pelagics Network, a group representing fishermen and processors tied to the menhaden industry, have pushed back on the Center for Conservation Biology’s research.
“A struggling predator does not by itself prove a menhaden harvest problem,” the group said in a recent statement. “The 2025 Atlantic menhaden assessment found the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring.”
A spokesperson for a leading menhaden fishing firm, Ocean Harvesters, stated the “suggestion that the fishery’s catch is hidden from scientists and regulators is wrong,” pointing instead to federal catch records and a daily logbook database—though both have access restrictions.
America’s “Reduction” Fishery
From the chilled estuaries of Nova Scotia to the brackish bays of northern Florida, massive schools of metallic menhaden form the ecological and economic foundation of the Atlantic shoreline. Following blooms of phytoplankton, menhaden migrate north in the spring and return south in the fall, offering a concentrated calorific meal for dozens of predators.
The largest commercial fishery, by volume, along the East Coast—second nationally only to Alaskan pollock—menhaden are a primary target of striped bass, predatory birds, marine mammals and fishermen alike.
In 2024, an estimated 410 million pounds of Atlantic menhaden was caught coastwide.
But menhaden isn’t the kind of fish you can easily buy at the supermarket.
Instead, roughly 20 percent of the U.S. catch is used as commercial bait for lobster and blue crab fisheries. The other 80 percent is reduced into fertilizer, livestock feed or dietary supplements, according to New Jersey Fish and Wild
